THE DESIRE GRATIFIED. Mis Royal Highseas Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, at the Villa Nevada, rose and gazed long and wistfully over the luxurious grounds before him to the deep blue sea beyond.l Turning at length to Captain Perceval, he said quietly, "Ireroeval, I would rather die here than anywhere else in IM world." Be died in that very room!—Extract from Wie Leeds Mercury, April let, 1884. Math looked he from the window; 'twas a scene Of beauty unsurpassed that met his eye. Ile spoke, that virtuous son of England's Queen: The world my choice, 'tis here that I would die." Were his thoughts turned to scenes that glorious are And fade not? Was he conscious of his doom? Could he foresee how soon both near and far The hearts of men would be o'erspread with gloom? Tint gaze must end; the Prince must needs retire; Since then far lovelier scenes he has espied; gracious God has granted his desire; His life is o'er. 'Twas in that room he died! A Royal mother weeps, overwhelmed with grief; God grant her strength to bear her bitter cross A widowed Princess mourns, nor finds relief; Her infant smiles, unconscious of its loss. And he, whose death has bowed those heads with woe To him it surely has brought glad release; Is drank the cup of suffering below; Above he findeth life, and joy, and peace. .—Leeds Weekly Mercury. THE CRAZY QUILT. I received, at the end of my journey. A welcome that made my heart ache, And into the pleasant guest.clascaber Was ushered at bedtime to sleep. The room was delightfully cosy, The furniture ciamien with care, While spread o'er the bed ro Was something I'd not ee..-1 elsewhere. It was fashioned of silks, velvet, satin, Of every conceivable hue, Embroidered with birds, beasts, and flowers In a manner most wondrous to view. But my limbo were so weary with travel, And so heavy with slumber my eyes, That I thonieht, "I'll wait until morning, And puzzle it out when I rise." T. dreamland I soon must have journeyed, For scarce had I chat out earth's scenes, When a floating procession of garments Advanced by invisible means. Thee catne from the southward in clusters, Tney came from the northward in troops, White east and the west seemed to rival All others in size of their groups. There were ball dresses, long past their splendour; White robes which some bride must have worn; Queer ribbons, old bonnets, and waistcoats; And from each one a section was shorn. Mak% jackets, skirts, aprons, and neckties— They hovered in groups o'er the bed, Ant with aspect of utter dejection, t ; Their phantom hands clutched at the spread. All night round the bedside they circled, And when in the morning I rose, My eyes in their stupefied vision, Could see bat a mass of old clothes. So when at the table my hostess Asked what sort of a night I had spent, I told my strange dream to the household, And begged to know what it all meant. For a time they looked at me quite puzzled, Their faces with wonder perplexed; At length my host cried, "1 have solved it ;" And laughed till I almost got vexed. He laughed while we plied him with questions, Engaged in merry word-tilt, Then gasped with what breath he had left him: "Yon slept 'neath my wife's crazy quilt !"

What goes most against a farmer's grain? His mowing machine. Taking things as they come isn't so very difficult It's parting with them as they go that's hard. We must necessarily live in the element we create around us. Then, to be happy ourselves, we mast make those aronnd us happy. Blessed is the man who has found his work; let him as i no other blessedness. Know thy work and do It; and work at it like Hercules. One monster there is in the world—a idle man. A little child, becoming wearied with the quarrelling aS two younger children over a glass of milk, exclaimed, " What's the use of quarrelling over that milk? There is a whole cowful out in the barn." At the late examination of a country grammar school, a elergyinan said that boys were of tan so excited when under- • an examination as to spoil many good papers by the mom curious blunders. For instance, a boy, after giving a very good description of the building of the ark, spoiled it by describing Moses as the builder; another, in answer to the question, "Suppose Queen Victoria had died in childhood, who would have succeeded to the English throne?" wrote "her eldest son." The celebrated mathematician, Sir James Ivory, was in his obscure early days a teacher in the Bergh t4chool of Dundee. One of the Bailies of the town having paid a visit id inspection to his class-room when he was teaching the elements of geometry out of the first book of Euclid, the homely, and no doubt otherwise shrewd enough, magistrate duly reported that he thought Jamie Ivory had been ap- pointed to teach mathematics, and yet he was no further than the ABC! A RUM—During the formation of the North Midland Railway, in 1837, an excavator went into a public-house at Inlay Cross, and calling for a glass of ale, entered into con- versation with the landlord, in the course of which the dis- honest practices of the men working on the line were dis- cussed. This person, who pretended to be a sort of overlooker, said that he had the good fortune to have an honest set of men under him, and that he was about to treat them with a epallon of gin as a reward for their industry and good con- duct. He then produc-d a gallon bottle, which he had pre- viously half filled with water, and requested the unsuspicious landlord to add "two more quarts of gin," which was ac- oordingly done. On a request for payment being made, he intimated to the landlord his intention of paying at a future day; bat mine host, having no faith in excavators, refused to trust, and two quarts of the liquor were consequently repoared from the bottle; after which the wily rascal, chuckling at his success, retired with his two quarts of water ingeniously converted into capital half-and-half grog. THE MIRACLE OF THE Wm.—Captain Cueynghame, in his "Recollections of Service in China," says, in some in- stances they looked upon us as gods, in some as devils, and in all as a very extraordinary race. As an instance of this, I will here relate a most absurd story which was told me by an officer at Nankin, and which will go far to show the fear with which we were looked upon by this superstitions race. Meer my friend had visited the Porcelain Tower, being some- what fatigued, he stepped into a barber's shop, and by way of employing his time he desired the barber to shave his head. This gentleman wore a wig, but which, for the sake of 000lnese, he placed in his pocket; this operation of !haying, so common in China, was speedily and quickly executed, the barber seeming to be delighted with the honour ef shaving one of the illustrious strangers. Pre- viously to his leaving the shop, and while the man's atten- tion was called in some other direction, my friend replaced his wig upon his head, little thinking of the result of this simple process; no sooner, however, had the barber turned roved and observed him, whom he had so lately cleared of every vestige of hair, suddenly covered with a most luxu- riant growth, than taking one steady gaze at him, to make sure he was not deceived, he let fall his razor, cleared his counter at a bound, and running madly through the crowd which was speedily collected, cried out that he was visited by the devil. No entreaties could induce him to return until every Englishman had left the neighbourhood; so pal- pable a miracle as this being, in his opinion, quite beyond the power of all the gods or demons in the Buddhist calendar. ON THE Witmato Fecuray.—For a man who has a cer- tain gift of, writing to say, "1 will make the most of it while the public likes my wares—as long as the market Is open and I am able to supply it at a money profit -such profit being the sign of liking," he should have a belief that his wares have nothing akin to the arsenic green in them, and also that his continuous supply is secure from a degrada- tion in quality which the habit of consumption encouraged in the buyers may hinder them from marking their sense of by rejection; so that they complain but pay, and read what they complain. Unless he has ;hat belief, he is on a level with the manufacturer who gets rich by fancy wares eelmiredeurith arsenic green. He really cares for not sing but hie income He carries on authorship on the principle of the gin palace. And bad literature of the sort called ' lolliteheff le spiritual gin. A writer capable of being popular' CAB only escape this social culpability by first of all getting a profound sense that literature is good for nothing if it is not admirably good; he must detest bad literature tee imutiry to be indifferent about producing it if only other people don't detest it. And if he has this sign of the divine - affiatue Within him, he must make up his mind that he most not pursue authorship as a vocation with a trading determination to get rich by it. It is in the highest sense lawfal for hint to get as good a price as he honourably can eer the best work he is capable of; but not for him to force or hurry his production, or even do over again what has already been done, either by himself or others, so as to ren- der his work no real contribution, for the sake of bringing uP his income to the fancy pitch. An author who would keep a pure and noble conscience, and with that a develop- ing instead of degenerating intellect and taste, must east oat of hie arms the aim to be rich. And therefore he must keep his expenditure low—he mug make for himself no dire necessity to earn sums in order to pay bills.—Fram George Riot's Jerseys. Wilksison (under whose superintendence the work had been carried out), a number of gentlemen as- sembled to see the silo opened. It is about 10ft, square and 10ft. deep, and was filled on October 30th with grass grown round the bridge, put in when wet with dew. The grass was trodden down by a number of men, some salt being added from time to time. A layer of mats of the couhtry was placed on top, then about 113 in. of earth, and on that a quantity of old iron, which raised the pressure to about 2001bs. per square foot. When opened on the 6th ult., about two inches on the surface was found to be mouldy, but the remainder was for the most part in excellent condi- tion. The salt did not appear to be an advantage, how- ever, for wherever it had been added a black " vien" ran through the ensilage. The lower part of the wall on two sides sloped inwards, and here the ensilage clung to the walls, and was not so well pressed as elsewhere. On the whole, however, the ensilage was in capital condition, al- though the grass from which it was made was of very poor quality. It was readily eaten by the cattle, and, with one or two exceptions, by the horses also. It is believed that this process will be of great advantage in India especially in districts where green fodder is not easily obtainable in

the hot season. Dm}maxim; CATTLB.—At the petty sessions held at Drumconra, Co. Meath, on March 19th, Thomas M'Ardle Watt prosecuted by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals' for cruelly ill-treating 34 bullocks by causing their horns to be cut off close to their skulls.' James Cahill, the bailiff of the defendant, stated that the 34 beasts been dishorned for the purpose of preventing the cattle .om tearing each other when being fed in the yard, and as a matter of convenience. Mr. George M'Carthy, RM., the presiding magistrate, dismissed the case on the grounds that, in his opinion, the practice of dishorning cattle was not cruelty within the fair meaning of the Act of Parliament under which the prosecution was brought. He agreed to state a case for the opinion of the superior court. The prac- tice of dishorning cattle is not very prevalent in any part of the Uaited Kingdom' or, for that matter, in any part of the world. If properly done, however, and at the right time, the operation could not be so painful as that of castration, and could not amount to more than a very fractional part of the sum of the suffering endured by each beast from the horns of other cattle. There is no occasion to use far- fetched arguments on the score either of humanity or of economy; as, for instance, that if all cattle were to badis- horned to-morrow, the price of boots and shoes would come down, or any other special pleading. Yet, as a matter of fact, the largest amount of damage to hides is from horns, next from warbles, and last of all from the butcher's knife in careless dressing. The whole matter lies in a nutshell; wild animals need their offensive and defensive weapons, and when these animals are domesticated these offensive and defensive weapons become dangerously useless. This is be- coming recognised to an extent which will in all probability lead sooner or latec to the dishorning of cattle as a general thing when they are about one year old. Ms. J. HOWARD AND THE CATTLE DISEASES BILL.— Mr. James Howard, in a letter to The Times, endeavours to prove that there is no important difference between the first clause of the Cattle Diseases Bill as originally drawn and the clause as amended by the Lords. He says :—" It will be seen that the main alteration made by the Lords is in transposing the negative 'not' from the end to the beginning of the clause, and this, it is alleged, hrs effected a vital change. In the debate upon the second reading I main- tained the contrary. I will not repeat the exact illustra- tion I used on that occasion, but when in conversation the other day with the chairman and general manager of one of our principal railways I put the case as follows :—Sap- pose you had a rule that whenever the locomotive superin- tendent was satisfied that an engine-driver was not sober he should prohibit his driving,' &a., what effect would be pro- duced by making the rule run thus:—' Whenever the loco- motive superintendent was not satisfied the engine-driver was sober he shOuld prohibit his driving,' &c.? The discre- tionary power in both cases would rest with the locomotive superintendent; and in the matter of importation of cattle, in both cases it would rest with .tae Privy 'Council." Mr. Howard' proceeds to another point, as follows now come to the present proposals of the Government. By Mr. Dodson's amendment the clause is to be restored to its original form, plus the following important words and to the administration of each laws,' ttc. The contention on the part of those who considered that the original proposal of the Government did not go far enough was that, although the laws of a country might be satisfactory, they might be very laxly administered; and that there was nothing in the bill to bind the Privy Council to make inquiry. To my mind the addition of the above words implies that it will be the duty of the Privy Council to satisfy themselves as to the administration of the laws of a suspected country, as well as to all the other circumstances set forth: Lastly, Mr. Howard makes an appeal for unity :--• Without enter- ing upon the question whether the Act should be a per- manent or a tentative one, as proposed by the Gov- rnment, I desire to appeal to the agricultural party in the House and in the country upon the desirability of joining hands over the first clause. If the original clause of the bill, with the amendment proposed by Mr. Dodson, is likely to accomplish what we desire—as I believe it Will—will it not be unwise In us, confronted as we are by a formidable opposition, to quarrel over the phraseology ?" RURAL NOTES.—A Manchester Guardian correspondent writes :—The pleasant rain which has fallen during the past week has had a most agreeable effect upon vegetation and bird life. We may expect to see the swallow and white- throat any day, for they are quite due now. Birds have made rapid progress with their nesting, and nests of the earlier breeding kinds are very numerous. I have seen a number of plovers' eggs. Ten days ago I saw a robin's nest at Nateby, and the young were almost ready to emerge from the shell. In that locality robins have been exceedingly scarce all winter. In South Lancashire, robins, wrens, and tits have been uncommonly numerous, and the distribution has not been equal. On the Brock and other tributaries of the Wyre, along which I have walked many miles, wagtails are exceedingly plentiful; also along oar Lancashire Yar- row; but these were probably, when I saw them, only par- tially destributed for nesting. At a place near Goosnargh, a hole in the wall has been the nesting-place for pied wag- tails, for twenty years in succession—l do not say always the same ;pair, but always a pair,—and on the Ilth of March the pair which had evidently occupied the hole last year were observed to arrive. On appearing overhead they gave an exclamation and then dropped by the hole, looking thoroughly worn out and tired. Presently they began to arrange their plumage, and by and by one of them dropped in the hole to examine it. It came out, and then the two birds beganito feed, and afterwards took possession. Green- finches are still in small flocks. A friend who rides on the borders of Pilling Moss informed me that on a recent visit there he had seen a flock of about 40 wild geese flying very low. He had also seen what he thought was a crane, which was feeding in one of the many moss ditches. It was a very tall bird and above the usual size of the heron, with which he is very familiar; but I doubt its being a crane, although it is reputed that at one time there was a cranery on the south side of Pilling Moss. A friend has informed me that herons have lately appeared in the neighbourhood of Claughton Park in unusual numbers. The skylark on the uplands north of the Ribble is much more numerous than it was a few years ago, and we have many more of them in South Lancashire. Chaffinches are unusually numerous in most places that I have visited. With regard to the skylark, I regret to see that some of the Cheshire farmers think them very destructive of grain. On the grass lands of North Lancashire, where one can travel miles without seeing a field of grain, these birds are now in great force, and are as numerous as in any part of Cheshire, and I have had about 100 miles of a ride through the latter county this week. Magpies are more numerous than usual in Lancashire and Cheshire. We have been told that the stockdove does not breed in Lancashire. Don't believe it; I have found it, and a friend who is as well able to speak as any man in the county has found it. With regard to the fruit prospects, there is plenty of plum and pear bloom.—A correspondent, writing from North Lancashire on the 3rd, says :—" I do not think the pewit has increased greatly in numbers in this neighbourhood, although there are not so many eggs taken as formerly. Several years ago a person was commissioned by a dealer in London to collect all the fresh pewit eggs he could. He obtained from an area of 10,000 acres as many as 8,000 eggs in a year, and never less than 5,000, which continued for four or five years. If the eggs are taken a second or third time, the birds will lay later on, and I hays found them amongst corn two feet high. Many nests escape in the meadows. Four years ago, after the Wild Birds Act came into force, this collection of pewits' eggs was discontinued. A very few are now taken to the local market, and one would have thought that there would have been a decided increase in the number of birds, but I do not see that they are appreciably more abundant than in a good year in the past. A given area, it seems, is only equal to maintain a given number, and the surplus goes elsewhere. Pewits are this season very numerous on the slopes of the Bleasdale Fells, and have been so for many years past. 'lNnow.—Fucheias The potting and stopping of these must be regulated by the time they are required to be in flower. If wanted at the end of July they should receive their last potting at the end of this month. They flower more freely when the pots are packed full of roots, and their pinching may be discontinued a month after the last potting. It must not be understood by pinching that a cer- tain length of the shoots must be taken off, which is what is actually done by those who ought to know better. We have grown plants a yard high and the tame in diameter in twelve months from the time they were put in as cuttings, but this was not done by reducing the plants an inch or .two every few weeks where the plants required stopping. As soon as the leaves which will form the fourth joint are fairly seen, we remove them with the point of a sharp pen- knife, and the plant may be termed stopped. The result will be that two or three shoots will proceed from each side, and these, when long enough, are served in a similar manner.

He wants clilaene liardy, easy to rear, with tendency to rapid growth, early develop- ment, and capability of attaining a fair size; all this, with the finest quality and greatest quantity of flesh attainable. Moreover; he wants them clear of feathers on the leg and foot, otherwise they are ill fitted to a farmyard in dirty weather." It will be seen from all this that the Plymouth Rocks excel as an all-round fowl. They are good layers and table birds, adult birds reaching ten to twelve pounds in weight; are good sitters and mothers, though nothing like the Cochin, which is such an inveterate sitter that it has cora- pasatively little time for laying. The statement made in the second extract given is a remarkable proof of this, namely, that "there have been but two days on which I have had no eggs from my birds," considering that the breed is a sitting one; they are very hardy, and can be kept on any soil; and, finally, they are not flyers, and can, there- fore, be kept within reasonable limits. To those who wish for layers, first of all we should not recommend the Ply- mouth Rock, nor yet to such as desire primarily table birds, but where the requirement is for a useful breed, good layers, yet good enough as a table fowl for market purposes, and of large size, it is eminently suitable. SEASONABLE HINTS. It will be found, as a rule, with the present mild weather, that eggs will begin to be very plentiful, and chickens will also begin to crowd the runs, so that extra room will require to be given to them. When sitting is done, and eggs can be spared, they can soon be sold for table purposes, thou& there will be a demand for some time yet for eggs for sit. ting. So far as the chicks are concerned upon farms and such places as offer plenty of room, there is no difficulty whatever, as the coops can then be widely scattered; but where the space is limited, then it is necessary to make sorne other arrangements, and these had better be in the way of breaking up the breeding pens and giving the elder chicks the space.

in the order of prelirence for them. The vote will be counted to the candidate against whose name the figure 1 is placed; but after any candidate had re- ceeived enough votes to secure his election the vote will be given to the candidate marked number 2. The result would be that each party would carry its best man; while whichever party was the stronger would also bring in its second candidate. This is surely as it should be, and Liverpool would under this system be fairly represented. Under a system of mere majority voting, on the contrary, the majority only, not Liverpool as a whole, would be represented. Let us suppose, for instance, that two Liberals and two Conservatives were standing for three seats. Then each Liberal would place 1 and 2 against the Liberal candidates in the order of his preference. The Conservatives would do the same, and the result would be that each party would carry its strongest candidate, while whichever had the majority would also bring in the second. Under this system no dictation by agents or committees would be require, and leading statesmen would be sure of election. The system was recently tried by Mr. Arnold Forster in a Board school, and it was found that the school children understood it quite easily. Again, Mr. Bompas arranged for our society to have 20,000 voting papers filled up, and then counted as they would be in an ordinary elec- tion. This was done without any hitch or difficulty. Those who may wish to join our society are requested to comMunicate with Mr. A. C. White, at 9, Bridge-street, Westminster. We do not ask for money as a condition of membership, but are of course grateful for any donations. We maintain that proportional representation is the right, fair, and just system. It would free the electors from the dictation of committees or caucuses; it would give to minorities a fair hearing; and lastly, by it, and by it alone, you can secure to majorities their just preponderance. If our opponents still deny this, we challenge them to point Out the fallacy of our argument, and until they do this we confidently claim for it the support of all true Liberals.

INGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. this Board was held in the Workhons.,War- .'ednesday morning. There were present—The -f or (Alderman Harrison), the Rev. G. F. Roberts' Dr. Mackie, and Major Cartwright; Messrs. Greening, Jolley, Blackhurst, Cooper, Brown, Appleton, Derbyshire, Walms- ley, Caldwell, J. Houghton, W. Houghton Balharry, R. Worthington, Swinton, Gibson, Grange, Hunt, Greenall, W. D. Jeans Bonnell, flumphreye, Kilehall, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE•CHLIEMBE. Major CARTWRIGHT said he bad the pleasure a fortnight ago of proposing that the cordial vote of thanks of that Board be given to the chairman, Mr. Greening, and from the feeling of the Board oa that occasion there appeared to be a unanimous opinion that he should be re-elected. lie (Major Cartwright) therefore had very great pleasure in nominating their old chairman, Mr. Greening, to the post fvr the ensuing year. lie verily believed it was the first time that a chairman had been proposed who had had the opportunity of presiding over the whole Board, for as thex all knewbefore they had triennial elections they hail annual elections, and there were always some new members—some old ones gone out and eome new ones come in. But under

present circumstances every member of that Board had had the privilege and honour of sitting under their friend, Mr. Greening, as their chairman. He need not say that he be- lieved their chairman had given satisfaction to every mem- ber of the Board—(hear, hear)—and he was certain that in the future no one would doubt his conduct. The manner in which Mr. Greening bad conducted the business of that Board was quite sufficient to justify him (Major Cartwright) in saying that he hoped they would give him an unanimous vote. He did not think he could say anything more in Mr Greening's favour. He was so patriarchal looking aud so well known to them all.—Mr. COoPnit seconded this pro- posal, and trusted that the vote would be unanimous.—The Bev. G. F. ROBERTS supported the proposal, and said the way in which the chairman had conducted the business of the Board daring the past year was the best proof of his fitness for the . post.—Mr. APPLI- - also supported the propoeal.—Mr. Haranisoic said that from the consensus of opinion there was on the last occasion they met there it was a foregone conclusion that they should re-elecL their chairman. He thought it would be a graceful tribute to his merits to elect Mr. Green- ing again a chairman of the Board, a position of which any man had a right to be proud.—Mr. Greening was then unani- mously elected chairaian.—Mr. (*REINING, on taking the Chair, thanked the Board for unanimously re-electing him chairman. He emphasized the word "unanimous," because he would certainly not have occupied the chair another year if there had been a contest. It was only on account of the vote being an unanimous vote that he undertook the duties of the chair. What he had done last year he hoped and believed had been appreciated by the whole Board. • There had been nothing extraordinary that he knew of; he hut simply conducted the business as well as he possibly could, and he was well repaid by the:manner in which they had received those services. As to the future, they did not knew what it would be, but he should endeavour to conduct

the busimss of the Board in as straightforward and as simple a manner and with as few words as it was possible for him to do it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BLACKIIIIRST then moved that Mr. Cooper be re-appointed senior vice-chair- man. Mr. Cooper, he said, was ono of the oldest members of that Board—he was going to say the oldest, but if not that he was very nearly so. fie had known • Mr. Cooper as long as he had been a member of that Board, and had seen the very great pains he had taken in anything hi isad had to do for the welfare of the Union. Mr. Cooper had been senior vice-chaii man for two or three years, and, he thought, had given every satisfaction.—The Rev. G. F. Ronstrre seconded this proposal. Mr. Cooper, he said, had held a similar position before, and there was every reason why they should again put him into that office.—The proposal was then carried—Mr. HARI/Isom nominated the Rev. G. F. Roberts ae junior vice-chairman. (Hear, hear.) He need not say anything in Mr. Roberts's praise. The un- pretending and simple manner in which he did everything, the zeal he brought to bear upon, and the good common- sense which marked everything he said and did on that Beird pre-eminently established his claim to that position. He (Mr. Harrison) hoped Bt/LllO tisne to see him in a more exalted position, which he was sure he would adorn. (Hear, hear.)—Major CARTWRIGHT seconded this proposal. He had known Mr. Robets for a great many years, and knew him to be a gentleman. (Hear, hear.) Like Mr. Harrison, he hoped to see him in a more exalted • position, but that would come by and by.—Mr. JOLLEY and the CHAIRMAN also suppoi ted the proposal, which was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN moved a resolution to the effect that the Guardians, elect,cl or ex-officio, be allowed to visit the Work- house and Industrial achools at their discretion.—Mr. DARDISHIRK seconded this proposal. It had, he said, always been understood before that any Guardian could visit either , the schools or the Wei kbouse, but it had never been printed. —Major CARTWRIGHT asked if the resolution referred to Sunday/J.—Tot CHAIRMAN: I should assume it refers to any day.—Major CART WRIGHT said it was his friend (Dr. Mackie) who put that question into his head, as he himself did not care about coming —The CLERK said they had , Church service at the Workhouse on Sunday.—The CHAIR• MAN: Yes; you can come to the service if you like.—Dr. Macxus said that was just the reason why he wanted the question asked.—Mr. Elanarsow understood that a Guar- dian had a right to visit the Workhouse at any time with- out a resolution.—Major CARTWRIGHT said that was not SO; the question '•ad been tested in the South of England.— The CURL explained that Guardians were just as other in- dividuals unless they had the power of the collective body. —The tesolution WAS then carried. The clerk then read the following letter from the treasurer:—" According to the list of cheques signed by the Guardians, the balance I hold, which is already one-half the minimum sum which was agreed the treasurer should hold, will be exhausted and the account considerably over- drawn on the present occasion. lam quite agreeable to the advance provided it is temporary, bat it may be well that the position of the accounts should be explained to your Board.—J. AN OPPORTUNITY FOR CHARITY.

Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in moving the confirmation of the School Attendance Committee's minutes, referred to the case et a boy named John Warrington, who had run away , from the school and gone into another district. The reliev- ing officer of the Union into wh ch the lad had gone brought him back, and now claimed his expenses. They should also be very glad if gentlemen who were planting would send their supetfluous roots and dowers to Mr. Mines, the schoolmaster —Mr. CALDWELL, who seconded the confirmation of the minutes, said the lad Warrington who had been mentioned was quite a notable lad. He thought he took his peculiarities and eccentricities from the town. Laughter.) He certainly was a nuisance, and the sooner they got rid of him the better, for they all remember the saying that when one sheep went wrong it led the other into mischief.—The minutes having been con- firmed, the CHAIRMAN moved that 8s 6d, the expenses paid tor bringing the boy back to Warrington, be paid.—This was agreed to. div.p: GI,.NERAL NEWS.

The Duke of Cambridge tern.inated his visit to Ports- rnoath on Tuesday, and returned to Loudon. &roma Irnsamv.—A stormy vestry meeting took place at at. James's, liatcham, on Tuesday. The Protestant party in the parish attended in force, and protested against the Ritualistic practices of the vicar. The Duke of Edinburgh landed at Malta on Monday, and met with a loyal reception, though, in consequence of the general mourning for the late Duke of Albany, the honours show to his Royal Elighnese were quiet and euodued. The War Office have decided to place 12,000 more Martini- Henry rifles at the service of the National Rifle Association. The latter have resolved that all* prizes may now be coua- Peted for with this weapon, and to add £1,200 to the value ef the prize list for the next Wimbledon meeting. KILIAN') ON THE RAILWAY—Mr. Wolfe, the station- master at Hockley railway station (Great Western Railway), Birmingham was killed on Monday whilst crossing the line from the up platform to the down to meet a stopping train. Mr. Wolfe had been at Hockley station 20 years, and WAS much esteemed. TILE " WHITE " ELZFRANT.—Sworn charges have been Preferred before the Philadelphia Society for the Prevention ef Cruelty to Animels to the effect that the whiteness et the fore feet of the so-called white elephant was produced by artificial means, and that there were in Liverpool 50 ePplications of whitening and sizing, closing the pores of the beast and occasioning sores that have endangered its A Ceroacu Bummer, Dows.—Wadsley Church, near kheffield, WAS partially destroyed by fire OD Sunday. The roof was ignited by sparks from a c'finmey attached to the heating apparatne, and before the Shetield Fire Brigade Could arrive the flames had extended the 'mole length of the Church. The roof fell an hour after the discovery of the eatbreak, causing great internal damage. The building WAS 'Seared. LORD BIACONSIMILD —The statue of Lord Beaconsfield, executed by Mr. Boehm, and placed in Westminster Abbey, 55 pursuance of a vote of the House of COMDIORS, is now in its position in the north transept, midway between the *tattles of Sir Robert Peel and the two Cannings. in accord- ance with the coarse followed in all similar Cases, there has been no public ceremonial of any kind. The inscription is let yet added. SIXTEEN FISHERMEN DROWNED.—A terrible accident, se, Ya an Aberdeen telegram, bas occurred at the Park Islands involving a loss of 16 lives. Two fishing boats, each with a crew of eight men, and heavily laden with fish, were caught in a gale and capsized. Several other boats were in the vicinity, but owing to the heavy sea that was on were unable to tender any assistance. Most of the men have widows and children, and in both boats there were cases in which fathers and eons went down together. Falk', QUARREL AT S&.—At Hull, on Monday. Adolph Gatv, a fishermen was charged with the manslaurhter of Charles Berton, cook on board the Hull smack Woodlark, en the 10th met, when the vessel was in the North Sea. The prisoner and Barton were engaged in heaving up nets, when the former is alleged to have struck Burton, who returned the blow. Other blows followed, and both men fell over- board. The prisoner was rescued, but, although every effort was made by the rest of the crew, Burton WAS drowned.— Remand ed. HEAVY FORGERY ay • Snowey Mit• Shell, a lad of sixteen, who was apprehended at Perth last Week, on a charge ef forging and uttering a cheque for £650 In the name of his employer on the Union Bank at Aberdeen, was on Tuesday charged with the crime before the magie- tratee and committed for trial. When apprehended £6OO were found in the boy's possession, and a gold watch, which shad purchased as a gift to a young lady in the south. The accused had been in the habit of reading literature of the "penny dreadfui " description, and to this his crime is attri- buted. Stu WILFRID Lawson ON THZ FRANCUISM —Speaking Oft Monday night, at Cockermoutb, Sir Wilfrid Lawson said tile effect of the Franchise Rill would be that Parliament Should obey the will of the people. He spoke of Mc. Goschen U resembling Mrs. Partington, who tried to keep out the antic with a bemom and a pail. The great breakers of Democracy were rolling in, and no human hand could stay their invincible and majestic advance. He could ask t_rhether they were satisfied with the result of aff eirs is the a" an, and inveighed against the aggressive policy of the ti"ernment which had caused the peopl.., to 'sup full of horrors." r SCARE AT ROCK F RlM—Early on Saturday, the in- sabitants of Rock Ferry were mach alarmed by a violent explosion accompanied by all the outward effects of a smart earthquake. There was A violent tremor of the earth, houses racked, and crockery was rattled about in the most alarming manner. As some wild stories had been current the pre- !ions evening regarding the arrest of dynamite fiends" at Birkenhead, the people concluded that an in ernal 'Machine outrage had occurred somewhere in the district. It transpired, however, that the "outrage" had been perpe- trated lay some workmen employed in the river to blow up Lbw remains of the sunken wreck of the reformatory ship Clarence. .

STRIKESi SCOTLAND—The paddlers employed at the North British Irouworks, Coatbridge, struck work on Mna- daY, in consequence of a dispute with Mr. Ellis, the pro- Prietor, as to extra work on Saturday. The works were closed, and fully 500 men will be thrown out of work. For 25 years Mr. Ellis and his men have been on most amicable terms.—The iron and steel workers employed by the Clydes- dale Works, Motherwell. the property of Messrs. McCorkin- dale and Co., struck work on Monday night. Notice of a reduction had been given 14 days ago, in which the men refused to acquiesce* About 600 hands are usually em- ployed at the works. Later information is to the effect that the strike is at an end, the firm having withdrawn the proposal to reduce wages. DEATH OF Mat. H. J. BTRON.—The death is announced of Mr. H. J. Ryron, which took pines on Saturday, at his house in Clapham Park, London. The pulmonary com- plaint from which he suff-qed had compelled him to spend mach of the winter at Hastings, where of late he had seemed ' somewhat better, and had even attempted to continue his work for the stage. He had, however, long been missed from the social gatherings which he used to enliven by the quint, dry humour that derived so much of its point from Ito prompt spontaneity, and so much of its charm from its apparent unconsciousness. His best play was, perhaps, " Cyril's Success f." his most successful one was, of course, "Our boys," the run of which at the Vaudeville was an event without parallel in theatrical history. By playgoers Mr. Byron will long be remembered as one ef the most fer- tile contributors to their entertainment, and by his acquain- tances he will long be regretted as the brightest of coin- Paniens and the cheeriest of friends. GLADSTONN ON FRUIT FARMING.—(To the editor of the Examirter.)—Sir, Referring to the Premier's speech at the annual rent audit at Hawarden, Mr. Gladetone is incor- rect in stating that preserves are charged from 7d to 9d a 111, and that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German and American fruit growers. All the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, black currante, damsons, and blackberries used ley me are entirelrEnglish—no foreign whatever being used—and to Prove that the quantity is not particularly small, my usual "moo's make is :—Gooseberry, 300 tons. Raspberry, 300 tom • Strawberry, 200 tons. Black currant, 400 tons. Damson, 500 tons. Blackberry, 100 tons. And they can be bought retail from ready-money grocers in two and three- pound stoneware jars it the following prices :—Gooseberry, aato so per lb. Raspberry, 6d to flid. Strawberry, gd to ~.t4l. Black currant, 50. Blackberry, si.d. Raspberry and Y.ooE:eherry, al. Plum, 4d. Greengage, 51. Damson, ,V tours Orange Marmalade, 4d. Jars extra, one penny each. , I/0e Wis. P. HARTLIY.—BootIe, Liverpool. oroortl'oter GLUe Lata.szs.—At the quarterly meeting of theS o c t ai, he ncheister and District Committee of the Liberation d at the offices, 4, St. J imes's Square, Mr. Jesse BrYant in the chair it was unanimously resolved, on the MetiOn of Mr. Rdward Cooper, seconded by Mr. J. R. Cros- geld, "That this committee, having had placed before them the tech' connected with the Stockport glebe leases, are of *pinion that the Rector of Stockport. by demanding a rack rental on the renewal of the leases now falling in, is infi ct- in; grievous injustice on the present leaseholders, and is doing violence to the pp rit of the Act under which he takes kis power. The committee consider that the enormous in- crease of revenue which the Rector seeks to grasp, ought, even if it in legitlrdately obtained, to be devoted to the good of the public, .andmot to, the enrichment of a State ecclesi- astic, inatunuctaas it arises out of public property. The committee further point out that the action of the Rector illustrates *heir contention—that the connection- of Churph and State helos to secularise the clergy, and to silence the bishops in the presence of legal injustice* tends to injure the character of the Christian religion, and is an evil that ran be remedied only in the way proposed by this society," EASTER MANOITITRIS AT PORTSatoreert.-With the advance of five marching columns on Portedowe Hill, on Saturday the Easter manoeuvree practically commenced. The Duke of Cambridge arrived at Havant about an hoar before the contest.began. The object of the battle was to check the advance of the northern force, and prevent the captive of Portsdown Ridge, overlookiog the harbour and town of Portsmouth. Colonel Brodigan, Gloucester Regiment, com- manded the defending force, consisting of only two regi- Wants of regulars and two of volunteers, while his base necessarily extending nearly six miles. The attacking force mastered five strong brigades, with gatling gains. The de- fenders were quickly driven in on the right and left, and the attack soon concentrated on the centre. The London Scottish were the first to engage the defenders' line. The mounted vedettes had been driven in, and the action soon became general. In the result the defenders were c uneletely routed, after an hour's fighting, the attackers gaining pos- session of Portsdown Ridge. Two sham fights. in which both regulars and volunteers participated. took place on Monday at Portemouth ani Dover. In the former c tee the battle was a continuation of Saturday's operations, and, briefly stated, was an attempt on the part of an invading force from the northward to carry the Hilsea Lines, protect- Lag Portsmouth. before a relieving army could intervene. , More than 20 ow men were actually engaged in the sham light. In the result, the defending force was completely driven back, and the relieving force also suffered a severe check. Thoniill the work was hard and continuous, great credit is awarded to the volunteers for their willingness and marked ability in extended inanceuvres of this kind. The operations at Dover were not upon a large scale, consisting mainly of the "arranged" defeat of an invading force Which was supposed to have landed and marched towards London, 1 raying troops to occupy the ground ne • the town. The invader was allowed temporarily to drive h., a strong bpdY of defenders, but coining under the heave :es of the Castle and adjacent Certifications, he was (on paper) repulsed With heavy loss. There was also a general " engagement " at Aldershot on Monday between the Northern and Southern f"cea, numbering altogether over 10,000 men.

FUNERAL Or Csuarms ReLDE.—The remains of Mr. Charles Boade were interred on Tuesday in Willesden churchyard. The hearse was an open one, and the coffin was covered with flowers. Mr. Charles Dickens and Mr. Ur. A. Sala were present. ATTACH ON Jews IN IRIL.A.ND.—e. young man, named Nash, was remanded at Limerick, on Tuesday, charged with taking part in a recent attack on the Jews, when windows were broken and many injured. A Jewish witness declined, in the absence of the Old Testament, to be sworn. Ciatcw.—There will be three representative matches be- tween England and Australia, besides engagements with the Gentlemen, the Players, the North and the South, CAM• bridge past'and present, the University Elevens, and all the best counties. A novel featara of the season will be the visit of a team of American amateurs from Philadelphia. Amor AT Hts POST.—At Oldham, on Wed.iesday, Baxter, engineer, was fined 404 and costs for a breach of the Mines Regulation Act. Dsfendant whilst in clamp of a colliery engine fell asleep and allowed the cage to be drawn over the head-gear, with consequent damage to the ma- chinery. No one was injured, but ninety men were im- prisoned in the pit for some hours. Tam Panxima.—Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left the Durdaes on Tuesday afternoon in a closed carriage for Holmbrirg, the residence of Mr. Leveson Gower, 17 miles distant. 'The Prernier,'who had relapsed a little, was, on Tuesday, better. Earl Grenville has also gone to Holmburg. The right hon, gentleman arrived at Holmburg shortly before five o'clock. Earl Granville followed the Premier in his own carriage. DEATH or Tan Bismor OF RIPON. The Right Rev. Robert Bickersterla, Bishop of Ripon, died at 1-30 p.m. on Tuesday. Dr. Bickersfeth matriculated at Camoridge in 1841, was ordained in the following year, and was consec- rated Bishop of Ripon in 1857. Ile was previously rector 'of St. Giles-in-the-Fields, London. The income of the See of Ripon now vacant, is £4,500. Leeds is the principal town within the diocese. • Munonn AT NORTH SHIELDS.—A single woman named Sarah Holmes was on Wednesday committed for trial at I North Shields on a charge of wilfully murdering her son, . aged eight years. A quarrel had occurred between Holmes I and the boy's lather, and after purchasing some "Vermin i killer" the mother administered part of the poison to the deceased, and took the remainder herself. The boy died, and Holmes had a very narrow escape. . I CURIOUS HIDING PLACB.—Elizi Baker, 18, wts re- I manded'at Wednesbury, on Wednesday, for bding on pre- 1 mine for unlawful purposes under singular circumstances. i On Monday night, upon a publican going to a wine barrel, he WAS unable to draw the wine, and on examining the bar- 1 rel he found the prisoner inside. The taps had been knocked out, and the wine allowed to waste. roe prisoner said she was concealing herself from a man who had thrtatened to assault her. • _ . .

A FRXIAN MANITBSTO.—A manifesto signed by the Sec- retary of the Fenian Brotherhood has been issued "to all Irishinen." It declares that never did Ireland have such an opportunity as the present. It is claimed that to the Fenian Brotherhood is due "the honour of inaugurating scientific warfare," and the brothers in organisation are urged to "per- severe vigorously in the glorious war' and strengthen the ranks; "then, it is promised, they will witness "a free and regenerated Ireland." LIMERICK AND THB IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. The freedom of the city of Limerick was on Monday conferred on Mr. Michael Davitt and Mr. Dawson, M.P. A great de- monstration took place in honour of the event, but the Con- servative members of the City Council absented themselves. After the ceremony a public meeting was held, and Mr. Davitt denounced "landlordism " as being the cause of the troubles in Ireland. Mr. Gray, M.P„ should have been presented with the freedom of the city, but was unable to attend. TRH ABSCONDING Wonxuorsa GOVERNOIL—The defal- cations in connection with the flight of Mr. Anderson. the Governor of the Liverpool Workhouse, will be much larger than was at first anticipated. It is stated that £5,000 would not cover all his deficiencies. The whole of this loss does not, however, fall upon the ratepayers. In this .05,000 are included L 2,600 or so borrowed at various times from Liver- pool gentlemen, members of the Select Vestry, and others. A large sum of money, the property of inmates of the work- house and of persons sent to the county lunatic asylum, is missing. EDINBURGH TBRCBNTBNARY FESTIVITIES.—The proceed- ings in connection with the Tercentenary festivities at the Edinburgh University commenced on Tuesday, when the annual students' graduation ceremonial took place. In the evening there was a reception of visitors and alumni at the Museum, followed by a torchlight procession, in which several hundreds of students took part. Wednesday was signalised by a special service in St. Giles's Cathedral, which was attended by a brilliant company of University members and foreign guests. There was a luncheon in the afternoon, and a e•nroersazione and ball in the evening. TBEI Qualm's VISIT TO TILL CONTINENT.—The Queen and Princess Beatrice and a number of ladies of the Court, left Windsor at five o'clock on Tuesday evening for London. Her Majesty passed through Waterloo shertly before six, for Port Victoria, where she embarked on board the Royal yacht Osborne, for Flashing, on her way to Darmstadt, on a visit to the Grand Duke Louis of Hesse. Her Majesty boked remarkably well considering her recent bereavement. The wedding of Prince Louis of Battenburg, and the Prin- cess Victoria of Hesse has been definitely fixed for the 30th instant. According to present arrangement the Court will not return te England until the 3rd of May. ATTRIMBD MIIRDBR Or FITL PIRSONS —A. Dungannon correspondent telegraphs that a deliberate attempt was made late on Monday night to shoot a Catholic party of five per- sons who were driving through Dungannon. At the turn of the road, just beside the entrance gate of the residence of Mr. A. Dickson, M.P., four men emerged from the hedge, went over to the car, stooped down and looked into the faces of the occupants, and then, as soon as the operation of " Make ready: present: fire," could be gone through, balls whizzed past the terrified group of five who sat on the vehicle. The car was only about a perch from them when the first shot was fired. It had not gone another perchl when a second shot followed. Those fired upon had a, miraculous escape. _

POOLE ELICrION.—The nomination took place on Tuee- day : ['homes Chatfield Clarke (L), Westbmrne-terrace, Hyde Park, London, and Oakfield Wooton, Isle of Wight, architect and surveyor; William James Harris (C), Linden Gardens, Bayswater, Middlesex, and Hal well Manor, Devon, corn factor. At the last election the deceased member, Mr. C. Cchreiber (C) was returned by a majority of only six votes. On Thursday the election resulted in the return:of Mr. Harris, the Conservative candidate, by 877 votes against 815 recorded for Mr. Clarke, thus reaffirming its veraict at the general election of 1880, when Mr. Schreiber was re- I turned by 854 against 848 votes given to Mr. C. Waring. The constituency is a small one, and has not usually iodi- cated the current of political opinion in the country. At the general election of 1888, when Mr. Gladstone gained a large majority, Poole returned a Conservative; in 1874, when the Tory party was carried into power, the same con- stituency returned a Liberal in the person of the Hon. E. Ashley; and in 1880, when Mr. Gladstone was again triumphant, it elected a Conservative. Poole evidently goes against the stream. Tiaz LATH DIJIR OF ALBANY: LBTTER FROM THE QUIIIIN.—Sir W. V. Harcourt, by command of the Queen, forwards the following letter from Her Majesty for pabli- cation in the newspapers:—" Windsor Castle, April 14, 1884.—1 have on several previous occasions given personal expression to my deep sense of the loving sympathy and loyalty of ray subjects in all parts of my Empire. I wish, therefore, in my present grievous bereavement to thank them most warmly for the very gratifying manner in which they have shown not only their sympathy with me and my dear so deeply afflicted daughter in-layr and my other children. but also their high appreciation of my son's great qualities of head an heart and of the loss he is to the country and to me. The affectionate sympathy of my loyal people, which. has .never failed me in weal en woe, is very seething, to my heart. Though mach shaken and sore'y afflicted by the many sorrows and trial which have fallen upon me during these past years' I will not lose courage ; and with the help of Him who has never forsaken me will strive to labour on for the lake of my children and for the good of the country I love so well as long as I can. My dear daughter-in-law, the Duchess of Albany, who bears her terrible misfortune with the most admirable, touching, and unmurmuring resignation to the will of God, is also deeply gratified by the universal sympathy and kind feeling evinced. towards her. I would wish, in conclusion, to express my gratitude to all other countries for their sympathy; above all, to the neighbouring one where my beloved son breathed his last, and for the great respect and kindness shown on that mournful occas'on Vteronra. R. and I." LORD CHURCHILL AT BIRMINGHAM. Lord Randolph Churchill on Tuesday made his first appearance before the Conservative electors of Birmingham as a candidate for their suffrages. FOREIGN NEWS.
THE SOUDAN. RUMOURED FALL OF KEIARTOU

..-- SUAKIM, MONDAY, 1 P.M.—lt appears that ttie intnded meeting between the Sheikh El Morghani and °the- sheikhs, followers of Osman Digna, has fallen through in con- sequence of a rumour that Khartoum, as well as the station at the Fifth Cataract, have been captured by the rebels. CAIRO, SUNDAY, 1•25 A.M.-..NeTIS has been received from Berber to the effect that communication both by land and ' water isinterrupted, that the forces of the rebels have been I materially augmented, and that they have made raids -upon the environs of that town. The Governor of Berber appeals ' for the aid of English troops. SUNDAY NlGlT.—Three more Sheikhs ef the Amass tribes have arrived here, asking to be relieved from the poll tax. They declere that the English Government is everywhere relied upon and that they want to see no more of the Egyptians. They were pleased to hear that the Enirlish troops were staying. The new Egyptian troops are ridiculed. The Egyptiein officers do not even understand their men, as they are unable to speak their language.

• DESPATCHES FROM GENERAL GORDON. CAIRO, WIDNIRIDAY.—Sir Evelyn Baring to-nay received the following telegram from General Gordon, dated the Ilth inst. A spy from Saleh Pasha, on the Blue Nile, reports that he is all right, and has 500 horsemen and 57 boatloads of grain. Internal dissensions are rife in Kordofan, in con- sequence of which the expedition which the Mandi was preparing against Khartoum has had to be abandoued. There seem to be two parties in revolt against the Maid Salab's effort to capture the Sheikh El Obeid be failed. Kassala is all right, and Sennaar also." CAIRO, WEDNRSDAY EVINING ---Zebehr Pasha has ill- iseived the following telegram from General Gordon this afternoon, dated April 7th:—" I have appointed you Assis- tant G..ivernor General of the Soudan. You will advise me on your arrival at Berber, and if possible I will send you two steamers. These, with the other two steamers now at Berber, will provide you with iron upon parapets in order to protect the troops on board. Take also as many as you can of the Galyieen tribe and make frequent skirmishes, but do not expose yourself." The above telegram is unintelligible here, because Colonel Stewart, on General Gordon's own preposal, hes been ap- pointed Assistant Governer General of the Soudan, and also because the Galyieen tribe have revolted. The telegram makes no mention whatever of the disapproval of the British Government to the appointment of Zebebr Pasha as his successor, which was known to General Gordon. ZESEHR PASHA AND THE SOUDAN. ..

Catno7P-munsnev.—Zebehr Pasha has refused the ap- pointment o! Assistant Governor General of the Soudan offered to him by General Gordon. THE CRISIS IN EGYPT. CAIRO, SUNDAY NlONT.—Yesterday the political crisis assumed a new phase. Nubar Pasha went to Sir. E. Boring and tentatively suggested that Omar Lufti should be ap- pointed Minister of the Interior in place of abdel Koder, stating that each was the express wish of the Khedive. Sir E. Baring very curtly begged Nubar to return to the palace to express his surprise at such a suggestion, which was utterly impracticable. Mr. Clifford Lloyd, on bearing of this fresh intrigue, instantly wrote to Sir E. Baring to the effect that should Abdel Lacier be dismissed to make room for Omar LOU. the incarnation of all that was bad of the old Turkish school, he would resign forthwith. This, of course, further strengthened Sir E. Baring's bands, and the plan was peremptorily nipped in the bud. Since this, Nubar Pasha has again talked of resigning, but has been persuaded or coerced into retaining office for the present. The chief concession made to him lies in the fact that, in future, all orders, kc., of the Ministry of the Interior should be signed by the Minister, and not by Mr. Clifford Lloyd alone. At the same time Nubar Pasha has been given to understand that though in theory Mr. C. Lloyd's position is the same as that of any Egyptian Under-Secretary, who may be dis- missed at the will of the Minister, the present state of affairs here precludes the carrying out of this theory into practice. The prominent part taken by the Khedive in the late crisis is noteworthy, as it constitutes a reversal of the usual order of things, in which the Ministers have been accustomed to make a stalking-horse of the Khedive irostead of being put forward by him. Canto, MONDAY.--The British Government have sub- mitted proposals to the Great Powers for the settlement of the financial difficulties of Egypt. The nature of these pro- posals is unknown here, except that the disbanding of General Wood's army is included in them.

CAIR-07T—ECUR-SDAY.—lntelligence received here from Ismailia states that a death from cholera has occurred in board Her Majesty's Indian troopship Crocodile, homeward bound, between Lake Timsah and Port Said. Ihe Pilot, on landing at Port Said, was placed in quarantine. FRLDICE AND CHINA. SONTAY, &WlRRAL—lntelligence. dated the 9th inst. received here from the French camp before Hone Hoe, states that from ten o'clock in the morning of that day lentil four o'clock in the afternoon, the batteries Nos. 80 and 25 bombarded the 'villages leading to Hong Hoe, as well as the citadel. The Chinese, who ofttred no resist once, evacuated Hong Hoa after haying set fire to the town, which is now in lames. The French shells set fire to several places in the town, and compelled the inhabitants to take to flight across the Bamboo bridge facing Hong Hoe, on the left bank of the Eloukoi. The distance, however, was too great for the French fire to reach the bridge. Part of the Chinese fled in the direction of Phulang, and part towards Dauvang and Than Pim The Chinese who occupied Hong Hoe came from Yunnan, and were commanded by General Cbam. Smawcarar, TUBSDAY.—The Viceroy of Canton has been publicly degraded for disobeying orders. The officers re- sponsible for the less of Bacninh have been condemned to be beheaded. The Governor of Yunnan has been ordered to Pekin for severe punishment. Affairs at Pekin are critical. PARIS, Turesney.—A despatch received here from Hong Etna, dated the 12th inst. announces that General Millot occupied that place at nooe on that day without fighting. The enemy had completely evacuated the town and carried off their artillery. They also destroyed some of the houses as well as the magazines in the citadel, which was defended with a double range of resent batteries. PARIS, TIIRSDAY Entmsro.—The Minister of Marine has received a telegram from General Millot, dated to-day, an- nouncing the capture of Hong Hoa. He says the French artillery fire had a terrifying effect on the enemy, and that soldiers and sailors behaved with their usual gallantry. PARIS, WIDNISDAS —The National says that the state- ment that the French Government had informed the Government of Pekin of its intention to demand a war in- demnity is confirmed, but adds that up to the present China has made no reply to the communication.
- - . FRANCE.-MINISTERIAL DECLARATION OF POLICY. .

PiItIGUICTX, TUESDAY EVENlNG.—Speaking at the ban- quet given here this evening M. Jules Ferry, the Premier, I alluded to the foreign policy of the Government, and re- marked that most of the foreign questions which were await- I ing solution when his Cabinet assumed office had been settled. France, he went en to say, was a maritime power, and had interests in all parts of the world; but she was also a continental Power, and could not allow foreign hands to be laid on any interest which she could legitimately call hers on the continent of Europe. After some reference to Tunis, the Premier proceeded to touch upon affairs in Ton- quin, where, he said, the military question had been dis- posed of, the news having just reached him that the troops had entered Hong Hoa. M. Ferry paid a warm tribute of praise to the soldiers and sailors engaged in the expedition who had proved themselves fully equal to encountering all the perils and labours of the task assigned to them. STATUE TO THE LATE M. GAMBETTA. CUKOR% Morrnay. —The statue of the late M. Gambetta was unveiled with much ceremony at 3 p.m. M. Jules Ferry delivered a speech, in which he expressed his deep regret for the premature death of M. Gambetta, which, he said, .1 left a void that could be filled by no one else. The Minister eantinued—ln future the country and Gambetta are un- separable. In to-day rendering this solemn homage to Gambetts we are only apotheosising the country. (Ap- plause.)—General Campenon, War Minister, said-The army will never forget the part played by Gambetta, whose voice was the voice of France herself, and whose words will live far ever in the memory of Frenchmen, teaching them to love their country to the death. Roma, moILNU2yD.—ERA OsirckFenliVnEg aBnOdLDwIhEo le slaughter was perpetrated at Naples last night at the Piss 'falcons Barracks. A Calabrian infantry soldier, who had been chaffed by his comrades, waited until they had gone to bed, and then seizing a rifle and cartridge pouch, and extin- guishing the lights, began firing on them. The panic in ' the dormitory was indescribable. All who could fled. One wounded man, unable to gain the door, jumped out of the window, breaking his legs. The assassin made next for the I non-commissioned officers' room and shot a sergeant, whose pouch served to replenish his own At last, after having Arad 57 shots, with the result of killing five men, wounding , three, and causing two more to throw themselves out of the , window, this human tiger was grappled with and disarmed by three of his comrades.

LORD SALISBURY AT MANCHESTER.

On Wednesday evening the Marquis of Salisbury ad- dressed a crowded meeting of the Conservatives of Man- chester and the district in the Free-trade Hall. Mr. Houlds- worth, Ml'., presided. Lord Salisbury, in his opening remarks, referred to the depres4ed condition of trade, and said that it was natural to ask What, in that state of things, was the Government doing? Was its policy such as to diminish the tension and guard against the dangers under which we suffer; or had it been, on the contrary, of a nature to aggravate them? He condemned Mr. Chamberlain's Shipping Bill 'as harassing:, and his language as insulting to the great shipping interest. His public statements here not unlikely to deter men from investing their money in branches of trade which were essential to the country's pros- perity. So with regard to land; such was the language em- ployed towards the landed interest that no one knew what might be in store; people refused to tie up any more of their capital in land lest la the legislation which Mr. Chamberlain threatenid they might lose it. Abroad the effect of the Government policy had been to allow markets once open to Britain to be stolen from is. The Congo Treaty, ter instance, would have the effect of putting a highly protective prohibitory power between British in- dustry and the consumption of the vast native populations, of Africa. In Madagascar also and in Central Asia other powers were being allowed to interfere and to raise a barrier of hostile tariffs. Why, he asked, is our ,Government power- less to do its duty by the commerce of this country? It was because they had sacrificed the great arm of this coun- try, our military credit. Everywhere, in all its foreign affairs, they found the stamp of failure. In the Transvaal, in Zulnland, in Afghanistan, they reversed the policy of their predecessors • their action was stamped with the brand of impotence; and it was their impotence which they had succeeded in persuading the Asiatic and the African was the chief characteristic of the policy of Great Britain. As to Egypt they professed to follow the policy of the late Government. They followed it for two years; they caricatured it; and by sheer negligence and irresolution they allowed its chief results to be sacrificed. Their present policy he declared was a policy of afterthoughts. As to the future, the prospect darkened every hour. Our diffi- culties increased with every fresh act of imbecility on the part of the Government. If he were asked what should be their policy he should be surprised at the question, for upon no point was public feeling more pronounced. It was clear that whilst we occupy and hold the power in Egypt we must, in every sense of the word, govern Egypt. We had been told that the policy of the present Government was to "rescue and retire." If they could not retire better than they could rescue they would not make much of their policy. But he would rather define the present policy of this coun- try in Egypt as to govern and restore. In saying that he did not wish to express any opinion as to the ultimate and distant issue of events, he was quite aware of the international difficulties which would pre- vent us from forecasting in permanence or for any very distant period the attitude of this country towards Egypt, but it was obvious that we should have to stay in Egypt "for so long as the period to which the an- ticipations of practical politicians usually extend." With reference to the immediate future, with which practical politicians have to deal, it was ebvious that we should have to remain the Governors of Egypt, and so long as we remain so no international consideration should prevent ps from giving to Egypt that to which she had a right—a irm and effective Government. It was not, however, a policy that was wanted, but workmen to carry it out. It was no use giving the best models or the best tools to people who, were incompetent to handle them. (Cheers.) At the close of Lord Salisbury's speech a resolution con- demnatory of the Government was moved by Sir R. A. Cross, M.P., seconded by Mr A. J. Balfour, M.P., and passed; as was also one "deploring the continued efforts of the Radical party to sow dissension between class and class and to harass the various interests of the country," moved by Mr. Marriott, M.P., and seconded by Mr. Tomlinson, M.P. Lord Salisbury made up for his omission to discuss the question of reform on the previous evening. In the after- noon he was presented with an address by the Lancashire Constitutional Union, and in his reply dwelt upon tEI necessity of maintaining the integrity of the empire, and upon the probability of an early dissolution. But his molt important speech was reserved for the banquet that took place in the Free Trade Hall in the evening, and it was then that be discussed the question of reform. He ad- mitted the need for reform, but declared his inability to understand why Sir W. Harcourt should exalt over the great majority on the second reading of the Franchise Bill, and Bait! this was merely the result of squaring the Irish vote. The bill he regarded as a crude measure, intended to secure a new lease of power, and though he had net said what the Lords would do with it, he assured Sir W. Harcourt that his bluster would not influence them, and that it had yet to be proved that the country wanted reform without redistribu- tion.

THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO DARMSTADT. DARMSTADT, THURSDAY, 940 AM —Queen Victoria and Princess Beatrice, accompanied by their suite, arrived here at a quarter-past nine o'clock this morning, by special train from Flushing. The Royal party was received at the rail- way station by the Grand Duke, the Princesses Victoria and Elizabeth, and Prince Henry. At the special request of Her Majesty, there was no official reception. The public were excluded from the platform. A large number of people, in- cluding many English residents, assembled near the station to witness Liar Majesty's arrival. Tea Queen appeared to be in good health. Her Majesty, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and the Grand Duke, drove in a carriage with four outriders to the New Palace, where the Queen and the Princess will remain, retaining only the Marchioness of Ely and Lady Churchill in attendance. The rest tithe suite, will be accommodated at the old castle. The Osborne had rough passage crossing to Flushing. Mr. Jocelyn, the sritish charge d'affaires, attended privately at the eta- ' don by Her Majesty's request.

Canter Cnonca VESTRY MEETING.—The annual met''- tag of the parishioners was held in the vestry of the above church, on Monday evening, "to examine the accounts of the churchwardens for the past year, and to appoint war- dens for the ensuing,year.' There was only a small attend- ance of the parishioners, namely, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, M.A., F.R.S , rector (in the chair); and Messrs. John Southern aid Lewis Birchall (churchwardens), Reginald Owen, sen., George Brimelow, and Edward Monks (sexton). —The churchwardens submitted their accounts, which showed that they had a balance in hand at the beginning,of the year of £6 14s 4il, and that the receipts from the volun- tary rate were £8 108 3d, and the collection at the last har- vest festival £9, making a total of £24 4s 70. The expen- diture for the year was £2 4s 3d, leaving a balance in the churchwardens' hands of £3 Os 40. The organ fund account showed the monthly offertory on behalf of the fund since Christmas, 1883, to be £lO 18s id, and the expendi- ture for coals and paraffin oil for warming the organ £1 5s 3d, leaving a balance in hand of £9 12a 10d. The ac- counts having been examined, were passed on the motion of Mr. Owen, sen., and seconded by Mr. Brimelow.—Mr. Owen, sen., moved, and Mr. Hunt seconded, that Messrs. John Southern and Lewis Birchall be re-elected church- wardens for the ensuing year, which was carried.—Votes of thanks closed the proceedings.

PR ESCOT. VESTRY MEETING.—Tbe annual Easter meeting of the parishioners was held in the vestry of the church, on Tues- day morning, the vicar, the Rev. H. A Macnaghten, M.A., occupying the chair. A motion for the election of two war- dens instead of four was rejected by a majerity of 10 votes. Messrs. W. L. Evans, 11. Cross, A. F. Evans, and J. K. Slack were then re-elected wardens for the ensuing year. TEMPERANCE MEZTING.—A meeting of the Preacot branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in the Houghton-street Schools, on Monday evening. The entertainment consisted of a service of song, entitled, "For Harry's sake," given by the members of the first class of the Girls' Sunday School, assisted by the members of the Church choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Baylis. Miss A. Driffield presided at the harmonium. The connec- tive readings were read in a very impressive manner by the Vicar; and the songs and solos were very well received by the audience, particularly a round called "London street cries" and the chorus "Laugh and grow fat." The meet- ing was exceedingly well attended, and at the close several persons came forward and signed the pledge. UNITED METHODIST FRIN CHURCH.—The annual public tea meeting in connection with this place of worship was held on Monday evening, and was very well attended. After tea a service of song, entitled, " Given in charge," which set forth the benefits of temperance and the miseries of in- temperance was given by the chapel choir, composed of 40 voices. The readings were given by the circuit minister, thb Rev. C. W. Hopper. of St. Helens. The music, which was well-rendered and much appreciated, was under the direc- tion of Mr. R. Hayes, the choirmaster. Mr. T. Willis pre- sided at the organ. The service, which was of a very im- pressive character, was rendered still more effective by the aid of limelight views. Whitfield, Hatton, Beasley, J. T. Hall, W. Goldsworth (surveyor). and Henry Cross (clerk).—As this was the first meeting of the new Board, Mr. Preston was elected to preside.—On the motion of Mr. Hall, Mr. C. Spenceley was appointed chairman of the Board for the ensuing year.—Appointment of Committees.—The following members were appointed as the General Purposes Committee: Messrs. Fogg, Preston, Whitfield, Hewitt, and McEgan. The Finance Committee was constituted as fol- lows: Messrs Hewitt, Hall, Beasley, Hatton, and Fogg.— It was decided to levy a a general district rate of is 6d in the and the bill of expen-es (£23 Is 8d) incurred by Mr. Fogg as returning officer in the recent election was passed for payment, after a little discussion.—The mode of collect- ing the voting papers in contested elections was raised, and Mr. Hewitt afterwards moved that in future elections the voting papers should be collected in boxes and not in bas- kets as heretofore, and the motion was passed.—This was the only business of interest.

AGAINST A MAGISTRATE AND GDARDIAN.—At a meeting of the Visiting Committee, held on the Bth intent, it was stated that one of the county justices and a mem- ber of the Prescot Board of Guardians, had recently visited the Union Workhouse for the purpose of obtaining informa- tion which might be used to the detriment of another mem- ber of the Board, and a motion was passed condemning the visit as uncalled for and contrary to a resolution of the Board previously passed. After the minutes of the committee had been confirmed, Captain Willis called attention to the matter. He believed that he was the ex-officio Guardian alluded to. The Visiting Committee of the County Justices at Rainhill Asylum advertised for tenders for the supply of milk to the the Asylum. Two tenders were sent in—one from the late contractor and another from a new man, and the rumour was that the Guardians of that Union had been dissatisfled with the quality of milk supplied to the new Union. He was anxious to prevent any injustice being done to him, and he accordingly visited the House, being perfectly ignorant of any resolution having been passed to the contrary. He simply came to ask a question of the Workhouse Master, whether or not the Guardians bad been dissatisfied with tbe quality of the milk supplied by the man in question. That was the only question be asked; that was the only informa- tion he received, and he thought they would all believe after what he had said that. he did not deliberately set at naught a resolution ef the Beard —After some remarks from Mr. Newsome and others, Mr. Dobell said: After hearing Captain Willis's satisfactory explanation, I move that it be accepted. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. T. Chambers had great pleasure in seconding the motion.—Mr. Tyrer thought it was much ado about nothing, and the motion was then carried. On a sun dial which stands upon the pier at Brighton is inscribed this most hopeful line: "'Tis always morning somewhere in the world." The best receipt for going through life happily is to feel that everybody, no matter how rich or how poor, needs all the kindness he can get from others in this world.

A life without joy passes away unprofitably, sheiding around it only gloom and sorrow. But joy does not mean levity, witty sayings, or repartee: it is habitual serenity. MR. PARNELL ON TES FRANCHISE BlLL.—Speaking at Drogheda, on Tuesday, on the occasion of the freedom of the borough being presented to him, Mr. Parnell, M.P., said by the operation of the Franchise Bill the representatives of the Irish people would be able to stand in a foreign as- sembly as true and unanswerable exponents of the people's will. He advocated increased attention to returning Nation- alists on the Elective Boards. SENTENCE ON A DEFAULTING COLLECTOR.—Mr. Higgin, Q.C,, presided on Monday at the opening of the Salford Hundred Quarter Sessions, held at the Assize Courts, Strangeways.—Alfred Herbert Allen, a collector of rates, was arraigned on the charge of embezzlement, and pleaded guilty. It was stated that the prisoner had embezzled alto- gether £1 332, belonging to the ratepayers of Sal(ord. On behalf of the prisoner it was stated that he bad been tempted to commit the crime through unfortunate speculations in property. The court sentenced him to 15 months' hard labour. LORD SALISBURY IN AN ARBITRATION CASE. An ar- bitration case, in which Lord Salisbury and the Cheshire Lines Committee are the parties concerned, came before Sir Henry Hunt at the Surveyors' Institute, Westminster, on Thursday.. The railway committee have taken 43 acres of land from the manors of West Derby and Little Woolton, and the question to be decided is what interest Lord Salis- bury had in those estates as lord of the manor. His lord- ship, according to the evidence of his surveyor, is entitled to about £750. The committee contend that it 4 is 2d is all that is due to him. The arbitrator reserved his award. ALARMING ACCIDENT TO THE IRISH MAIL.—The Irish mail train from Holyhead ran into an engine outside the railway station at Chester, on Thursday afternoon. The passengers were much shaken, but no one was seriously hurt. A Chester correspondent says that when the train was leavin% Chester station by some mistake it proceeded along the stied line instead of the main line, running into some locomotives standing there. The locomotives were damaged, but the engine of the mail train was only slightly injured, and was able to continue the journey. The (way officials state that only one passenger complained of being shaken.
