Mr. Oreenwood, South wane, presided, course of an address expressed the hope that a separate de- partment of Education would be established with Mr. Mun- della at its head. The expenses of the union last year ex- ceeded the income by £l5O. On Tuesday there was consi- derable discussion regarding proposals to create a fund for supporting members' rights, and to reorganise the Union On what is known as the "Manchester scheme," the sibscrip.." tions being increased and the benefits of membership corres- pondingly enlarged. Both were carried. A rtsolooli condemnatory ef the " merit grant" to schools was carried by a large majority. Deputations from Belgian, Scotch, and Irish teachers' associations were 'received during the day, and congratulatory ad Ireames were delivered. On Wednesday Conference discussed the subject of over•preeinse ip education. Mr. Collide; of Redbill, condemned the system ,of " payment by retiults," and urged that Reboot managers should be allowed 'greater freedom in nreser.tin " backward " pupils for examination. A resolution to that effect was adopted. Tile conference was concluded by a dinner in the evening. On Thurslay a proposition from Bristol that children need not be presented foi..i.smination Unless having made three hntadred attendances raised a long discussion. The resoluOon *again-led, also one supporting Mr. Brodrick's motion in Parliament regarding pensions t') aged teachers.

We append the results:— SAILING MATCE.—For this race seven boats had been en- tered, viz :—Lord Ramsay, W. Swift, captain; Queen, W. Watson, captain; lied Jack. J. Leigh, captain; Chuck Ho, W. Wilding. captain; Primrose, L. Spencer' captain; Deer. foot, T. Skellhorn, captain; and Spud, W. Leigh, captain. The starting point was at Fidler'e Ferry', and the,finishing point at Mandock. The following is the order in which the boats arrived :--1, Spud; 2, Red Jack; 2, Deerfoot ; 4, Primrose. The prizes were £3, £2, il 10s., and 15s. FOUR-OARED Recz.—First prize, £2; second, £l.—There were two crews entered for this race under the captaincies of L. Spencer and T. Skellhern. The first prize was taken by L. Spencer's crew, and the second by that of Skellhorn. PAIR-OARED RACl.—First prize, £1 10s.; second, 10s.; third, 55.-1, S. Spencer, 2, R. Warburton, 3, T. Skein:torn. There were only three entries for this event. 4. Scurmuto Ric.—First prize, Al 10e. ; second, 10s. ; ' third, 51-1, John Skellhorn; 2, Thomas Skellhorn ; 3, S. Spencer. There were five entries for this event.—A stern scull race, for which the prizes were .£1 and 7s. 6d. respec- tively, was won by B. Griffiths, Samuel Leigh being second. 100 YARDS HANDICAP (YOUTHS UNDER 164 First prize, value £1 55.; second, 10s.; third, 71. 6d.—First beat: The whole of the five who were entered for this heat ran, the resul tor the race being that G. G. Titchard, of Warrington, came in first, closely followed by J. L. Peers, of Warring- ton. For the second heat there were four entries, all of whom ran. This heat was warmly contested by R. Tickle and J. Fair, both of Warrington, and ended in a dead heat. The two foremost in each of these heats ran in the final, which was won by J. L. Peers, 5 yards; R. Tickle, scratch, being second; John Fair, 12 yards, third; and G. G. Titchard, 12 yards, fourth. Peers and Tickle were, however, objected to as being over 16 years of age. 120 YARDS HANDICAP.—First prize, value £3; second, £1 10e.; third, lOs —First heat: 1, Thomas Sepbton, Bur- tonwood, 6 yards,l3 4-550 c. Second heat :1, E. McEvoy, Warrington, 3 yards, 14sec. Third heat: I; E. Ellinson, Rushohne, 5 yards, 13 2-ssec. Fourth heat: 1, J. Davies, Manchester, 41 yards, 13 4-ssec. The final heat was a well- contested race, Davies ultimately winning by about two yards. Ellinson was secondoind Sephton third. Tiro MILES BICYCLE Recs.—First prize, value £3 ; second. £1 10s.; third, 10s.—The starters in this race were W. Worsley, Marston, scratch; E. Kenyon, Manchester, 50 , yards; J. B. Webster, Warrington, 20 yards; T. Craddock, I Warrington, 140 yards; Walter Massey, Warrington, 150 yards; W. H. Bataan, Warrington, 200 yards. The ground over which the race took place was not at all suitable for bicycle riding, being so uneven as to jerk the bicycles in al manner which must have been very unpleasant to the riders, and also to prevent any rapid riding. When about half the distance had been traversed Webster, who was pushing forward in a promising manner, fell from his machine and did not again remount. Bellian also fell out at an early part of the race. Towards the close of the race, however, a very close struggle for premier position took place between Massey. Worsley, and Kenyon. Kenyon was to the fore at the commencement of the last lap, but after that both Massey and Worsley pushed past him, and the former won by half a wheel, Kenyon coming in third, about half a dozen yards behind Worsley. QI7ARTIR MILE HANDICAP.—First prize, £3; second, £1 10s; third, 10s. First heat: 1, R. Johnson. Bradford, 12 yards; 2, J. ROVISOO, Warrington, 17 yards; 3, F. Board- man, Warrington, ld yards. Second beat: 1, B. Pierpoint, Warrington, 12 yards; 2, J. Haslam' Manchester, 9 yards; 3, J. Buxton, Warrington, 18 yards. The final heat was won by R. Johnson, who beat J. Haslam by about three yards, Buxton coaling in a very good third. QUARTER MILE HURDLE RACE.—First prize, £3; second, £1 108 ; third 10s. There were five competitors turned out to contest this event. T. Howard, Rusholme, 12 yards, won somewhat easily; F. Tabbott, of Crewe, 8 yards, was second; and R. F. Cooper, of Warrington, 23 yards, was third.

BCllool..—The ladies' Committee of the Royal Society for_ the _Prevention of Qrnelty to Animals has awarded a prize and certificate to Edward Kerry, a scholar of the above school, for.the etellence of his essay on -"Short reasons for kindness to dumb animals.' It was for. wardedlarst rntinfh Iti the Minna competition 'among scholl lays in-elerberitatry school*. • UPARISEI ,CH aeli —Tee decorations af the above churclell for the Easter Day services Were extremelv pretty atid7 effective. A fine collection of flowering and ftilliage plants • was most artistically; arranged in the chancel' by the Ref:l_laq J. Barton. The otiler parts of e the decorative' 'work -wskleiti undertaken hy.the following Wiles and gentlemen, and fleeted the greatest credit on'tthem :—The pulpit and thii?'l, lectern by lira. H. Hosking, Miss F. Husking, and Mr. 6.4:"" Braking; the pillars by Mies L. Poore, Miss E. Eyre, au-I Miss E. Martin; the font by the Misses Gibbs: the text in front of the gallery by the Misses Lewis; and the win- dows by Mrs. Barton. The plants and flowers, both hardy and greenhouse, were kindly lent by Mr. H. Baxter (of The - Towers), Mr. J. Birchal Mr. H. Bromelow, Mr. E Johnson (Lawton Mouse), Mrs. J. Owen, and Mrs. Barton (T6* Vicarage). The musical portions of the services were capit- ally rendered by a full choir. Mr. G. Eyre, of London, presided at the organ on behril of Mr. C. Collins, the organist. VESTRY MEETING.—On Tuesday evening, the annual vestry meeting was held in the National Schools, when the Rey. J. Barton, MA., vicar, preeidod. There were also present Mr Ashton, Mr-E Johnson Brown, Mr E Poore, Mr J Birchen, Mr Leires, Mr T Crowther,Mesers W and Owen, Captain Phillips, Mr G Eyre, Mr E Johnson, and others. Mr oore was re-elected vicar's churchwarden, and Mr .7 Eirchair churOwarden for the congregatiOn. These gentlemen were al tin again appointed lay representatives. The churchwardens' accounts for the year ending Easter, IsB3, were read by 'Mr Poore, accepted, and passed. The customary votes athanke were given to the churchwardens, and to the memlFws of the church choir, for their services during the past 3;,-ar. Mr J Birchall responded for the wardens, and Mr E Johnson-Brown for the choir. A vote of thanks for the energetic and successful exertions of the late Mr.!" Whi,ttaker and Mr W Owen, in connection with the completion and decoration of the interior of the church, was passed unanimously ; and thanks were also given to the • ladies who bad presented articles of church furniture. Thai question of further enlargement of the National School* was disemssd at some length, and it was agreed that a pill of extension to the front. proposed by the Vicar, being thil most ,practicable, and open to the fewest objections, should be carried out.

div.head: WINbFORD.
div.p: WINbFORD.

WHARTON —On Wednesday, there was a soirée held in the Wharton National Schools in aid of the choir. It con- sisted of songs. glees, recitations, NC., given by the choir asd other friends, who turned in to aseist. Though but an ex• periment in its present form, it has proved a success, and will encourage the choir master and conductor, Mr E. Singleton, to try it again. EASTERTIOIL—The day being beautifully fine, Good Friday was very generally observed as a holiday. A goodly rumba availed themselves of a trip to Liverpool from Over and Wharton station, and many went in the afternoon to a cricket match at Minshull. There were tea meetings at Swanlow Chapel (Wesleyan), Over Congregational (which was held in the Marshall Memorial Schools), and the United ' Free Methodist Church, all of which were well attended. In each case there was a meeting in the evening, when recitations, dialogues, and songs, by the Sunday school scholars, Jtc., were given to large and interested audiences. In the churches there was the usual services morning and afternoon. St. Chad's had an evening service, that in ths afternoon being for children. On Sunday, St. Chad's was beautifullT decorated, Mrs. Turner, of. Over Hall, and Mrs. Knowles, -of Darnhall Hall, having kindly given a quantity of hot-house flowers for the purpose. Monday being Bank Holiday, most of the shops were closed. . Tarn SALT TRADIL—The demand during the past month has been much below the average of sever tl years, and as brine has remained abundant (although showing already signs of decrease) the make has much exceeded the demand; the natural consequence has been a lowering of prices, as the list below only too plainly shows :—Common salt is going at Bs, butter ditto 95, Calcutta ditto 8s 63, shuts stoves 10s, handed squares 163, best fishery 12s, second ditto 101,qac- tory, filled with sacks, 26s 81, best Prussian rock 63, pickled lump rock 9s 61, ground rock for agricultural and chemical purposes first quality fine 7s, rough es, rough riddlings for ship salting 6561, soiled agricultural 13s 6d, The salt freights to America run as follows :—Charlestown 3s; Savannah 4s; Wilmington 23 8d ; Baltimore, steam, 41 and 43 61 ; New York, steam rates up to lOs and 10 per cent; Boston 3s, steam; St. John's N.B ,ss; Halifax 7s and 6s 9d; or over 133; Quebec 33 &I and 3s; to Asia, Calcutta very little done at 18s; Baltic, Wyburg Se; Cronstadt 55 on offer; Nerve 75 6d; Revel ss; Newel, Pillan Dantzig 5e on offer but no business done; North Sea, Harlingen 8s ; Nor h Cape 5s 61. The Standard publishes an account of a cockfight for £3OO which took place on Monday in the neighbourhood of the Metropolis. The scene drscribkd was of a most brutalis- ing character, and it is to be hoped that the "main" for a future day arranged at the close will be the means of enabling the police to bring the lawbreakers to justice.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

HUTTON CHIJECH.—The services at this church have been well attended, the sermon in the morniug being preached by the Rev. W. T. Southward, M.A. of Cam- bridge ; and in the evening by the vicar, the Rev. Cane' Penrhyte. The church was very tastefully decotated, the most prominent objects being the carved screen a: d the west font, the former being surmounted by an illuminatioe on a white ground "0 death where is thy sting," "0 grave where is thy victery ;" and below a device is primrores "He is risen, as He said." ST. BANTHOLOVEVI'S Cruuce, Rosv.—The Easter de- corations at this church were of a striking character, great attention having been paid to the chancel, which was wreathed with beautiful and rare cut cowers, the table being ornamented with vases of choice amities, groups of lilies on either side adding .to the effect._ The services
were conducted by the vicar.-the Rev. G. J. Banner and the

musical portion was well rendered by Mr. Hough (organist) and au efficient choir, which included Best's arrangement of the Easter ,hymn Te Deem, Winchester in F., and the anthem " Tuis is the day" (Sewell.) CIICECH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETT.—An en- tertainment was given in the Huyton and Baby Schools on Wednesday evening by the members of the Hnyton Band of Hope brooch of the abive society. The first pert of the proceedings consisted of a tee, with which the young folks were regaled, and was heartily enjoyed. When the tables were cleared, the parents, friends, and general public were , admitted, and Can-in Peorhyn took the chair. An interest- ing programme was then gone through and elicited much ' applause and laughter, especially the dialogue, "The tee- total barber," which was done in character. Prizes were awarded by vote of the audience to the following, for the best rendering of songs and recitations :-1.5.., J. R Webster ; 2nd, Earnest Reichardt, for recitations; A. Nelson, .1. Birchall, and Edgar Birchall. Miss Fieldwick played the accompaniments, and the proceedings closed with presents of sweetmeats to the members. Sr. Micsrases Clnuncer —The Easter vestry meeting was held on Thursday evening in the fluyton and Roby schools, the Rey Canon Penrhya presiding. The accounts presented by the churchwardens showed total receipts £482 13s 141, the expenditure £478 6s up, leaving a balance in hand of £4 7s Oil. The accounts were passed unani- mously. The Vicar regretted that his warden, Mr W Busby, could not again stand, so he would appoint the parishioners' choice of last year, Mr W H Crook. Mr Thomas Glover, on the nomination 'of Mr Busby, seconded by Mr E B Williams, was elected peoples' warden; and the following gentlemen were elected sidesmen :—C Cooper. J Fountain, T Evans, and E C Lewenton; auditors, F T Team and E Airey. The Vicar produced and read the charities accounts, 1 of which there are four, namely :—The Birch charity £590 'consols, Church lands at West Derby realising about £l2, the Webster dole, and the recently addediWillink charity. He took the present opportunity of informing the parish that it was the wish of the son of Mr Willink that he should have permission to place a stained glass window, in memory of his father (the donor of the above charity), in the church. He need hardly say he cordially weleomed the proposal. Attention was called by Mr Cooper to the dilapidated condition of the new addition to the church yard. The warden, Mr lithely, said he had ben in commu- nication with Mr Hale, Lord Derby's agent, and the reply he received was that they would plant the new portion with shrubs as had been promised when the church yard was re-bnilt. The Vicar said there was another difficulty, the new portion was not consecrated, and it was not likely to be, so a division or boundary would have to be s own. A lively discussion took place on the questiqn of appropriated seats, initiated by Mr Williams, who said he bad to be in churn 10 or 15 minutes before service cons- menced to secure an un-appropriated seat for his family, whilst through the service the appropriated seats, especially in the evening, were not half filled, He was supported in his statement by Mr Newsy and Mr Moss. The wardens and Vicar explained that all the seats were free when the service had commenced; bat the explanation did not satisfy Mr Williams, who charged the wardens with neglect of duty in not attending to strangers. This was b-ing warmly denied by Mr Crook, when Messrs Lerenton and Cooper in- terposed, and a vote of thanks was eventually passed to the retiiing officers, and else to the chairman. A MAD BLACESMITH.—A blacksmith, named Thomas Rigby, of Raehton, near Leek, was on Thursday conveyed to the Stafford Lunatic Asylum. A week or two ago he demolished his sinitby and uprooted numbers of trees and planted there again root upwards. Two magistrates on Wednesday had an interview with him, and signed an order for his removal. LIBERAL MEETING AT FAILSWORTH —Mr. W. B. Briggs was present on Thursday evening at a Liberal meeting at Faiisworth, and delivered a speech in support of a resolution which was passed—expressing confidence in the Govern-- ment, satisfaction at the majority by which the second. ' reading of the Franchise Bill was carried, and asking for the frupoort of Liberal members of Parliammit in the passing of the measure through Committee. TILE FENIAN ARRESTS.—The Government have deter- mined to take up the prosecution of the dynamiter Daly, arrested at Birkenhead. In addition to making this an- nouncement, particulars have been sushi by solicitors of the Treasury as to the preliminary tnagieterial proceedings at Liverpool police-court. Daly has had an interview with his solicitor, Mr. Quelch, and admits only a slight anqulintance withr fi qn teEpgt i'°l o visits t o E fn'i ringiann,grn ha, as a fellow-lodger. As to his, as alleged by Mrs. Egan, he declares they are purely imaginative. TSB ROME SECRETARY AT DEREY.—Sir WM. HarEOurt speaking to his constituents at Derby on Wednesday even-• ing, entered on a somewhat lengthy criticism of the atti- tude aissumed by the Opposition during the past session. Kw characterised the Oevernrcent majority as a conquest rather than a 'victory, and maintained that the Tories, un- able to meet the Franchise Bill in open tight, had resorted , to all sorts of unusual tactica to delay and obstruct the Bill. He accused the Opposition of having no intelligible policy of its own, and asserted that that of the Government, which proposed to enfranchise two millions of people, was backed by the popular voice. He refused to believe, until he knew it. .that the House of Lords would, at Lord Salisbury's bid- ding, throw out the Bill; and referring to the desire of the leader of the Tory peers to have a dissolution, said the Go- i vernment would dissolve in their own time and not Lord satisbury,s, He defended the Egyptian policy of the Go- vernment, and with regard to tieneral Goidon, said the latest news from him did not inilicete that he considered. himself in any danger. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1884.

LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has studied and acted upon the philosophy of the Yankee who said—" Great is cheek." He is cheek incarnate—not, let it be understood, in ven- turing to assail Birmingham as the strong- hold of Liberalism, but in the brazen way in which he turns facts topsy-turvy in order to present the semb.ance of a case against the Government, and, more particularly, that pet object of his a'version—the Radical party. He knows what he is about—in his way; he is trying the role which BaNjAtang DISRAELI essayed in his younger days. He evidently believes the Tory party is lamentably short of talent, and "go," and if 'ne can show that he possesses in some degree both these qualities, he is convinced that it will more quickly bring him to the front than any display of sterling merit. It is true that he has no new theory to propound; he has no new depar- ture to propose in the way of policy; he is not possessed of a genius, like his prototype, for the adornment of generalities; but he has no scruples and plenty of cheek, and, however much he may disgust Conservatives of tbe better class, it can hardly be denied that he is making headway with the rank and file of the Tory party. He lays himself out for those who don't read and who don't th ink, and it thus happens that the more extrava- gant he is, and the further he gets from the fact, and the louder they cheer. His speech is therefore of sonie interest as showing how far the force of folly in these latter 'days may go, and this must be our apology for such attention as we may give it. What a burlesque of political history it is to hear of the Tory party as initiating the Factory Acts It is notorious that in the various divisions on measures relating to factory legislation there was the most curious cross-voting—the ques- tion never at any time being regarded as a party one. And how delightfully gullible LORD RANDOLPH must have thought his audience when they swallowed his reference to what the Tories have done in the way of better defined relations between the employer and the working man. It would have gone down, we do not doubt, if he had said the Employers' Liability Act was carried by the , Conservative party. But stay, their particu- lar virtue is "the faithful development of the Education Act," an act passed when ,Mr. GLADSTONE was last in office—an act which the Tories at the time tried to mutilate—an act which Tories seek to burke to-day. where they have the upper hand, in almost every town in England and Wales. Lord RAN- DOLPH tries to be merry over the Liberal watch-cry—" Peace, Retrenchment, and Re-

I form " ; but he makes nothing of it. As to peace, he says the Radicals "allowed the Government during the whole of tl?e protracted session to carry on warlike operations in Afghanistan; " but he doesn't tell the Tories that the "warlike operations" were those which were actually in progress when the Government came into power; nor does he say that the Govern- ment, as speedily as was consistent with safety, brought peace to Afghanistan and India, completely feversing, as the Con- servatives themselves confessed, the disas- trous policy of their predecessors. A more absurd reference could not be made; but he acts on the principle that it is as well to "go the •whole hog" whilst you are at it, and so he turns next to the policy of the Government on the oocasion of the revolt of the Boers of South Africa He blames the Radicals that they permitted the Government to suppress that revolt by force of arms, impudently oblivious of the fact that the Tory party at the time were incessant in their denunciation of Mr. GLADSTONE for listening to the peace party and finally mak- ing reasonable terms with the Boers, instead of butchering them to make a British holi- day And so with Egypt--.' the Radical party have not only not censured, but they have connived at and consented to the most sanguinary and the most fruttless military operations which history can recall." This is a pretty statement to come from a politician identified with the party that by means of the Dual Control sowed the wind .hat others might reap the whirlwind. He knows per- fectly well that if the present Government had hesitated to keep faith with the. KHEDIVE by putting down ARABI PASHA, the Tory party would have been the first to assert that the flag of England was being trailed in the mire. And why does he assume that the Radicals should attack the Government for doing the right thing? It is no part of their creed to break faith in national engagements, however much they may question the wisdom of certain undertakings, or to act as though it were never justifiable to draw the sword. Lord RANDOLPH'S Radical is very much akin to his lordship; he is, politically speaking, a man of straw. Coming to the question of " Retrenehmet,t," we find the same sort of juggle with words. There is the "lie which is half a truth," and which, as we are told on good authority, is "ever the blackest of lies." Quo- ting figures as to national expenditure, Lord RANDOLPH tries to make it appear that the Liberals are spendthrifts compared with the Tories, but he does not say how Much of the Liberal expenditure which he deals with has gone towards paying Tory debts. Has he quite forgotten the TEN MILLIONS which the Tories were to the bad when they went out of (Alice, and which the Liberals have had to meet? Taking Mr. GLansioNE as an authority—and we think he is good yet against this random representative of the CHURCHILLS—ne find that, comparing the first three years of office of the present and the late Administration, the Liberal Govern- ment stand 18 millions to the good as against their predecessors, having amongst other things paid off no less than iz millions more of war debt than was paid during the first three years of the BEACONSFIELD Ministry. Roundly speaking, the f ones added :Ten Millions per year to the national expenditure during their last control of the purse strings— the total running up from £75 000,000 to £85.000,000, and yet, including the Two Millions of loan to India which has since been tightly converted into a war sub- sidy, they were Ten Millions 'behind nothing" when an indignant nation sent them to the right-about When Lord RANDOLPEI points to the high expenditure of Mr. GLADSToNE'S Government—caused in so large a degree by the deficits and bad management of BEACONS- , FIELD and Co --/!e occupies a somewhat similar position to that of the associate of 3 spendthrift who should " cheek " the " guy'ner " for spending so much money lo clearing his son's estate. As to Reform, well, there is the Irish Land Act, the Arrears Bill, the Burials Bill, to say nothing of changes in Patents, Bankruptcy, and Game Laws, and last, but not least "the humbugging Franchise Bill." But the wise man of Wood- stock has a way of his own as to these things; he closes his eyes to them, and then when they are no longer visible to him he is ready to swear they are non-existant. This may do for some "sleepy hollow" of a pocket borough, but it will not do for wide-awake, go-ahead Birmingham.

The Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS, of St. John's 'Church, Earlestown, has brought, to borrow a Lancashire phrase, "his pigs to a bonny market." He has been appointed to minister to the people of the parish —to preach and practice goodwill amongst men—and he has done it so effectually that he has got the will of almost everybody in his parish. He has foolishly raised, as so many of the clergy of the Church of England have done, the question of authority, and would appear to be ready now to sacrifice everything, except " his living," to he gratification of an ill regulated imperious self-will. The origin of this dispute between parson and people is a " trifle light as air," but from want of tact and common sense, to say nothing of Christianity, the Vicar hash fostered the quarrel until the " scenes " at St. John's have come to rival those of a " sensation " theatre. Mr. MAT- THEWS has, in his way, discharged the organist because the organist would not take upon himself to discharge a member of the choir who was not even to be heard in defence as to a trifling charge which was brought against him. The p= ople's warden and sidesmen would not be party to proceed- ings which they regarded as tyrannical ; the organist, Mr. Durman, had been appointed at a vestry meeting, and they bade him keep his place. The result has been that on two Sundays there have been two organists, th. Vicar's man and the people's man, the struggle culminating on Sunday in Mr. Dur- man, backed by the church officials, being left in possession, while the Vicar beat a re- treat from the church amid a storm of hooting, making "confusion worse Con- founded" by the announcement that there would be no service there that day. The people, however, had in the evening a sort of service in the open air, and next night, being that of the annual Vestry Meet- ing, they' had it out " with their Vicd.r. We commend the lengthy report we have given of these proceedings to the attention of our Church-going readers, and put it to them whether they do not think the ,emedy fcir such unseemly squabbling is not, as suggested by a local Churchman, in Dises.aulishment: It is no wonder that parishioneis e galled into saying irritating things when they are teminded by their spiritual pastor and master that, fume and fret as they may under tir. yoke, he is "there for lift." They may toil and spin and gather gear for the Church ; an, cl then have the door locked upon them tn. e moment they want to exercise' a reasonable

iceinChurch affairs. Vhe,thousand souls fr the parishioners are AS nothing to the ".corporation sole" in the shape of a Vicar who has a living "'for life." It is lot always. of course. that the parish priest ahuses his opportunity, but when he does, lie in this ,instance, it becomes evident that it la the system which is really bad, and that a can only be remedied by setting the Church free. With a free Church:in a free State, such men as Mr Marrinws would not "for 111:e " be permitted to "play such fantastics kicks before high heaven as make the angels weep." They would be justly set aside as unsuitable for the high office to which they hitVo been called.

WTHHIES PARISH CHLIRCE.—We understand that the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, has made arrange- ments for two coratee to aid him ia the multifarious labours of his parish when Trinity term commences. One of the gentlemen possesses a title, and both are gentlemen of ability. and energy, but their names have not yet been made public. A FIRE AT WESTON,—On Wednesday morning at Weston Point, a wood shippon belonging to Mr. Samuel Bennett, grocer, was burnt to the ground and two pigs which it contained were killed, but were in such a condition as to permit them being used for human food. The shed which adjoined the shop had a tarred roof, and it is supposed that a spark fronl.a neighbouring chimney had alighted upon it and commenced the conflagration. The damage is estimated at £lO, the structure being insured in the Lancashire Assu- rance Company for that amount. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORIL—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the following persons were each fined 6d, and costs 4s 6d, for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—James Prescott, William Edwardson, William Schumann, Ann Evans, John Hughes, George Whitley, James Carr Mary McDonald, James Fal- low, Michael Grennan, Charles McKenna. James Tierney, John Tracey, James Hynan, Joseph Hickey, Dennis Malone, John Shanley. and John Power (two cases). Mr. G. H. Denby prosecuted on behalf of the School Board, and the cases were proved by attendance officers, Messrs. Davies, Joyneon, and Rowe. A. Row AT THE BLUR BALL INN, RUNCORN.—On Thurs- day, at Runcorn Police Court, James Crompton, A strong- looking yeung f/dlow, WAS charged with assaulting Robert Dwyer, the landlord of the Blue Ball Inn, Fryer-street. Accompanied by several young men, the prisoner entered the Blue Ball on Monday and asked to be supplied with liquor. The landlord supplied the prisoner's companions, but as he was under the influence of liquor he declined to serve himoind asked him to leave the premises. He refused, and the landlord placed his hand on his shoulder with the intention of enforcing his request, when the mi. 'toner struck him, and seizing his finger between his teeth bit it severely.—A fine of 20s and costs was imposed and

He pointed out Ith*Tt was the usual practice to drive cattle from Stanley -r4et Widnes atone the hialtway, but the defendant, flir°ol,...leing that the cow in question was foot-sore, departed niu"' the usual course and sent the animals he had pur- n o • -Bed bY t-ai t Ditton This showed that he was nzio__ • . to avoid anything in the nature of cruelty. The own bad cost the defendant £27 10s and it was to his ani";n'nterttt not to illtreat the beast as the flesh of the al Would be iniared,...--The Bench did not consider the elle, a I, in 'id one and indicted a penalty of Is, and costs 12s, "cl.l adee, •

defendant pleaded guilty.—P.C. Emmons stnied-that at half- past three on Saturday afternoon he was sent for to a house In Penketh-lane. On arriving there he saw a woman named Wilson, who said she liad been badly beaten,b the prisoner He could see that ehe had. On entering the louse he found. the defendant lying on a sofa, and asked him what he had done. The defendant replied that it was for spite, and he would "do six months for the woman." Spencer, who was in the house, spoke to the defendant, who immediately inenpad up and beat her aavagely about the head. The wit- ness succeeded in throwing him to the ground and placing the "snaps" upon him. He took from him the large pieeo of wood produced, which be was using as a weapon, the girt Spencer having seized a poker to defend hereelf.—The woman Wilson was called to give evidence, and she entered the witness box in a beastly state of drunkenness.—Super- intendant Williamson c tiled the attention of their worships to the matter, and they expressed their astonishment at her state. She WAS removed and the prosecutrix Spencer took her place, but she was found to be in an even worse state of intoxication, and unable to utter a word intelligibly. She was taken from the court. a WAS stated that the young women were catainly not more than 20 years of age, and that the prisoner had been:heir companion for the past five weeks.—Mr. Rigby said that when two girls. wt.° wore little more than children, appeared before the court in a positive state of drunkenness, it was a state of affairs that called for the interfermce of some authority.—Superinten- dent Williamson pointed out to the Bench that the polite bad no power to interfere with the cases. Proceedings for the suppression of such houses as those where these girls were harboured rested with the ratepayers, who would have to lay an information, and there was a natural hesitation on the part of people engaged in business to come forward and give evidence.—r. Rie)y said if the police had trouble in putting iu motion the necessary machinery, he thought it was a case for the Improvement Commissioners if it was one of their funetions.—Strperintendent Williamson said un- fortunately these houses were in respectable parts of the town, and 'annoyed a respectable class of the community.-- Mr. Rigby observed that this was a most flagrant case. Ile girls not only carried on their orgies in the houses, hut they were continued in that court, and the intervention of ' eome authority Was imperative. If there WAR a difficulty on the part of the rolice, the Commissioners might consider it 1 their duty to interfere. There were all the elements of a conviction in tide case, and he did not think it could be too emphatically stated that such a state if affairs was a etcandal to the town.—The Bench then fined the defendant 20s and ems, or in default a month's bard labour.--We understand the young women will be summoned to appear at the next court day.

div.p: 'IRE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1884.

ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—At the works of Messrs. Vickers and Sou, Widnes, on Wednesday, a boy named John Walker, of Halebauk, had his leg broken. He was playing with a coil of wire, when it fell upon him and broke his ' right leg. He was taken to the hospital, where he is being lattended by Dr. McDonnell. WIDNES CHURCH OF ENOLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. —Tnere was a moderate attendance at the weekly meeting of the Widnes branch of the Church of England Temper- ance Society on Thursday, when the Vicar presided and delivered an address. Mr. Foley also spoke. Au entertain- ment of songs and readings was given by Miss Show, Messrs. White, Morgan, Moss, and Atherton. THE 11111301 C PUPIL TRACHEA AT WIWI/C.a.—MY' hetOiC act Of Thomas Phillips, son of Mr. John Phillips, builder and contractor, Gladstone-street, Widnes, has received sui,- able recognition. It will be remembered that Phillips rescued a little boy from drowning in a pool of water at Halton View, and the teachers and scholars of the Warring- ton-road Board Schools, where Phillips is a teacher, have presented him with a silver lever watch as a token of their admiration of his bravery. The parents of the rescued boy testified their gratitude by subscribing to the testi- monial. A Sitrarrut. Touts LOCAL BOARD Etscriox.—At Widnes , Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Shanahan, a strong- looking fellow, was summoned for threatening to assault James Gaghan, a grey-haired old man.—The complainant stated that on the sth inst. he was standing at the door of his own house when the defendant came np, and after cursing him said, " You traitor Carey, your days are num- bered. You have not long to live." The complainant ex. plainsid that this conduct arose because he declined to Can- vass for the candidate Quinn, and he did so for the Owners' and Occupiers' Association. There had been great animosity shown against him by the defendant since the election. —After hearing the evidence on both sides the Bench dis- missed the ease. _ _ _ .

A WIDNES Prinucam FlNED.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. J. C. Gamble, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, William Wilkinson Lewis, keeper of the Bridge Inn, Church-street, Widnes, was summoned to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness to take place on his premises. and also a charge of selling intoxicating liquor to a drunken person.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defendant.—Ser- geant Robinson deposed that at a quarter to eight o'clock on Thursday night, the 3rd inst., he visited the defendant's house in company with P.C. Laing. In the vaults he found a man named John Harris sitting asleep with his head lean- ing upon his breast. As be went towards Harris the bar- maid shouted Waken him up," and be (witness) replied, "If I have anything to do with tbis man I shall very likely lock him up." The barmaid and the landlady immediately roused him up, and he then saw that Harris was drunk. On the table in front of Harris was a pint bottle full of beer; and the barmaid said it WAS a pint of beer which she would not allow him to have in a pint pot, and she placed it in a bottle. Harris seized the bottle and walked out of the house with it. On getting into the open air, however, Harris could scarcely walk, and the constables " aaw him home." —P.C. Laing confirmed this evidence.—Mr. Swift addressed the Bench at some length, pointing out that the defendant had managed the house respectably for four years. He observed that owing to two magistrates mot being present at the last sessions the cask was adjourned, and he could confidently state that it had already Cost the defendantmore than the highest penalty that could be inflicted under the Act. Harris, he was told, had been " doing " three months in gaol, and this seemed to have made him rather weak, and affected his capacity for drinking beer. At one o'ciock on the day in question he entered the Bridge Inn, which was in charge of Mrs. Lewis and the barmaid; the defendant I being away on business. Harris having no money sat in the place quietly reading the newspaper, but during the ' aftemooo be wits Owed to several dritike, lie was served • I with a pint of beer to carry away, paid •by a man named ' Spencer, but, becoming drowsy, he fell asleep.—Mrs. Lewis was called, and stated that Harris was not drunk. It was pointed out to her by Superintendent Barker that he fell against a wall, and had to be assisted home by the police. She replied that that WAS his way of walking.— Mary Emma Aspinall, barmaid, said Harris was not drunk when the police arrived at the house. The beer in the bottle was what had been left by his mates.—George Corns, John Birchall also stated Harris was not drunk, but another wit- ness, Alfred Brassington, admitted in cross-examination that Harris was scarcely sober.— Elie Bench dismissed the sum- mons of supplying drink, and fined the defendant 20s and costs 18s for permitting drunkenness--Harris, who did not appear, was fined lOs and costs.
VESTRY MEE riNGs. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCII•

The Easter Vestry meeting in connection with Runcorn Parish Church was held on Monday morning, under the presidency of the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were present the Rev. R. Edwards, Messrs. W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, J. Brundrit, J.P., J. K. Digges, E. Marwoctl, G. Suintnei field, and W. Sutton (clerk). The churchwardens' accounts showed that the receipts from all sources, including the balance from last year, amounted to £lB7 7s 21, while the expenses were £179 lie 9d, leaving a balance in the bands of the churchwardens of £7 15s sd. The total collec- tions for the year for all purposes amounted to £262 18s. —The accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. J. K. Di4Ats, seconded by Mr. Briscoe.—The Chairman said Mr. Brundrit had, at his earnest solicitation, consented to be his churchwarden for another year. Re was sure that anybody who saw the way in which the services were conducted, and the provision made "for all persons, and the consideration shown by the officials, would greet this decision with satis- faiation.—On the motion of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by Mr. Digges, Mr. S. Crosby was re-elected "outer warden." Mr. Briscoe was re-elected sideman on the motion of Mr. Sutton, seconded by Rev. R. Edwards, Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Whittaker were appointed the lay representatives at the ruri-decanal conference. The ringers were engaged for the next year at a salary of £B, with permission to collect gratuities as heretofore.—On the motion of Mr. Briscoe, a vote of thanks was passed to the choir for their services during the past year, and on the motion of Mr. Digges a similar compliment was paid to the chairman for presiding.

income bad been £B6 17s 4d, while the expenditure wal £3 os 11d, leaving a balance of £3 13s ad in the hands of Lim wardens.—The accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. Fisher.--On the proposition of Mr. Lea. seconded by Mr. Yates, the thanks of the vestry were accorded to Mr. Annett for his decorations to the chancel and for his ser- vices as choirmaster.
NEW CEIURCH FOR RUNCORN.-LAYING THE CORNER STONE.
The first dublic demonstration la connection with the new

church of St. Michael and All Angels lock place on Thurs- day afternoon, when the corner Atone was bid by Major J. Cavendish Orred, of Meidwell Rail, in the presence of a large assembly. The erectiou of the edifice is rendered necessary by the settlement of a large population ou the south bide of the Brideewater Cute', the educational and spiritual neede of which have been lo eons extent met by the estetnishment there of the Newtown Mission. A school chapel wee opened in 1866; cod since that time it hes been used aa a public elementary echeol on week deys with an average attendance of about 110 children, and oa toe Lord's ' Day as a Sunday school, attended by upwards of 130 scholars, while divine service Was performed morning and evening. Several years ago the church authorities deemed It advisable that a permanent church should be established in the neighbourhood, and their plans received a welcome and decided impetus by the presentation of an eligible and valuable site in Greenway-road. The designs for a church capable of accommodating 600 worshippers were obtained, the estimated cost of the erection, exclusive of the transept, the tower and the chancel,being £3,000. Earnest and energetic steps were taken for raising the requisite sum, and a mons- ter bazaar in midsummer of last year realised upwards of £l,lOO, while subscriptions amounting to about £1,400 were promised, and ere this have doubtless been collected. Late in the autumn the builders commenced preparations for the erection of the edifice, which, when completed, will consist of a nave 86 feet by 27 feet; north and south aislee, each 77 feet by 13 feet; an apsidal chancel 41 feet by 25 feet; a baptistry 10 feet by 10 feet; a choir vestry 18 feet by 12 feet; a clergy vestry, with separate entrance and conveni- ences attached, 12 feet 6 inches by 12 feet; an organ chamber, formed in the square of the tower, which will stand in the south Bide of the chancel. with arches opening into the chancel and south aisle. The entrances will be through porches at the south-west corner of the building and at the north-east side, folding doors for the prevention of draughts being fixed. An exit door will also be placed on the Greenway-road side. The church is designed in the early &notated style of Gothic architecture, with traceried and mullioned windows in the aisles and clerestory and east and west ends of the church, the treatment being exceed- ingly delicate and beautiful. The clerestory is to be supported on an arcade of twelve pointed stone arches, which are in their turn supported by octagonal and circular shafts with richly moulded beees, and carved end moulded capitals, which form a handsome and striking feature of the interior. Ihe tower, which will occupy p south easterly positien, will be 18 feet square. flanked with buttresses ef massive proportions, and will rise te a height of 60 feet above the groued. The spire octagonal form will rise to a heigbt of 86 feet above the square of the tower, which makes a total height of 146 feet above the ground level The whole of the walls are to be of Runcarn red sandstone, faced with the same stone in regular courses. The wood work of the roof, benches, dm, is to be of best selected pitch pine varnished. The feet of all the principals are to be supported on carved red sand- stone corbles. The ceiling of the chancel is to be of wrought matched, and that of the aisle and nave to be iolsstered. The floors are to be of wood blocks, laid in herring bone patterns on asphalte. This system has the! effect of reducing the loud echoing sound so frequently I heard in churches. The vestries are to be divided by a groined partition, which can on emergencies be folded back to throw the room into one. The , roofs are to be covered with IVestmoreland green slates, the ornamental ridges to be 9f terracotta. As previously stated the walls are to be finished in plaster internally, and to be painted in a light shade of colour. The glazing is to be of rolled, toned, cathedral glass in geometric dead patterns. The contras; entered into between the Building Committee (whieli Consists of Sir Richard Brooke, But., Rev. Canon Barclay, Messrs. J. Brundrit, S. B. Chadwick, E. A. Chorton, C. W. Hezlenurst, F. A. Lake, M. Steele, W. Whittaker, C. Wigg, and G L. Wigg) and Mr. Richard Beckett, of Hartford, the builder, is for the nave, aisles, and porches alone, but it is confidently expected that orders will shortly be given for the ckancel, tower, and spire. The site of the church occupies the whole of the space between Greenway-road, Fox-street, Eaton-street, and Shaw-street. The corner of Shaw-street is to be rounded off in a large sweep to allow of a geed approach to the station, and the street is- also to be widened a feet at the lower end of the site. Mr. H. Coward, of Runcern, is clerk to the works, and the edifice is being erected front the designs and under the superintendence of Messrs. T. D. Berry and Son, architects, of Liverpool. Considerable pro- gress has been made with the structure, the foundations having been laid, and the outer walls are several feet from the ground. For the convenience of those taking part in the ceremony on Thursday, a platform had been improvised, and from prominent positions about the site flags fluttered in the sunlight. The R -v. Canon Barclay, MA., occupied the chief position on the nlatfortn, on his left being Ledy Brooke,eMiss Brooke. and Mtjor Orred. The clergy were represented by the Revs. J. J. Bryant, W. Preston, J. Mid- den, F. M. Arinson, R. Ed wards (curate in charge of New- town Mission), H. B. Blogg (Frodshain), E. Mersden (Aston), J. Lockwood (Halton), Lyon Bennett, and E. A. Begot. Amongst those present were Drs. McDougall, Steele, Carruthers, Lieutenant• Colonel Ashton and Mrs. Ashton, Messrs. C. Wigg, J. Brundrit, J.P., R. M. Brooke, .1 P., A. thomas, IP., F. A Lake, A. Buck, W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, W. Shaw, J. F. Claudet, R. Lea, M. Barker, dic. Grouped round the front of the platform were the chorister:: tom the Parish Church and the scholars of the Newtown Mission, who had walked in processional order from the schoolroom. The Rev. Canon Barclay commenced the ceremony with a short prayer, and then was sung the Psalm " 0 how amiable are Thy dwellings. thou Lord of Hosts," the choir being conducted by Mr. J. J. Johnson, organist at the Parish Church. Other devotional exercises followed, after which Lady Brooke, in the name of the stallholders at the late bizaar, presented a handsome silver trowel to Major Orred, ac- companying the gift with a few suitable remarks. The trowel, which was beeutifully chased with the Cenen- dish crest, a hare with three barley-corns in its mouth and other designs, bore the following inscription, " Pre- sented to Major John Cavendish Orred on the occasion of laviog the foundation stone of St. Michael and All Aneels, Runcorn, by the stall-holders of the bazaar held to raise funds for this church, April 17tn, 1884." With the assist- ance or the architect and builders, Major Orred then placed the stone in its position, saying "In the faith of Jesus Christ, and in honour of St. Michael and all angels we place this corner stone in the name of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost." Beneath the stone was placed a bottle containing the Liverpool llferoury for that day and the coins of the realm. The ins Tiption on the stone was as follows;—" An GLORIAM DE' ET IN HONORER S. MICHAELIS ET MOULIN ANGELORIIN HIINC LAPIDEM ANGI7LAREM POSDIT J. C. OREED, ARELIGER, XVII. DIE APRIL'S, 1884."

Major Orred, in a short address, expressed his very great pleasure and satisfaction in having been permitted, through God's mercy and by their kindness, to perform this most solemn and interesting ceremony they had just seen taken place, the first he had had the oppertunity of assisting at. He begged to thank the ladies who had held Btalls, to whom so much of the success of the baz ear was due. He earnestly trusted that when this beautiful building wee, by the blessing of God, completed, it migh,t form a haven of rest to many a poor weary soul. In these days of open and avowed atheism, and when so many clever but misguided individuals tried to argue themselves almost out of their own existence, and seemed to find it impossible to accept any- thing in simple faith, or which they could not prove by hard and fast mathematical rules, he as a small landowner in the County of Chester felt it a peculiar privilege to have been enabled to give a site for a building entirely devoted to God's services and to the spintual needs of 4 000 emits on on this site of the bridge. He WAS , bound to thank their kind friend and good vicar Canon Barclay, following him to dedicate this church to St. Michael and All Angels— " God's soldiers "—having had the honour of serving in the army of a good, thorongh earthly sovereign and it bring possible for him to make a free gift of the site, he trusted the title might not be deemed inappropriate. This beaotiful memenito so kindly presented to him by Lady Brooke on behalf of the stall-holders' should always be t-easured and paced by the side of three others given to his father when he laid the foundation stones of St. Paul's Chtplch, Tranrnere, Church of England Schools at Tranmere, I and Church of England Schools at Weston, the latter 21 years ago, in the hope that his children, should they be I spared and have the opportEnity, migot, on seeing them, be ' urged to do what in their power lay towards promoting our Christian religion and doing good to those around them. In con- clusion, he asked for their kind offerings towards the build- in fund, begging them all to remember that the widow's inite was quite as acceptable in the eyes of our Blessed Redeemer as tbe offerings of the rich and great. He ex- pressed a hope that before the completion of their present contract the committee would be in a position to proceed with the chancel and that toe nave and chancel might be opened together. The "offerings" placed on the stone amounted to - £57 7s 3d, in this being included £2O which the children at the mission had collected by means of cards dnring the past month. After singing and prayer the proceedings con- cluded. In the evening a special service was held in the Parish Church, but there was only a moderate attend ince. The prayers were read by the Rev. C tun Barclay and the Rev. R. Edwards, the Rev. T. M. Armson reading the first lesson and the Rev. J. J. Bryant the second. The Very Rev. Dean of Chester preached an oppropriate sermon. The anthem, " floe Lord is King," was rendered by the choir daring the evening, Mr. J. J. Johnsen being the organist. A collection was made on behalf of the building fund.
Mr. Parnell, preslding ite meeting of the National League in Dublin on Wednbsday, said the emcees of the organisation was evidenced by the flow of funds and the nurnber of branches.

The third trial. of the Westmeath murder conspiracy case, fixed to commence in Dublin, on'Thursday, has ben again PostPoned in consequence of the procurement At the last moment of additional evideece on the part of the Crown. Mr. Joseph Arch, addrersing an agricultural labourers' gathering at Evenly. fkorthampton, on Thursday, said that when they obtained the vote they !Mould urge the abolition of the law of settlament and the tiD _r action at a Med/51UP for the compulsory cultivation of land capable of producing food. Thomas Roe, of Lower Trinity -street, BirminL;ham, was returring from Pour Oaks Park Races, when, on alighting from a train before it had stopped. he Flipped between the platform and the carriage. He was terribly craebed, and I-wee conveyed to the General Hospital, where he died yester- day morning.

div.head: FARNWORTH PARISH CHTIRCH.
div.p: FARNWORTH PARISH CHTIRCH.

The annual meeting of parishioners was held in the chan- cel of the church, on Monday evening, the Rev. G. Bond, vicar, in the chair. There were also present :—Captain H. Bruoner, Messrs. R. Kidd, W. A. Watts, H. Lea, M. Taylor, John R. Whalley, J. Lea, J. W. Davies, Hanckle, and J. Hunter.—The minutes of last meeting were read and con- &med.—Captain Brunner submitted the churehwardens' accounts. At the beginning of the year there was a balance in hand of £8 18e, and the amount received by collections on accouot of church expenses and church repairs was D 441 16s 10d. In addition there had been received small some which brought the receipts to £l9 21 7d. The expenditure, bad been £13(3 Es 110, being 12s 8d less than last year.— The Chairman observed that considering that a collection was made at each service, they could not expect much for special services, but he hoped next year would be better in that respect. lie trusted they would be aisle to raise some- thing towards the restoration of the church, the seats in which were very uocomfortable.—Theacoounts were passed, on the motion of Mr. M. Taylor, seem:Hied by Mr. Watts.— The Chairman announced that their kind Rad •dear friend and useful churchwarden, Mr. Brunner, had resigned, and in . eulogistic terms he proposed that a hearty vote of thanks I be tendered to him for his past e-rvices.—Mr. Kidd seconded the motion, which was cirried.—A similar compliment was also paid the other churchwardens, on the proposition ,of Mr. Davies, seconded by Mr. Whalley.—Captain Brunner suitably replied on their behalf, and explained that he had resigned because he thought the office of okurchwarden ought not to be held continuous by any one .person. A change was desirable from time to thne.—The Chairman then appointed Mr. Peter Longton as his warden, represent. log the Widnes township in the pariah. The following churchwardens were also appointed :—Bold, J. R. Whalley; Cuerdley, M. Taylor; Cronton, W. B. Longton. The Chairman bserved that Mr. Albert Gray had introduced into Parliament a Bill for the purpose of causing parish churches to be governed by a council elected annually by the ratepayers who would have votes whether they were Churchmen, Roman Catholics, or Dissenters. From what the Chancellor of the 'Diocese said at a Ruri-Decanal Con- ference, a short time ago, be took it that if they elected a council fairly representative of the dietrict to eensult with the clergyman on church matters to represent grievances, and to take-care no anomalies were permitted, they would save the erpense and the turmoil of an election by the popular vote. They had such a council in St. Mary's parish, • Widnes, and it worked well. This council would relieve him of financial and other matters, and he would have more leisure to attend to the spiritual necessities of the parish- ioners. He suggested-that the following gentlemen should act as sideemen and constitute the council :—Drs.:Looth and Cooper; Messrs. H. Brunner, J. Brock, Hanckell, J. W. Warning, J. Glover (Cronton), R. Kidd, T. Shuttleworth, Jun., W S. Pritchard, C. E. Barlow, 1. Lea, T. -.Baker, J. Whitfield, J. Newton, W. A. Watts, J. W. Davies, H. Lea, Bul long h, and J..lmi.on.—The Chairman's suggestion was adopted, on the proposition of Mr. Hauckle, seconded by Mr. H. Brunner, both of whom considered the suggestion a good one.—trotes of thanks were accorded to Mr. W. A. Watts for hie services as choirmaster, and to the chairman for presiding. Mr. Bench's suggested that the Widnes Local Board should throw open Pex Hill as a secreation ground, but no definite reeolution was pl-iced before the meeting. Before the meeting concluded, the Chairman said it had been stated that .the services at the church were b•icorning almost too ornate, but he asked them to remember that if they had to hold their own against other parishes, they must make their services as popular as possible, and live up to the standard of the day. If other people had good aer- vices they must have them there too; therefore do not let them ,be led aside by any narrow prejudices.

div.head: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the National Soho°le, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Wright Williams. 'There was a good attend- ance, amongst those present being Messrs. F. H. Pankburst, J. B. Liaison. James White, W. Treacy, den., W. Treacy, j .u., L. ;inertias, F. Cave, H. W. Wharton Atherton, J. Dickson. A. Edwards, H. Beacham, and Chadwick. The minutes of the last meeting having been read and passed, Mr. unison (the vicar's warden) presented the annual finan- cial statement relating to church expenses. The receipts, including a balance of £lB 135 7d from 1862, amounted to £147 Os 9d, and the expenditure to £134 28 61-d, leaving a balance in the hands of the wardens of £l3 4s 20. The btlance of £lB Ils tip was transferred to repairs fund No. 2 by vestry resolution. Tura only moneys that had not been received in the ordinary way of offertoslee were the pro. oaeds of the annual tea party, £lB 135 7d; ground rent, £8; proceeds if excursion to Myr and Llandudno, £6 141 Bd. The expenditure included several extraordinary items, their wish having been if possible to wipe off repairs fund No. and they had consequently carried no accounts to it. Dur- ing the year the footpath to the church had been tiled at a cest of something like £II ; the roof of the church had been a source of treuble, and had cost the sum of £l4; whilst they had carried out certain decorative alterations to the chancel at a cost of about £7. In answer to a question, Mr. linisem said there was a balance of £6 Ifs 101 d due on the repairs fund No. 2, and the gates about which there was a dispute had not been paid for.—Mr. James White said he and Mr. Treacy had examined ths accounts, which com- pared very favourably with the previous year. He pointed out Haat there was £6 ide 1011 due to Mr. Irnison on the repairs fund, and he did sot think it right that that gentle- man should be cut of pocket —On the motion of Mr. Treacy, jun., seconded by Mr. Edwards, the accounts were passed, the Chairman remarking that the duancias of the church were a source for great congratulation.— Mr. W. Treacy, see , proposed that the repairs fund No. 2 be closed, and that the slim owing to the treasurer (Mr. Itnison), £8 16s 1011, be the first charge on the balance transferred to the new churchwardens.-Mr. Wkittle seconded the motion, which was carried.—ln appointing his warden for the ensuing year tke Chairman referred wi a regret to the retirement of Mr. Liaison from the position of vicar's warden, but was glad to be able to announce that he would continue to labour in the parish, and had promised to take charge of the church Muir. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks having seen accorded to the retiring wardens, the Chairman appointed Mr. Fred Neil as his warden, and on the motion of Mr. Dickson, seconded by Mr. W. Tracy, sen., Nlr. Lewis Kilcross was re-elected people's warden.—lt was decided that the number of sidesmen should be increased from 16 to 20 in view of the increased work which would ensue upon the opening of St. Paul's Church, and the following gentleman were appointed: Messrs. Pankhurst, Shore, Hughes, Williams, Edwards, Treacy, sem, Jones, Wharton, Lowe, Lord, Cave, Beacham, Farrant, Wharton, Chadwick, Dwerryhouse, Watson, Whittle, Richards, and Treacy, jun. The thanks of the Meeting were accorded to Messrs. James White and J. Matthews for their services as lay representa- tives, and to Mr. Chadwick for the excellent way in which he had performed the duties of vestry clerk, and the gentle- men were all mappointel—A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman conolutled the proceedings.

The annual meeting of the parishioners was held in the Girl's School, on Tue 3 ley evening, under the presidency of the Rev. J. I.)ckwood, and there was a good attendance. The churchwardens' accounts showed that the receipts, in- cluding a balance of £l7 17s from last year, amounted to £B3 45 6d, and he expenditure was £93 53 3d, leaving a balance of £lO Os 91 duo to the wardens. The accounts were considered satisfactory and passed. It was stated that the amount realisan by collections in the church for various purposes was £l3B. Mr. T. F. Acton was re-appointed vicar's warden, and on the motion of Mr. D. T. Baguley (retiring warden), seconded by Mr. J. W. Haddock, Mr. J. J. Yapp was elected parishioners' warden. Messrs. T. Wright, Joseph Stokes, A. Woodier, and J. Rutter were ap- pointed sidesmen, and Messrs. T. F. Baguley, and T. Wright were appointed ruri-decenal representatives. The choir were heartily thanked for their pest services; and a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the vicar for his active la- bours in the parish, as well as his kindness and attention to the sink and needy. The Vicar suitably responded, and the meeting closed,

div.head: IT. ASSIROSH CHURCIL
div.p: IT. ASSIROSH CHURCIL

The first annual vestry meeting in connection with this church was held on Thursday night. The Rev. S. A. Spooner presided, and there was a fair attendance. The Chairman observed that the unanimity with which he was called to the incumbency was very grateful to him, and it would be his desire to work as far as possible in accordance with the general feelings of the parishioners, lie hoped that they would try to work with him, and that the inter- change of counsel would be mutual. Ile appointed Mr. E. Carey his warden.—Mr. Caliendo: inquired if Mr. Carey was eligible to act as warden, and the Chairman replied that al- though Mr. Carey did not reside in the parish, he was a regular attendant at the services of the church, and in choosing Mr. Carey he was quite within the spirit of the law•—On the motion of Mr. Williams, seconded bv Mr. Mercer, Mr. Valentyne was unanimously appointed people's warden, and the following were elected sidemen and church counsel :—Messrs. Richard Barker, T. A. Ballough, W. S. Callender, John Goff, Henry Johnson, T. W. Hunter, S. Kidd, R. Latham, It. Mercer, T. Minton, W. Newton, R. Riley. Joseph Williams, W. Carlile, William Smith, jun., and W. Hill.—Mr. Riley was thanked for his services as secretary and treasurer during the past year, but declined to be re-appointed, and on the motion of 14:. Goff, seconded by Mr. 11. Glover, Mr. Mercer was elected to the position. —After votes of thanks to the various officials and the chairman, the meeting concluded.

He would do his best to work the Board through as well as he could. He thanked the members very much for the honour they had done him. THE ELECTION •CE COMMITVEES : D. O'KEEFFE ON THB KINGMALEE.-0E the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded Iby Mr. Pankhurst, it was decided that there should be seven committees as usual.—Mr. Carey and Mr. Midwood had each drawn up a list of committees, and some conver- sation took place upon them. The members of the High- way Committee were appointed, and these six gentlemen were proposed to form the Gas and Water Committee. After he had made several interjectory remarks about there being Earls of Warwicks on the Board, Dr. O'Keeffe moved that no committee should have more than five members. He added: As long as we have Earls of Warwick here I am not going to sit on the Board —The motion was seconded by Mr. Johnsec.—Mr. Midwood moved an amendment that no limit be fixed to the nember of members on the commit- tees, and this proposition being seconded, was carried.—Dr. O'Keeffe declared that he would not vote at all.—Mr. Jahn- son moved that Dr. O'Keeffe's name be added to the Gas Committee.—Dr. O'Keefe : I move that Mr. Sadlor's name be added.—Mr Carey: You will have the whole Board on it Dr. O'Keeffe.—Dr. O'Keeffa : Quite right—The Chairman: We shall be kept here all afternoon.—Dr. O'Keeffe: Quite right. It is Mr. Carey'e fault. I know who is the king-maker here. Let Mr. Sadler los put on.— Mr. Pankhuret-: It amounts to this, that the Gas Committee will be so large that it will be able to carry anything at the Board.—Mr. Wright: Mr. Pankhurst must take his share of blame he wanted it.—Mr. Pankhurst: Certainly I did.— Dr. O'Keeffe: If we are going to have this a matter of ridicule, I shall make it as ridicelous as possible. Under , your presidency I think it is ridiculous enough already, and if it ie going to be made ridiculous I want to make it still mere.—The Cha rman: I cannot understand what 'AI% .O'Keeffe means by the Board being ridiculeue under my management —Dr. MlCeeffe: I can see how it is done. We have got a king-maker here.—The Cluj man: If you wish to say anything, sir, you must stand on your feet. I will not bear anything unless a member stands on his feet and addresses the chair.-Dr. 0 Keeffe made an inaa- dible observation, on which the Chairman said: Stand up, sir. If you mean to address the Board, if you Llltala to say anything to the Board, stand up. Gentlemen, you will re- member that at the beginning of the year I had to ask you it ..you had coefidence in me as chairman. There have been such remarks made to me by Dr. 0 Kee& as I don't CllOO3O to tit under: and I ask you to say, gentlemen, whether you have confidence in me or not. (Veices: We have.) lam envy to have to make such remarks on the first occasion ef being elected chairmen.—Dr. O'Keeffe: I have the greatest contieence in you and the greatest respect for you. There is no one more willing than lam to uphold the dignity of the position you occupy here, and as long sal am a member of the Board I shall certainly do everything in my power to uphold your position as chairman of the Beard, which you %kill occupy with the same dignity you have done hitherto—The electina of committees then proceeded without further altercation, with the following result : Highway, Building, and Street: Messrs.. Midwood (chair- loan I, Johnson, )-'aoktatirsr, Sadler, Dutton. —Gas and Water: Messrs. Forster (chairman), Pankhurst, Webster, Wright, Gasket!, Mid wood. Hospital: Messrs. Sadler (chairman), Houghton, Dutton, Martley.—Heezith : Dr. O'Keeffee (chairman), Messrs. Houghton, Martley, Johnson, Carey.—Seteerage: Messrs. Carey (chairman). Dutton. Midwood, Handley, Webster.—Finance: Messrs. Handley (chairman), O'Keeffe, Wright, Midwood, Gaskell.—General Purposes: Chairmen of the committees and Messrs. Pank- I buret, Wright. and Gasket). There is nothing new under the sun not even the divided skirt. I made this discovery the other day whee trying on a suit of clothes fresh home from Japan. A not unimpor- tant portion of the costume is a loose pair ef trowsers, which, when worn, folds over in plates that give it the appearance of an ordinary skirt. In the interests of science I ventured to submit the things to the inspection of a dis- ciple of Lady Ilaterton, who at once admitted that in every respect the girment modelled on a fashion thousands of years old in Japan is identical with the divided skirt pressed as a novelty upon the favourite attention of English ladies. The Royal Academy is never overburthened with striking subject pictures, or historical episodes, now that portraiture holds its sway, and more room is found for landscape than in days of old. Still there will be this year a few tale-tel- ling Works besides Mr. Waterhouse's "Oracle." 11r. Orcbardson's "Marriage de Ceuvenance," which, though similar in motive to episodes related on canvas by Hogarth, Mr. W. P. Frith, 14 A., and other moralists, will come to us newly-dressed under the brush of one of our few strong his- torical painters. The artist has in this instance deserted Shakespeare and history for a too frequent scene in social life. A htrihand and wife, vrtainly not a happy pair, Bi t opposite each other at a dining table ins room sumptuously furnished, and they are surrounded apparently by every luxury save that of harmony. The lady is probably little over twenty, her husband being considerably her senior. They are already wearied of Each other, though they have but just started in the race of life before them. We shall &leo see this year a well-worn subject from Scripture his- tory which, curiously enough, two academicians have lately chosen for their theme. Mr. Goodall, R.A., as well as Mr. Long, LA., has painted a " Flight into Egypt ;" bet, for- tunately, as one artist has already exhibited his picture in hond-street. the two works will not in any way clash. The Sultaa, come people may learn with interest, is a great pigeon fancier. A friend of mine just home from Eastern travel, came upon a truly Imperial consignment of ' fancy pigeons which had been sent from the United States to C n Constantinople for the recreation of the Sultan. There were 250 birds in all, of the choicest breeds and many of them prize takers. There is a shrewd remark in one off Charles Dickens's novels—it was made. at the expense of the "charitable grinder" who subsequently htelo ybecame assistant to Captain Cuttle in keeping Sal p —that there is something demoralising in the society et pigeons, and that boy or man who keeps them inevitably becomes a a cheat. The Sultan has fallen liar and out of the front rank of politics of late years. It is, nevertheless, to be hoped that the axiom may not be justified i nhis OW Tie saying of a lady well known in London society is having a prosperous course just now, perhaps more particu- larly in Liberal circles. The lady, who lives in a famous , "long, unlovely street," and opens her house to all kinds

iOf people with the simple requirement that t hey shall be either clever or much talked about, recently had Mr. Chamberlain among her guests. "I am told you are a very dangerous man," she said to the President of the Board of Trade, "and will do all kinds of things if you live. But I'm not a bit afraid of you. We have the snobs On our side, and there are so many of them." Another story about Mr. Chamberlain, alse iceelli!, and else true. A very short time after be went to the Board of Trade a telegram arrived addressed to him by nano. ht accordance with practice it was opened by the chief cleat. IL was simply addressed from "Jessie," in a street in Pim— lico, and ran thus, "Come to me at once, lam very iii." This was an embarrassing position for an official te be Illacei! in. Mr. Chamberlain was out ef town, and there was un- certainty as te his present address. Tke telegram was urgent, and it seemed that something should be done. After consultation it well decided that a grave and elderly clerk should go to the address given, explain Mr. Chamberlain's absence, and sae if anything could be done. Os arrival be discovered that the sender of the telegram was Mr. Jesse Collings, the spelling of whose Christian name the telegraph clerk had improved upon. Ths rola; ions et Mr. Ceilings and Mr. Chamberlain were then, as now, akin to those of David and Jonathan, and finding himself suddenly takes ill in strange lodgiags, the newly elected member for Ipswich telegraphed to his friend, and incidentally scandalized the Board of Trade.

Chatto and Windus, is just out, and the only fault which can be found with it is that it was not published at least two months ago. The opening of the Parliamentary session appears the most convenient time for such a publi- cation, whereas, as a foot note indicates, "The Shilling House of Commons " was passing through the press at the time the result of the Huntington election, which followed on the elevation a Lord Hinchingorook to the peerage, was undetermined. This said, there remains to be added only words of praise for an indispensable little book, whieh is a marvel of condeusation, accuracy, and cheapness.
