LOCAL POLITICS.

hir,—Poer, dear Sir Gilbert! What; it is to hurt his feelings! It seems to me that the oftener he appears in public and the easier will be the task of defeating him at the next election. The Tories could not do the Radicals of Warrington a kinder service than to "trot" their man out as often as possible. I would suggest that the two last "speeches" (?) of Sir Gilbert should be printed, and a copy sent to every voter in the borough, as they display such a tborongh knowledge of politics, and give evidence on the parted their anchor of such statesman-like abilities, that it is a pity they should be buried in the oblivion of a contem- porary's columns. At the Tory meeting in Latchford the military-titled chairman [whom the workmen employed at some of the tanneries think so highly of, and have such cause to be grateful (?) to] said, "when Sir Gilbert goes to Parliament again we shall not expect him to speak more (?) than usual." Surely Captain Reynolds must have been joking, seeing that Sir Gilbert only spoke once during the whole SO years curing which he sat as member for the borough. Ah, well, he will never have the chance of speaking either "more" or less" in Parliament again. Mr. George Woods must have felt very uncomfortable during his own speech. To say that Sir Gilbert is a large em- ployer of labour and a benefactor of Warrington because be is a shareholder in Parra Bank won't wash, and is about as ridiculous a piece of "special pleading" as has been re- cently witnessed. What fools George" must think the Latchford Tories are to swallow such 'rot," and how he mast have laughed at their gullibility when be got home. When the old gentleman got on his feet for the moment he was, as usual, affectionate to everybody, and then he poured eat the vials of his wrath to a perfect "flood" of childish rdesardities. Truly, he is" done up," or he would not take offences° easily. As a public man aspiring to a most im- portant public office he must expect, and whether he does at net, he will receive, severe criticism. We have a right to ask, what has Sir Gilbert Greenall done for Warrington? Let the stenemasons of Warrington who starved in 1879 (while the new church at Walton was being erected by rearkmen from a distance), let these men answer. Let the shopkeepers who hear of the big hampers coming from Lowest marked "C.S.S." (Civil Service Stores) give their opinions on the subject. Let the officers of the Friendly Societies and Sunday schools tell of Sir Gilbert'e unbounded generosity to them? Let the treasurer of the new School of Art tell us what Sir Gilbert has subscribed to that noble institution? Let the officers of any public benevolent in- stitution in the borough inform us how much we owe to the ex-member's benevolence. Let the working men of War- rington who years ago were able occasionally to breathe the fresh country air, and at the same time indulge in the in- nocent, but attractive, sport of fishing tell us how it is that the waterworks and even other pieces of water over which Sir Gilbert has control is now closed to them? Let Sir Gilbert tell us how it is that the Sunday closing if public- houses, which once partially existed here, was completely prevented. Sir Gilbert Greenall a benefactor to Warrington? What a farce! Warrington has largely benefitted him and his. We have given him an egg, ay, and a big one too, and he has given us—a little bit of the shell beck again. As ter Mr. Robert Pierpoint, he displays the sort of Courage which might be expected of a bully, who always "hits a man when he is down." At each of the Tory meet- ings he has taken occasion to sneer at Mr. McMinnies' in- disposition, knowing that he is safe from the possibility of a return blow, and while he wishes to pose before the people of Warrington as a man of culture and a gentlemazi, he ohows in these references such an utter absence of " bon- hommie" that one's memory is forcibly reminded of his

The Liberals of Warrington have now had an opportunity of seeing what the Tories are made of. We have very little to fear, but we must not sleep, "not even nod." Let every roan. official, as well as volunteer do his duty, and Toryism in Warrington will receive its death blow at no distant date. —Yours truly, AN OLD BAD.

Sir,—Tisere seems to be a sort of talismanic effect about the above numbers. Whenever quoted, or wherever seen, they reuse the ire of our Conservative friends, and when I I read over your able leader in last Saturday's issue, where you refer to the great success of the Liberal party in the ' !Rouse of Commons, and quote the figures 130 with each evident satisfaction, I thought perhaps it would be as well to be merciful. If our frieods are chiefly of the fossil class, well don't upbraid them with it. It is a case of cause and effect carried out to its logical conclusions. Had the echool- master gore abroad a few years earlier there would Lave been fewer political fossils to-day. But the strangest feature about Warrington politics is that after scoring such a large majority at the hat election there should be even one in this town ef ours willing to believe that that dear kind old gent eman, Sir Gilbert, has the ghost of a dunes at the next election. at the commencement of the winter season it was given out by the two political parties that every effort would be made to educate and keep them- selves well abreast of current politics. Has this been so? Take the newspaper reports of the meetings of each party and what do we see?' The Conservatives at each of their ward meetings carrying round the figure , head of a Dorcas meeting, and saying, " This is , the politician you mast vote for." In nearly all cases this r advice has been received with suppressed laughter. Take stock of those occupying the platform. Why, it reminds me of the sketch recently given by " Verax," showing how all our Royal families were related by marriage. You , couldn't touch one without touching all. So with all our local Tories—not exactly in the marriage line, but trade. Take each one of the speakers and you find the "dear old , duck" je the main financial spring in some insignificant toffy shop or other. Lots of ways to pull the political wires besides those intended to be removed by the Corrupt Prac- tices Act! Another little matter may oe referred to, not of much moment, perhaps, but still showing pretty clearly how unselfish the Tory candidate is. For a great length of time the followers of good old , Isaac Walton have enjoyed the benefit of a day's , fishing at Hill Cliff reservoir, or at one of the pits in the district. All this is now a thing of the past. Very likely , some of those outrageous Socialists may think a day's fish- ing would help to soothe their nerves, and that a stroll round the reservoir would add something to their entomo- logical knowledge. Rash beings! If they venture to look I even on the side of the reservoir one of Sir Gilbert's game- keepers will be ready to pounce open him. Ha owns nearly all the land for mites around, and, not satisfied with this,l;e claims to own the birds in the air and all the poor little fishes. What a gobbler he is To stock the big pond he has had all the small ones dragged, and new the reservoir is se overstockel with fish as to become a nuisance. And still a poor man MUCt sot have a day's fishing. Talk about the dog in the manger; it was nothing to this, for selfishness could no further go. He a benefactor te the town? Non- sense! Now I would ask your readers to look at the other picture. No carrying about a figure head ; the Liberal party has honestly tried to teach the whole town, not just their own party, what was going on in the political world. All the current subjects have been ably dealt with, and the result is that the old gentleman stands a good chance of L,eeing " 529 " doubled.—Yours, April 15th, 1554. CLIFFORD DIX. POLITICAL PALAVERING. Sr,—Your columns in last issue afforded us a sight which, had it not been pitiable, would have been ludicrous. I refer to your report of the Tory ward meeting in Latch- ford. Here we have the pitiably ludicrous spectacle of a good old country gentleman leaving home and home com- forts at the instigation of a crew of mercenary Tories—who thus drag upon the purse and person of this poor old man— for the good of the cause and not without a thought for themselves—and put him in that place for which Heaven at least never fitted him—a political platform' there to be a torture to his hearers, a grief and terror to his friends, and a laughing-stock for his political opponents. Than this, I know of no sight more pitiable. Here we have a gentleman advanced in years, endowed with great wealth, but with so tittle wisdom that he allows himself to be pushed into public life as the lay figure to be drawn from by the Tory artists, or rather as the formless nugget, to be wrought .3r these political goldsmiths, who, probably to console them- selves for the Tory job, they bate made appropriate some of the chips. Can any, except the very blindest of his par- tisans, suppose for a moment that it is the man and not the money thus eagerly sought. . Who that sees this limp lay figure, so void of that political vitality—the backbone, so necessary in a candidate for Parliamentary honors—ges- ticulating at ward and tea meetings, tittering vapid nothing and empty platitudes, could so far forget themselves aé to imagine that a "fit and proper person" to represent this important borough? I say this is nothing better than the worship of the Golden Calf, a temple for the worship of which is even now being erected in Sankey-street. Now, whatever respect I may entertain for Sir Gilbert Greenall in his proper and private capacity as a country gentleman and a landlord-that respect ceases when he leaves "his—the sphere in which atone be shines—wed offers, or allows himself to be offered, as a cindidate for Parliamen- tary honors. Then he ceases to ha a simple and innocent country gentleman, and becomes, as the tool of an un-

scrupulous party, a person endowed with the possible poten tiallity of danger, as a clog to the wheels of progress political nuisance to be avoided, er, if incurred, to be got rid let speedily. But all this, while we have left poor Sir Gilbert stand- ing, the ghost of a politition, " lean , attenuated," feeding a vacuous audience with political " pobs " fit only for persons in their first or second child- hood. Whenever Sir Gilbert gets up we expect no exposi- tion or explanation of imperial policy, no well-weighed discussion on the momentous events of the day. We do net expect it and we certainly never get it. Bet in its place we always have a re-hash of the old cry of "no surrender." Exactly! No surrender of perpetual pensions—of the right of voting to working men outside the borough—no surrender of any portion of the tithes to the poor now so wrongfully misappropriated by the clergy. No surrender! No pro- gress is what he means. And had we had the great misfor- tune to have had him in Parliament this session be would have done his feeble best to have blocked the Franchise Bill; for he is "most loyal to the working men "and would not have had those of them who happen to reside over the borough border, troubled with votes. Again, has he not given the working men of Warrington every facility for drinking to his health even if it might injure their own? His peevish attack upon The Examiner I regard as the querulousness of second childhood. Your pages sometimes contain the bitter, if wholesome, medicine of adverse criti- cism which the feeble, mental digestion of the magnate of Walton cannot assimilate He evinces a child-like aversion to the bitter medicine that "will do it good," and would willingly dish the cup to the ground and scratch the nurse who offers it. He forgets that they who do not flatter are his sincerest friends. Probably he prefers hebdomadal doses of sugary Godfrey administered in a neutral medium. Evidently he does not like the other side of the question poked at him. He prefers the sootkings of assentors to the correctives of criticism. He is evidently no stoic nor in- deed a philosopher of any sort, but simply an old man— past whatever of best he may have had, who should never have been allowed Is leave the circle of home and friends to encounter the rough usage of political strife. Now I would ask my fellow townsmen of all shades of political complexion, is this the sort of material out of which to make a wise and judicious statesman? Is there in his exhibitions evidence of 'that grasp, comprehension, judgment we expect and must have in a would-be legisla- tor? No !—I am, Mr. Editor, yours, ice., JOHN PEERS.

A BICYCLIST AT FAULT.—Ernest Birch, a youth, WAS fined by Bird. I. Mantell 15s and costs, for riding with his bicycle on the footpath on the 31st of March. The magis- trate declared that bicycles were a frightful nuisance and a frightful danger. PARTINGION.—The Band of Hope in connection with the Congregational Church had its annual treat on Good Fri- day. There was a large attendance at the public tea held in the schoolrocm. The meeting was held afterwards in the chapel, which was filled. Too pastor occupied the chair. Several temperance melodies were sung, and recitations and addresses given. A very enjoyable evening was spent. Srsamorrs.—The anniversary sermons of Wesley Chapel, Cadishead, were preached on Sunday last. In the morning at 10-30 a service for the young was conducted by the minister of the circuit. In the afternoon and evening the Rey. J. Chalmers' M.A., of Manchester, preached two elt cellent sermons. The congregations were good, especially lin the evening. Collections were made on behalf of the trust fund.

DRUAKENNE.3B.—EdwIrd Godfrey was 'fined 7s 64 and costs for being drunk; Jslssz Hostrance, as and cotta; Jane Jennett, Is and coats; Michael Healey, Andrew Dogherty, Ann Dog- bony. each Is 64 and costs; Mary Daley, 15. and °Jets.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. Fred. Rigby and Mr. Jas. Handley. MlBo.ELLA.Nzotre.—Mary Martin was fined 55 and costs 9s id ?or using prorane humus" in Cooper street. on the sth April. P.O Bennett proved 1115 case.—Mary Ann Glover, on the evi- dence of P.O.Smith, was fined 103 aid costs, for having been guilty of a similar offence, on the 21st March.—For haying the chimney of his dwelling. in Rutland-street, oa fire, on the 801. Ap•II, Joseph Walker was fined 6d and 93 6d costa. P.O. Revlon proved the case. KEEPING 0009 WITHOUT LICZNSTA. Edward Johnson, grocer, Church-street. was charged with kesping a dog without i a license. A servant n the employ of the defendant appeared, and stated that the dI; belonged to Mr Steward, auctioneer,. of Fiodsham, and he produced a license given to him by that ga itleman. Sergeant Walley proved that the dog had been kept about Johnson's premises, and he bad told the person who now appeared that the license ought to be kept where the dog was. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.—Joseph Richardson, butcher, Bridgewater-street, was chaeged with having, on the 25th March, unlawfully kept five dogs, being a greater num- ber by two than he was licensed to keep. P.C. Cooper gave evidence, and the defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined Sc and costa for each dog; total tt 9.

Tussns.Y.—Before Messrs. W. L Evans and J. 0. Gamble. MIISOELL&WLO ITS —John Entwistle and James Parr were ft ned 2a 6d and costs for playing pitch and toss at Whiston on Sunday —James Gregg was committed to a month's hard labour for atiaaniting an old man named Moreland. and also flied 51 and costs or seven days for 'drunkenness —The Court was occupied a considerable time in hearing a charge of assauit preferred by Mary Ann Johnson agalost Joseph Goss. The plaintiff, who Is the wife of the manager of the club and headquarters of the fluyton Company of the 2nd Lancashire iEngineer Volunteers, alleged that during an altercation on Wednesday, the Ilth lust, on the above-mentioned premises, the defendant, who is brother to th 3 drill instructor, threw her down some steps. Mr. J. 0. Swat appeared for the defence. A number of witnesses were heard on both sides, and the Bench, considering she br..iught the triiuble on herself, dis- missed the case —Newman Banner. a pensioner In the Army Reserve, was brought up for £3 2s 6d, being arrears of an order made upon him of Is 6d per week for the maintenance of his mother in the Workhouie Hospital, Preecot Union. An order for payment of the amount or six weeks' imprisonment was made.—ltichard Carroll was fined Sc and coats for being asleep in his cart on the highway at Rainhill.—James Corner wee committed for trial at the next (1831Zeli on a charge of com- mitting an unnatural offence at Huyton Quarry on Monday evening last. ADULTERATION OF MILK William Hardwick of Eccleston- street, was charged with selling to Sergeant Bull, on March 24th, three half pints of milk, samples of which had been sub- mitted to analysis by Dr. Campbell Brown, public analyst, who certified it to contain 20 parts water to 80 parts milk. Defendant said that his wife managed the business, as he was employed at the gas works. The Bench held him responsible, and imposed a penalty of 20s and 18s costs —Henry Hatton or High street, was charged with • similar offence, the propor- tion in his csse being 15 per cent water. In reply to the charge, he said they used about two quarts of water to rinee the cans and added it to the 14 quarts of milk. The Bench considered it a deliberate fraud, and imposed a penaly of 44 aid costs.

-- , A Mortorawn ROASTED TO DEATIL—A negro who had brutally murdered a woman near Austin, Texas, last Satur- day, was chased and captured on Monday. He was taken to the scene of the crime by a lynching party numbering 100, and confessed his guilt. Ele was then roasted to death. GIFT OF A PHIL OF BELLS HT Tau PuEstrErt.—A spire is about to be added to the Parish Church at Peßmaenmawr, North Wales, where the Premier was accustomed to worship during his holiday resorts on the Welsh coast. When the spire is completed Mr. Gladstone will, it 13 stated, I ulfil a promise of presenting a peal of bells.

EARLESTOWN.

NON-PAYMENT OF RATES: APPLICATION FOR COMMIT- MENT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions. on Saturday last, Mr. Henry Houghton (rate collector) applied for a commit- ment order against Mrs. Noah, lately of Bridge-street. Earlestown, for non-payment of rates.—Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, represented Mrs. North. and asked for an adjourn- ment pending certain legal proceedings which were in pro- greas.—The application was accordingly adjourned until the first sessions in May. GAMING AT EAELESTOWN.—At the Newton Petty Ses- sion*, on Saturday last, Matthias Skidmore. Henry Berry, and Robert Riley, young men, were summont-d for gaming at pitch and toss at Earlestown, on the sth April.—Skid. more and Riley pleaded guilty, and Berry not guilty.—P.C. Jaunt deposed that on the forenoon of the sth inst. he saw the defendants in company with others playing at pitch and toss opposite the Griffin Hotel, Earle-etreet, Earlestown. He saw them exchange money several times.—The sum- mons against Berry was dismitsed, and the other two defen- shots were fined 25 6d and costs each. LETTER FROM MIA GLADSTONE —A week or two ago a large Liberal meeting was held in the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, at which resolutions in favour of Government bills were passed, and directed to be forwarded to the Prime Minister. The following communication has been received in reply :—" 10, Downing-street, Wnitehall, April 18th, 1884. Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Gladstone to inform you .that he has received the communication from Earlestown on the subject of the Franchise and " other bills, which you have done him the honour to forward to him.-1 am, air, your obedient servant,. G. W. Spencer Lyttleton. Mr. T. Howard."

OBSTRUCTING TUB HIGHWAY AT NBWTON. - Patrick Clarke was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, for obstructing the highway at Newton, on the 28th ult.—On the date named the defendant was in charge of a wagonette urawn by one horse, and was in Mill-lane with a number of others waiting to convey pas- sengers to the Haydock Park Coursing Meeting. The de- fendant left the stand and stopped the waggonette in the middle of the road, and though be was requested to remove it by a constable he refused to do so.—The defendant was ordered to pay the costs.--John Kettle was summoned for a similar offence, and the Bench imposed a fine of 2s 6d and costs.

ST. PETRY'S SINGING CLASS, NNWTON.—The seventh annual concert in connection with t.Peter's Singing Class, Newton, was held in the Town Hall, on Thursday evening. There was a large audience, and the platform had been tastefully decorated. The glees were given by the class, numbering 55 members, coder the conductorship V. Mr. Jos. Oven; and Miss A. Kitchen accompanied the singing on the

pianoforte. The programme was a somewhat lengthy one, but this did not deter the audience from demanding numerous encores, which were responded to by the follow- I ing:—Miss A. Carr, Miss A. Haynes, Miss L. Mayor, MUNI I A. Kitchen, Miss Percival, Miss A. Braddock, Miss A. Hewitt, Mr. McClure, and Mr. S. Swann. ALLEGED TRESPASS IN PURSUIT OF GAME AT BURTON- WOOD.—Before Messrs. George McCorquodale, R. Hough- ' ton, and T. J. Gillespie at the Newton Town Hall, on Sat- urday last, Thomas Heaton and Alick Skein were summoned ; for trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Burtonwood, in ' the occupation of Thomas Naylor —Mr. Moore appeared fpr the defendants.—The evidence was to the effect that the de- fendants were seen with a grin each on the land in question en the sth ingt., and they had something bulky in their pockets. They refused to let the gamekeeper see what they had in their pockets, but one of the defendants showed him a pigeon which they had in their possession.—Mr. Moore sub- mitted that the flefendants were simply shooting pigeons, and that the "something bulky" in their pockets was but their powder and shot flasks.—The case was dismissed. THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH Cnoiß.—Last week Earles- town and district was well placarded with an announce- ment that on Good Friday evening a "grand sacred con- cert" would be given in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, by Miss Mabel Harcourt, "Queen of the Stage," who has recently been appearing at the Alexandra Theatre, Earles- town. The bill also stated that Miss Mabel Harcourt had secured the services of the choir of St. John's Church, . Earlestown, and that Mr. H. J. Durinan would officiate as accompanist. The announcement evoked much conversa- tion in the town, and the engagement of the choir was generally looked upon as unfavourable to their cause in their present dispute with the vicar of the parish. On Good Friday morning a rumour spread that the concert was not to I be held, and this proved to be correct. One of the vocalists, who had to take the principal solos in the anthems, choruses, was unable to fulfil his engagement, and it was con- sequently decided by the choir and Mr. Darman to cancel their engagement. WARORATH CHURCH VESTRY MEETINIS.—The. annual

--- vestry meeting of the parishioners of EmmanneliChurch, Wargrave, was held on Tuesday afternoon, when the Rev. Canon Whitley (rector) presided. There was a fair attend- ance of parishioners. After the chairman had read the notice convening the meeting, the accounts shqwing a balance of over £l3 were read and passed. The retiring wardens were reappointed, viz., Mr. William Thompson (vicar's) and Mr. Thomas Hunt (parisionera'), and the fol- lowing gentlemen were nominated as sidesmen :—Messrs. Starkie, E. Davies, Tooth], Catterall, Bate, Kimbell, Peake, and Bradshaw. Mr. Jones was reappointed organist, Mr. Davies choirmaster, and Mr. James Houghton sexton. , Messrs. Hunt and Tootill were reappointed the lay repre- sentatives to the ruri-decanel conference to be held at Man- chester. The question of a settled list of subscriptions to the church was mooted, and alter some conversation it was left over for further consideration. ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, NERTON.—III aid of the funds of St. Mary's and St. John's Catholic Schools, Crow-line, Newton, a sale of work was held in the school on Monday and Tuesday afternoons, and on the latter day al.o a " drawing " for prizes took place. The arraneements for the sale of work were principally carried out by Miss Torpey, the schoolmistress, Mrs. Forster, Miss O'Neil, and others, who presided at the stalls. The latter were filled with an assortment of useful articles—the work of .the

scholars taught by Miss Torpey, and without exception they were neatly worked—reftecting credit on the juvenile workers. There was no formal opening ceremony, but the "sale " was well patronised on the Monday. The most interest, kowever, appeared to centre in the drawing for about 100 prizes—consisting principally of handsome oil 1 paintings—and which took place on the Tuesday afternoon. There was a large company present. The whole of the goods were disposed of, and consequently a good sum has been realised by the sale of work. GOOD FRIDAY AT EARLBSTOwN AND NEWTON.—Good 1 Friday was observed at Earleatown as a general holiday, all I the places of business and occupation being closed. From lan early hour in the forenoon to late in the evening the streets and roads presented a lively and animated appear- ance—pedestrians being clothed in holiday attire. Un- doubtedly the principal attraction during the day I was the charmingly-situated Newton lake, and some thousands of persons wended their way thither to spend an hour or two in the pleasant avocation of rowing or reclining on the grassy slopes near inear Castle Bill, bordering on the lake. Many hundreds of persons assembled in the afternoon at Wargrave Moss to witness the football match—Earlestown v. Preston Olympic.

The visitors came with A very strong eleven, while no fewer than five second team men were required to fill up vacancies in the Earlestown representatives. It was generally antici- pated that the home team were in for a defeat, but after a very fast and hard-fought game Earlestown retired the victors by three goals to none. In the everting the Primi- tive Methodists held their annual tea meeting, whhe similar gatherings were also held at Burtonwood, Haydock, and Ashton. ILLTREATING • PONT: THE ANIMAL SHOT.— At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, before George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, and T. J. Gillespie, Esqs., John Thompson was summoned for ihtreating a pony by working the same in an unfit state.—P.C. spencer deposed that he saw the defendant in charge of a pony and cart at Newton, wkile attached to the back of the cart was another pony. The latter was actually walking on three legs—one foreleg being so lame that the horse would have fallen if it had not been tied to the cart. He examined it and found that its fetlock was very much swollen and the horse ap- peared to be in great pain. He (witness) unloosed it and it was pat up in the Millstone Inn stable.—The defendant ' called his mother as a witness and she said that the horse was all right, but it had fallen on the morning of the day in question and hurt its fetlock. It was a valuable horse, and it was a great shame and a sin that it bad afterwards to be shot. If all ponies were to be shot for the same cease a great litany would have to be killed —ln reply to the Bench, P.C. Speccer said it was the defendant's own sugges- tion that the horse should be shot. It was in good condition, but was excessively lame—The Bench considered that the defendant had sustained a considerable loss through the pony being shot, and they had no wish to add any further trouble to what he had met with. They would, therefore, dismiss the case.

FOOTBALL —On Good Friday afternoon a match at foot- ball was played at Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, between the Earlestown and Preston Olympic teams. As the weather was beautifully fine there wss a large concourse of specta- tors. The visitors turned up with their best eleven, while the Earlestown first team was very poorly represented. The game was very fast at the commencememt,and bath elevens worked hard, and the Earlestoniaus won by three goals to none. All the three ties in the second round of the com- petition for the Earlestown and District Junior Challenge Cup were played off on Saturday afternoon last, and, singu- lar to say, the Earlestown and Newton clubs defeated their opponents, and in each case the score was two goals to one. The Earlestown 2nd team and St. Thomas's (St. Helens) let team met to decide their tie on the ground of the Earles- town club. As the two elevens had played a drawn game at St. Helens on the previous Saturday, additional interest centred in the game. The St. Helens team secured the first goal, but the home team afterwards pulled themselves to- gether a bit, and playing up in good style they won by two goals to one. The Newton St. Peter's and Haydock St. James's (2nd team) decided their tie on the ground of the first-named After a good game the result at the expiration of the usual time was a draw, and an extra half hour was consequently played, the Newtonians pulling off the game by two goals to one. Considerable interest attached to the meeting of the Earlestown Wanderers (Ist team) and the ti.vdock Temperance (2nd)—who played their tie at Hay- doCk in the presence of a goodly number of spectators. A hard-fought game resulted in a well-earned victory for the Wanderers by two goals to one—this beieg the first defeat of the Temperance 2nd team for the season. The ties for he semi-final took place on Tues Jay afternoon amid some xciteruent. The Wanderers 2nd and the Earlestown Club 2nd were drawn together, And they w;l1 consequently play off the semi-final tie of the contest.

div.p: TRDAY. APRIL 19. 1884.

EAELFSTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. —The anneal tea party in connection with this place of worship was held on Good Friday. Owing to the eminently fine weather there was not quite as large an attendance at tea as was anticipated, but at-out 100 persons partook of the good things provided. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by the resident minister, the Rv. F N. Shim- min, who, in his opening remarks spoke of Good Friday and its associations, and went on to point oat that by maui. fasting a spirit of self sacrifice people would best secure their own highest well-being as well as the highest well- being of others. He called attention to the het that they were fully committed to their scheme, building new schools, and said he hoped they would do their utmost in rendering the help and assistance that was required. Several recita- tions, readings, dm., were excellently given by the scholars, and selections of music were given by the choir, conducted byl Mr. Banton, Mr. W. Austin presided at the harmonium. A hearty vote of thanks to all who had assisted in the even- ing's proceedirgs, the choir and chairman, brought a very pleasant meeting to a close. PosTronnmarrr OF A MAIIRIADIL—The time-honoured adage that "There's many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip" has received a striking confirmation in Earlestown during the last few days. Sunday last was the "third and last time" on which the banns of marriage of a loving pair had to be " published " in the Church of St. John. and in view of that fact it had been arranged that the interesting ceremony, which usually succeeds, should take place on the following day (Monday). Due preparations to this end had been made and all the arrangements requisite on such occa- sions were duly completed. Unfortunately, however, when Monday morning came the sad news was known that the loving couple could not be united so early as was anticipated, inasmuch as the statutory declaration as to the publication of the banns of marriage had not been complied with on the Sunday. This, it may be explained, WAS owing to the fact that the banns were not announced at all on that day. No doubt they would have been given nut in due course had the usual services been held, but owing to the dispute the vicar ordered the church to be closed. Much sympathy has been expressed for the disappointed couple And their friends, ' who were put to a deal of unnecessary trouble and inconve- nience.

according to the notice. ("Not poßsible," and hooting.)—Mr. Nevin : It is impossible to do so, and I propose that we ad- journ. (Applause.)—The Vicar : It is quite possible.—Mr. Nevitt : It is not. (Applause.)—A Parishioner: There are more outside than there are in. (Disorder.)—The Vicar: I must have order before any business can be proceeded with. Don't all speak at once.—Mr. Nevitt again moved that they adjourn to the school-room with the permission of the Vicar. (Applause.) He suggested that only those who were householders or ratepayers should have a vote.—Mr. Corlett said it entirely rested with the parishioners. If thee:- wished to have the meeting adjourned to the school-room they could do it with a show of hands. If the Vicar would not let them have the use .4 the school they must go to a more convenient place for the parishioners. (Loud applause ) The Vicar: You have heard my expression of opinion that there are those in this room who are not householders, and I think in all fairness to others who are they ought to retire. (Voices: "Point them out,' and "name."—The Vicar: I will not name them—l will leave it to their lionour.—A. Parishioner: Don't leave it to their honour, point them out. (" That's it.")—Mr. Nevitt : I am in favour of the adjourn- ment to the school-room. (Applause.)—The Vicar: Is Mr. Maudsley a householder?—Mr. Mandalay: I retire with pleasure.—The Vicar: I only asked a question?—Mr. Mandsley : I will go out; it is only another specimen of your Christianity. (Applause.)—Mr. Corlett: I believe there are 200 or 300 outside who wieh to come in, but this place is certainly too small. That being so, it rests with yourselves to say whether the meeting shall be adjourned or not. (Hear, hear.) I therefore beg to propose that we adjourn to the school-room. (Hear, hear.) All in favour of that motion—The Vicar: If you please, lam in the chair. (Hisses.)—A Parishioner: Mr. Corlett is on his feet, and he should be heard. (Hear, hear.) —Mr- Corlett: Seeing that this room is too small. I beg to propose that we adjourn to the school-room —A parishioner: , I second it.—The Vicar: I decline to put that metion—if it be a motion—for this reason that I Dress for a transaction of business where we are. (Loud groans and hisses, mingled with cries of "We can't do it, &i.)—Mr. Nevitt : Who is in favour of the motion 2—All persons present held up their hands amid applause.—Mr. Corlett: Is there any amend- ment?—The Vicar: I understand that previous arrange- ments have been made with regard to an adjournment, with which of course I have nothing to do.—Mr. Corlett: The adjournment is pressing before you. There is not 'Ancient room for the parishioners to have a fair hearing to-nignt— (hear, hear,)—and it is for you to make provision for them. (Applause.)—The Vicar: After I have read your notice con- vening the meeting, we can very well do the business in this place. (Great aprear.)—Mr. Birkheed said that in every parish anywhere on earth if the vestry was found to be too small for a parishioners' meeting they adjourned to the school-room or some other place. (Cheers.) Their vicar knew that such was the custoM of the country, and unless they had to transact business of which they were ashamed there was no harm dose in holding the meeting in school. (Disorder.)—The Chairman: I will have order and quietness, please.—Mr. Corlett: Put it tithe meeting.—The Vicar: I must say you are not in order.—Mr. Corlett: All in I favour of the motion--The Vicar: He has no right to put it to the meeting. (Groans.)—Mr. Corlett: If you won't do it yourself, somebody else must. (Hear, Hear.)— A Parishioner called Out: "Mr.. Slinn's outside," where- upon the Vicar retorted: Mr. Winn ought to have been here before now.—Amid a scene of excitement Mr. k•linuaucceded lii forcing his way into the room with the books and ac- counts in his possession. fie was greeted with groans and hisses, and in his progress was somewhat hustled by the parishioners. He climbed over the table at which the vicar and reporters were seated and stood beside the vicar.—Mr. Corlett again appealed to the vicar to consent to an adjourn- ment. —The Vicar, however, amid considerable disorder, refused to do so.—Mr. Corlett (to the parishioners): It rests in your hends to have an adjournment—(cheera)—and will you please retire to the school-room. (Renewed cheers.)— The Vicar: I say you shall not retire to the school room. (Groans.)—Mr. Corlett, then if you won't let us have the school-room we will retire to the Cu-operative Hall. (Ap- plause.) We can go and we will transact the business with a chairman of our own. (Renewed cheers.) We will do that if Mr. Matthews won't let us have the school-room.— Mr. Taylor: If you retire Mr. Matthews and his friends will pass the accounts here and they willl call themselves the proper vestry meeting.—The disorder again continued for some minutes, amid which Mr. Birkhead maintained that the parishioners had a right to insist upon an adjournment to the school. room. Mr. Corlett: I

will put the motion for the adjournment to the school- room. (Applause.)—The Vioir : You cannot. (groans.) I say Mr. Corlett is out of order.—Mr. Corlett : All those in favour —The Vicar: He is not in the chair, and has no right to put a motion to the meeting. (Hisses.)—A Parishioner: Put the motion lourself, then. (Applause.)— The Vicar: I call upon Mr. Shinn to read the accounts.— .. ....

Mr. Slinn rose to comply with the Vicar's r;Cju-e;;:-b-U-i--he was inet with a perfect storm of groans, hissing, and shout- ing. Cries of "Turn him out" and "Take the books from him "were raised, and immediately afterwards those at the back part cf the room began to press forward, and in the confusion which ensued the chair- man's and reporters table was overturned ; the half. dozen representatives of the Press present being hustled and pushed about with the other persons at that end of ths roogn.—Mr. Corlett shouted at the top of his voice for order, the parishioners responding with cries of "Adjourn." —A brief discussion took Wane between the Vicar and Mr. Corlett, in the course of which the latter promised that if the Vicar would consent to an adjournment to the school- room he would see that none but householders resident in the parish were admitted.—The Vicar : Just one word, if you please. (Cries of 'Order.") I have asked Mr. Cor- lett if we adjourn to the school who are to go is P (" Parish- ioners" and "Ratepayers.")—Mr. Corlett : R itepayers or householders in the parish.—The Vicar: Then we will go to the school on that condition only. (Applause.) Shouts of " Chat's fair" and " That's all we want.") As the parishioners retired from the vestry it was noticed that some handreds of other persons had been waiting out- side, unable to gain admission. They accordingly pro- ceeded to the school, about two hundred yards away, and soon after the doors were opened the room was well filled. Several minutes were wasted in persons being asked to retire who were not householders in the parish, the Vicar stating that the hotter:lades of the parish were the Ilaydock railway down to the arousing over the London and North-Western line, then along the latter line to what is called the "Nine Arches," then along the canal, taking in the "Red louse" and all houses on the Common. If anyone resided outside that district he hoped they would retire. TIN ACCOUNTS.

The Vicar afterwardi"-calleii;;;;Mr. Slina to read the accounts—Mr. Nevitt: Before he does so I should like to ask is he reading this year's or last year's balance sheet ? When I was churchwarden last year the accounts were not passed, and I think we should pass them first. —The Viear: Were they posted on the church doors?—Mr. Nevitt : They were not passed. There was CS odd which you drew from your warden, and about which you would not give ns any account. As a churchwarden I thought you ought to give a proper account. (Hear, bear.)—The Vicar: With reference to Mr. Nevitt's assertion as to the money being drawn without his knowledge, I beg flatly to contradict it.— Mr. Nevitt: I did not say that—l only said it was drawn without my knowledge.--The Vicar said he would tell them the reason of that. It was money invested for the epecifie object of repairing the fabric of the ehurch, and it was his object to see that the money was not spent for any other purpose.—Mr. Taylor: Before Mr. Blinn reads the accounts will you satisfy us that he is a qualified parishioner?— (Applause.)— rhe Vicar explained that at the first forma- tion of the parish a gentleman was appointed warden who had resided out of the parish, and the same course had since been followed as it happened. The question of legality was raised some time ago, and he (the vicar) communicated with the Bishop's legal adviser, who replied to the effect that his non-residence in the parish was no disability whatever. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Slinn happened to reside a few yards over the boundry of the parish.—Mr. Corlett: You must understand that Mr. &inn is illegally in the office he holds at the present time, and so is anyone who lives out of the parish. (Applause.) They must either have property in the parish or they must live in the parish. (Hear, hear.) He added that he had no complaint to find with Mr. Slinn per- sonally as he had found him very pleasant te work with.— Mr. Taylor: Still it is an admitted fact that he is illegally in his office? ("That's it.")—Mr. Shun: If you desire I can retire from the room.—Mr. Taylor: Undoubtedly. (Cries of "No, no," " Let him remain."-The Vicar: I verily believe in my soul—(laughter)—that Mr. Shinn is not disqualified.—Mr. Taylor: Then why draw the boundary 1 line? (Applause.)—The Vicar: I say that having taken high legal opinion—A Parishioner: You will have it a High Church in a bit. (Hear, hear.)—The Vicar: Looking all around at the practice over the country, do all church- wardens live in the parish for which they serve ?--A. Par- ishioner. : They ought to do if they don't. (Applause.)— The Vicar:. Then it comes to this, that if they are not eli- gible for the office they bold those who appointed them are ignorant, and lax in their duty ?. ( Laughter.)—A Par- ishioner: That's one to you, for you. appointed him.—An- other Parishioner: That's a fact —Mr. Shinn made an at- tempt to leave the room, but was called back by the Chair- man,and Mr. Corlett also prevailed upon him to remain:- The Vicar: I look upon Mr. Shinn as a legal officer—(A Voice : " He's a legal imposter ")—and as not disqualified, , and I think it is unfair and ungentlemanly for any man, after Mr. Shinn has served two years, to ask him to.with- draw and leave the room. (Hear, hear.)—Voices: Then why did you draw the boundary and exclude others? (Ap- plause.)-Mr. Taylor: If you make a law you should carry it out.—(luterruption and disorder, in the course of which one or two persons were ejected from the room.)—Mr, Corlett thought they had better let bygones with Tegazd to Mr Slinn be bygones. At the present timo he did not think they had a right to interfere, as ' it appeared to have been the custom from the commencement. But in the future it would be their guide to elect officers who lived in the parish—(applause)—ana then if it was under the law it would save all Sorts of squab- bling. He quoted the opinion of Sir Robert Phillimore, .ihat a warden must have property in the parish or live in the parish; and he (Mr. Corlett) added that that ought to settle the matter—(hear, hear)—as it was a high legal authority.—The Vicar said Mr. Corlett had not told them the particular case upon which Sir R. Phillimore had ex- pressed the opinion, and observed that all parishes were not governed alike, and were not all under the same regime.— Mr. Corlett (holding up a book): Here is the law in my hand, and the laws have never been repealed, and it dis- tinctly says they must have property in the parish or live in the parish to be a warden. (Applause.)—After a further desultory discussion, Mr. Corlett moved that Mr. Slinn read I the nainutee of the last meeting. The motion was seconded

and passed.—Mr. Blinn proceeded to do so, but was fre- quently interrupted by cat-calls and other unseemly noises. The accounts for the year were next read, showing receipts £177 13a sid, and expenses £175 121 9id, leaving a talance of £2 Os Std. Accounts still owing amounted to £s.—Mr. Corlett proceeded to refer to the accounts at some length, remarking that the wardens had had to borrow about £l4 from the offertory fund in order to defray expenses incurred in the repair of the church, and since then Mr. Matthews had drawn £ll odd, which was an amount received yearly for the repair of the church. But Mr. Matthews would not hand over the £ll odd, but kept it in his pocket —(`• shame ")—although be knew that they (the wardens) had had to borrow money from the offertory. 'As a conse- quence of that they were not able to pay the church cleaner. (" Shame.") He had no right to hold toe money in his own hands—(applause)—but it should be inveetial in the bank in the names of the two wardens and the vicar. They had never seen a penny of the money. Did they call it fair? ("No.") They were not satisfied about it; the auditors that afternoon were not satisfied about it, and they would not pass the balance sheet in consequence of the money not being brought forward. They yet knew nothing i about t, but it ought to have been in the bank. (Applause.> I —The Vicar, in reply to Mr. Corlett, stated that the money had been left for a specific purpose, and be was determined that it should not be devoted to any other end. It had beim so on a previous occasion, but on the last occasion he drew the money. (A Voice: "And kept it too.") The Vicar said he could not honestly and conscientiously allow money for church repairs to go to church expenses.—Mr. Nevitt : But you did it before.—The Vicar I consented foolishly, I must say. (Laughter.) He added again that he could not let the money go until he was satisfied that it was re- quired for the specific purpose for which it was left.—A Parishioner: Why do you keep the money yourself? (Ap- plause.l—The Vicar: I will tell you why. lam here pro- bably for life—(Prolonged groans, hisses, and hooting, mingled with cries of "There's a doubt about it," and " Question.")—The Vicar: I am here probably for life— (Voices: "Change your living ")—and somebody must have possession of it.—Mr. Corlett: Put it in the bank.— (Applause.)—The Vicar: Have I ever objected to that? I have never been asked to pat it in the bank. (Hear, hear. —4. Parishioner : You ought to put it in the bank without being asked if you are an honest man. (Applause.) He added, that Mr. Corlett had tried to convey an unfair impression with regard to the amount of £ll odd which he (the vicar) held. He denied that he used the money for his own purposes—(applause)—and he had neyer refused to turn the money up for the proper object.— Mr. Corlett said that so long as money was owing why did Mr. Matthews hold it ?—A voice: It is not his own.—Mr. Corlett: You were asked for it, and you refused to give it up.—The Vicar : As soon as I am shown that the money is required for the repair of the fabric I will hand it over. Mr. Corlett: lam fully prepared to do it now. (Applause.) —A Parishioner: Who is responsible for the debts ?—Mr. Corlett: The wardens are.—The Parishioner: Then you ought to hold the money. (Applause.)—Mr. Birkhead sug- gested that they should refer the accounts to a small com- mittee who would thoroughly examine them and g, into the matter properly. He thought all monies belonging to the church ought to be invested in the bank properly.—The Vicar said he thought the church safe was as safe as any- where else.—Mr. Corlett said the money might be invested in the names of three persons, so that one person could not getat out himself. (Applause).—The Vicar said the money had been left for a special purpose and not to give to the churchwardens because their accounts showed a deficiency. —Mr. Corlett said that churchwardens should be church- wardens and not half churchwardens. (Loud applause.) He alleged that he had never been, treated as a churchwar- den since he had been in office. The Vicar had insulted him continually, but he had himself always acted as a gentle- man throughout the whole of the squabbles, and had ap- proached the Vicar with conciliatory measures. He did not for one moment think that the Vicar had used the money for his own purposes, but he left the meeting to judge for themselves, as it was not in the bank. (Ironical applause.) —The Vicar: This is a charge against my morality and honesty. (Derisive laughter.)—Mr. Corlett: What we want is the money put in the bank in the three names, and if Mr. Matthews will promise it there is an end of the matter.— After further discussion the Vicar consented to do this, amid loud applause; after which Mr. Corlett asked the parishion- ers if they thought the money borrowed from the offertory fund should be refunded by Mr. Matthews. (Cries of "Yes.")—The Vicar: I previoasly consented to spend £lB out of the repair fund, and about the applicition of it.l am not satisfied. Until I am satisfied about it I will not part with another farthing to anybody. (Hooting ) Mr. Corlett: He wants to go into other people's affairs, but I lave nothing to do with them. (Applause.)—The Vicar said he believed Mr. Corlett had never advanced any money personally.—Mr. Corlett replied that the wardens had paid a certain sum for repairs out of the offertory fund, and they now wanted the money refunding from the repair fund. If they wanted money, and knew where it was, they had a perfect right to go and ask for it. (Applause.) —The Vicar: Hear, hear.—Mr. Corlett: So long as you say that, will you kindly pay it now, Mr. Matthews ? (Roars of laughter, amid which Mr. Corlett held his hat towards the Vicar.)—The Vicar; All I can say in answer to Mr. Corlett's request is, as Paddy says—(renewed laughter, which was prolonged for several minutes, mingled with hisses and shouts of "He comes from Ireland," "Hear what Paddy says," eke.). The Vicar: If I owe it, lam able to owe it you. (Hisses.)—Mr. Birkhead again suggested that the question should be referred to a small committee. He propoaed that the accounts be left to the two wardens. the Vicar, and Messrs. Lane, Burchall, and Appleton to deal with. (Applause.)—Mr. Winstanley seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously.

div.head: EARLESTOWN CEUTRCH DISPUTE. SCANDALOUS SCENES.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN CEUTRCH DISPUTE. SCANDALOUS SCENES.

What was originally. a small personal squabble at the church of St. John the Baptist, Earlestown, has now de- veloped into a public scandal of a most painful and die- creditable character. The constantly recurring " scenes " and "disgraceful proceedings" which have been witnessed in the church Suaday after Sunday have not only been the theme of conversation of those resident ia the immediate district, but they have attracted the attention of people resident in other parts of the country—giving to Eerier!. town an unenviable notriety. Teem a narrow personal matter it gradually developed a bitter feeling between the vicar, choir, and congregation. This has given rise to numerous irregular proceedings in church, and can now only be designates' as discreditable to an extreme degree.

It will be remembered that on Sunday week, the Vicar declared from the pulpit that he bad fully made up his mind that Mr. Durman (organist) should not play the organ again, and he was prepared with another organist to take his place. This gave rise to a most unseemly disturbance after the evening service, and the parishioners freely ex- pressed themselves to the ettec: that if Mr. Darman did not play no one else should. This expression of opinion was forcibly carried into effect on Sunday morning last. The Vicar again secured the services of the gentleman from Liverpool, who attende I to play the organ on the previous Sunday, but when the sidesmen arrived at tbe church they proceeded behind the organ to prevent anyone " blowing" for the new "importation." Mr. Darman and the choir occupied their accustomed seats, but Mr. Darman after- wards went to the organ and sat down as if to play. The Vicar's warden (Mr. Shinn) requested him to leave, but Mr. Darman declined to do so, although the new organist still Sat near him. Shortly before the time for the commence- ment of the service, Mr. Darman began to play a voluntary; whereupon the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews), and the Curate (the Rev. 11. E. Smith) entered the charch from the vestry. They walked to the reading-desk, and after Mr. Darman had finished the voluntary, the Vicar, turning to- wards the congregation said: I have to announce that there will be no service whatever in this church to-day.—This statement gave rise to a most exciting and disgraceful scene. The congregation loudly hissed the Vicar, WllO retired into the vestry amidst a perfect howl of disapprobation; while many of the congregation seemed inclined to follow him I therein. One of the Vicar's friends or sympathisers was I violently pushed and hustled out of the church by about I half-a-dozen men; and after the commotion had a little subsided Mr. Darman commenced to play the " Hallelujah Chorus," and this was very heartily sung by the choir to the evident satisfaction of the eocgregation. Mr. Birkhead (sideman) afterwards stepped forward to the chancel steps and addressed the congregation as follows: —I cannot sufficiently strongly express my regret at the scenes that are now taking place in the name of religion and in the House of God. It is a shame to our common Christianity.—At this point the 'near entered the church from the vestry, and was greeted with hisses. As he looked at Mr. Birkhead, who had momentarily stepped speaking, Mr. Birkhead exclaimed "Yes, it's me," and the Vicar again retired amid groans and hisses. Mr. Birkhead (con- tinuing) said: If a little bit of forbearance and Christian charity had been exercised as it should be exercised, then these scenes would have been avoided. There is redress to be got in other ways, and, therefore, ought to be taken, and this sort of thing ought not te be repeated.—He then gave out several hymns, which were earnestly sung by the choir and congregation to Mr. Darman's accompaniment on the organ. After the Doxology had been sung, the choir pro- ceeded to pack up their books, with which they retired from the cherch along with the congregation, the time being about eleven o'clock. For some time the action of the Vicar in refusing to proceed with the service was strongly condemned by those who gathered round the church doors, and a suggestion was made that parties should remain in the church all day so that the Vicar,: could not close it be- fore the time of evening service. This course, however, was not adopted, as it was thought best to leave that matter in the hands of the Vicar. In the evening a large number of persons gathered in the vicinity of the chureb, but the Vicar carried out his inten- tion of not holding a service by keeping the church doors locked. Small groups gathered about the streets, and the state of affairs was eagerly discussed. After half-past six o'clock there would be some two or three hundreds present, and they retired to the plot of land fronting Williamson- square, with the intention of singing several hymns. The people'e churchwarden. the sidesmen, organist (Mr. Darman), and many members of the choir were present. Before any hymns were announced, Mr. Birkhead (aidesman) said they were lockA out of their parish church, and•coald not, con- sequently, hold their usual service. It was to be hoped that that dispute WAS nearly at an end, for it was a disgrace that they should be in that position, and still be unable to help themselves. But let them keep as well as they possibly could within the law, so that they could not be caught hold of for what they did. They were in the right at present. They had subscribed for a parish church, they had bought an organ, and it was not right that they should be debarred from having something to say in the matter. If it was ac- cording to law that a parson was to be the Pope in his own parish all he could say was that the sooner the law was done away with the better. (Hear, hear.) They were that night locked out of their parish church, and could not join in their usual service, but they were under the canopy of heaven stet they could join in singing one or two hymns. Several hymns were then given out and lustily sung by the congregation, after which Mr. Birkhead asked the company to retire quietly to their homes, and informed them of the annual vestry meeting which was to be held on the ft flow- ing evening. PARISHIONERS' VESTRY MEETING. TI7III7LTUOIIS PISOCENDINGS.

It is a question whether the history of recent years contain a record of such a scene of excitement and tumult at an Easter vestry meeting of parishioners as, that witnessed in Earlestowe on Monday evening. It was pretty freely understood that the grievances of the parishioners were to be thoroughly ventilated at the Easter vestry meeting, and it is needless to add that the vestry meeting for St. John's parish was eagerly awaited. According to a notice posted on the church doors it was to be held in • the vestry of the church at seven o'clock, but long before that time a large crowd of parishioners gathered at the entrance to the vestry, and somewhat excitedly discussed the probable consequences of the meeting. About twenty minutes to seven the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) opened the doors and there was imme- diately a rush for seate. The room was immediately filled to overflowing, every inch of sitting and standing room being occupied; while considerably inure than those inside were oatside pushing to gain admission. After the excitement iuside had a little subsided the Vicar said it was evident they had not room for all who wished to be present. ble sugges- ted that those who were not householders should retire and make room for those who were householders.—Mr. Nevitt (sideman): I beg to move that we retire to the school ; it is only right that we should have a place big enough. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Corlett (people's warden): Anyone who is here and does not pay the poor-rate or reside in the parish is not entitled to vote.—Mr. Nevitt : Is Mr. Slinn here? Blinn is not in the parish and cannot atteni. (Hear, hear.)—The Vicar: He is an officer of the church at the Present time.—Mr. Corlett : What transpires 'here let it be done in a legal and proper way so that anyone who does not pay the poor-rates will they kindly leave the roorn.—Mr. Birkhead (sidesman) said it was quite evident they could not get through the business there, and he thought they orght to adjourn to the school-room. (Applauee.)—A voice; Are the reporters householders? (Laughter.)—The Vicar: They are privileged generally.—Mr. Corlett: It is because they don't exercise a vote.— (le Vicar: I see that all householders have not yet retired.—The Vicar : We shall have to adjourn to the school-room. Of course, it rested with the vestry whether or not you adjourn—you have power to adjourn if you think proper.—The Vicar pointed eut that the time for the commencement of business, seven o'clock, had not arrived, and the remaining few minutes was spent in discussing the claims of certain persons to I), present. —At seven o'clock the Vicar proceeded to read the notice concerning the meeting, and said that notwithstand- ing what had been said about adjourning the meeting, be hwished te have the business gone on with in that place,

div.head: BUICTION OF WIRDENS.
div.p: BUICTION OF WIRDENS.

The Vicar said the next business was the election of officers. Of course he had his own right, which he would exercise, of appointing his own warden.—Mr. Burchall : I dispute that, sir. (Applause.) I hold in my band the canons of the Church of England, which anyone can get for a shilling, and they ought to be in everybody's house. With reference to the choice of churchwardens it says— " All churchwardens in every parish shall be chosen by the joint consent of minieters and parishioners, if it may be, but if they cannot agree upon such choice, then the minis- ter shall chose one and the parishioners another." Our first duty is to appoint two wardens, and I beg to propose Mr. khead as one of them. (Cheers.)—Mr. Corlett seconded the nomination, observing that all they wanted was honesty and straightforwardness. —The Vicar : I object to it. (Hisses.)—Mr. Taylor: Upon what ground. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. Birkhead said it was not the first time he had been objected to by a minister, and consequently he did not feel much hurt about it. (Laughter.)—Mr. George• Appleton had great pleasure in supporting Mr. Birkhead as one of the wardens.—Mr. Buithead moved that Mr. Appleton be one of the wardens.—The motion was seconded.—The Vicar :

I object to the appointment of two wardens by the parishioners. I do not at all object to Mr. Appleton's. appointment as people's warden, but I do object to Mr. Birkhead's appointment as people's warden.—Mr. Birkhead withdrew in favour of Mr. Appleton, who he said, was eminently fitted for the post, and capable of fulfilling its duties.—Mr. John Taylor was also proposed as warden.— The Vicar: I have to object to Mr. Taylor. (Loud hisses.) —Several persons: We don't object to him.—Mr. Corlett: Will anybody propose me as the Vicar's warden P—Mr. Taylor moved a motion M that effect amid cheers—The Vicar: I take an objection to that. (Hisses.)—Mr. Corlett (laughing): I knew he would do so.—The Vicar:. You who approve of Mr. Appleton as people's warden. (Cries of "Mr. Taylor also.")—The Vicar: I don't wish.to speak of- fensively of anybody. bat when I say so, I am advised that it is a fact, that Mr. Taylor is not eligible, not being a ehurchman.—Mr. Taylor: I am a churchman—was bred and born a churchman. At St. James's Church, Latchford, I was brought up, and my parents were church people. (Ap- plause.) I took my sitting at Crow-lane Congregational Chapel because I would not sit under you. (Cheers.) If you put me in as a warden the church difficulty will be settled in three months. (Applause.)—A Parishioner: We shall have Disatablialament before then.-,-eis the ;Vicar re- fused to submit the name of Mr. Birkhead or MrJraylor to the meeting, Mr. Btrkhead proceeded to ash thoselin favour of Mr. Appleton to hold up their hands.--The there-• upon left the chair, saying "Gentlemen, as far as I am concerned if thia is to be the procedure /close the meeting. (Groans, and voices: "You cannot."),—Mr. Birkbead: An. the, victr has vacated the chair, we can still go on with another chairman. After a pause: Do yore refuse to pro- ceed with the meeting P—The Vicar: Mr. Birkhead asks me if I refuse to go on with the meeting. I said that Ido refuse to proceed with the meeting if I am interrupted. Disorder.)—Mr. George Appleton was afterwards unani- mously elected one of the wardens, amid applause, tbe vicar putting the motion to the meeting.—The Vicar: The vicar selects and appoints his own warden. The people's warden is already appointed.—Mr. Nevitt : Who is the vicarltmar- den I' (Hear, hear.)—The Vicar: Mr. Nevitt says.it necessary you should know who the vicar's warden is. All lam disposed to say is that he is a parishioner. (Hisses, and cries of "Name, name.") No. I will not name him.— Mr. Corlett: I think we have a right to know who thissecret man is. ( Applause.)—A Parishioner: Perhaps he la" Skin- the-Goat "or "Number One." (Lend laughter.)—After considerabledisorder, Mr. Corlett said: This is a case of ob- struction, gentlemen.—Mr. Birkhead: If Mr. Matthews won't name the warden we had better name a warden for him. (Hear,. hear, and applause.)—Mr. John Taylor was there- upon proposed and seconded as a. warden.—Tho Vicar: Be- fore we proceed any further I would say that there is a certain paper to fill up, and until that is tilled up, signed, and presented at the proper quarters no election is valid under the law —After a squabble between the Vicar and Mr. Coalett about this matter. the Vicar said he would not for one moment deny having added another name to the paper.—Mr. Corlett: As wo have only onowarden, we have the right to appoint another. (Hear, hear.)—The Vicar: No. no.—Mr. Corlett : Well, we are going to put it to the test. (Applause.)—Mr. Birkhead: You have heard a pro- position, will you put it to the meeting .P—The Vicar: I say I object —Mr. Corlett: I beg to propose Mr. Birkhead as the Vicar's warden. (Cheers.)—The motion was seconded by Mr. Lane.--After further disorder, Mr. Corlett said: If it is your wish to appoint a Vicar's warden, you can do so. If he (the Vicar) leaves his place on his own account, this I meeting will lee adjourned to another night, and we will then have another jolly good do. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. George Appleton (the newly-elected warden) kereupon I stepped forward, and said if the Chairman would not put a vote to the meeting which was duly proposed and seconded, his duty as chairman would cease. (Rear, hear.) —After abother delsy, Mr. Corlett said if the Vicar would not proceed to business he would move that Mr. Appleton be the chairman.—Mr. Birkhead said he was of opinion that if the Chairman refueed to go on with the business his duty

as Chairman would cease. fie believed they were only doing justice to themselves in appointing a new chair- man. He load seen it done before, and he believed it was right to do it. On that account he had pleasure in second- ing the motion.—The Vicar: Before you put that motion have to say that I object to it (Groans and hisses.)—Mr. ilirchall submitted the motion, and it was carried unanim- ously.—Mr. George Appleton thereupon assumed the presi- dency—the hour being 10-30, the meeting so far having been lasted over three hours. Mr. Appleton at once pro. needed to put the motion to the meeting, that Mr. 13irkhead be the Vicar's warden, and it was agreed to unanimous'''. Three cheers for Mr. Birlitioad were called for, and the tip- peal was lustily responded to. Hisses and groans were given for the Vicar.—The appointment of sidesmen wag next proceeded with. The following gentlemen were pro- posed and seconded :—Messrs. F. Harwood, Lane, G. Owen, Burchall, Nevitt, Scott, Molyneux, and B. Corlett.—.T Vicar: I object—(prolonged 'limiest—l object to the follow. ing names--Mr. Corlett: The side wind is coming; leek out. (Laughter.)—The Vicar: I object to the following names :—Mr. Molyneux. Mr. Scott, Mr. Nevitt, Mr. Georg* Owen, Mr. Lane, and Mr. Corlett.—Notwithstanding the protest of the Vicar these gentlemen were appointed side/. men amid much applause.—Mr. Corlett: We have now II propose an organist for the coming year. (Cries of "W. ; Darman again.") I shall be very glad nocsonly to heat Mr. Durman's name proposed but anybody else's, and it will give this meeting a fair test of saving whe they 1141! I have. ("No one else.") I propose Mr. Durnaan.—(Cheers.) Mr. Birkhead : I have very great pleasure in seconding Mr. Durman's nomination. (Renewed cheers.)—The Vigo I think Mr. Corlett has been informed, or has seen informa- tion at any rate, in writing, or heard it said, that the sp. pointment of organist rests with the incumbent. (Cries of " No, no ;" "Who pays him ?" and general uproar.) therefore assert my right and claim rev right of appointing the organist of St. John's Church,: and I emphatically gh- I ject to Mr. Durman's appointment (Vigorous hissing and I hooting.)—Mr. Birkhead : It is just a case of—he objects, and we dare him to test it. (Cheers.) If the p.ople in the Church of England have any rights of such a nature worth competing for now is the time for testing them. (Applause.) I will say this—that if a congregation meeting under the Church of England ministers have nothing on earth to de but to find the money, to gratify a lot of ministers whether they like them or not, I say the sooner the Church is disestablished the better. (Cheers.) I have heard that the Bishop of Liverpool and lots of enai- nent men belonging to the Church of England wonder why' the Church of England cannot get hold of the manse& There is no wonder why the Church of England neler reaches the masses, because we seem to be driven like a lot of sheep to the slaughter—as if the only thing they want from us is money. If this is to be a test case let us test it to the last. (Cheers.)—The motion t -rat Mr. Darman should be re-elected organist was then put to the meeting and carried.—Mr. Birkhead said be had pleasure in moving that Mr. Durman's salary be £4O per year as usual —Mr, Lane seconded the motion, which was passed with acclam- mation.—On the motion of Mr. Corlett, seconded by Alt- Taylor, Mr. Stacey was re-elected church cleiner.—The list of elected officers was then read over, and the Vicar asked that his objrction should not be forgotten. (Hisses.)—/dr. Appleton said he would propose a vote of thanks to Mr. Matthews for conducting the first part of the business. -- Repeated hisses and groans were given, however, and the motion was not seconded.—.& vote of thanks was moved le Mr. Appleton, and accorded with cheers.— This brought the meeting to a close.—The Vicar asked for the police to he called in to protect him in retiring, and in a short time P.S. Commins and P.C. Lloyd entered the room. As the Vicar left the room in their company, he was loudly hissed and groaned at.

The Sporting Chronicle of Tuesday says :—" Sunda/ amusements at the St. John's Church, Earlestown, will be conducted as usual during the Easter festival—only more so." Such might, and should, have been the announcernest placarded outside the place of worship named, in anticips- Lion of Easter Sunday's advent, for we feel quite certain tbst many people, who might otherwise have attended and par- ticipated in the frolicsome amusements provided at the Earlestown church on Sunday morning last, only remainee away because they thought that even the noisy Christiansof that place would have sufficient common decency to Cur , pend their petty and discreditable quarrels on so bell, - Christian festival as Easter Sunday. Therefore a placard to the effect above suggested would, we think, have constitutes' a useful and eeneible announcement, considering the nature . of the programme which had apparently been specially Pft pared for, and which was carried out on Easter Sunday. may be remembered that on the previous Sunday the vicar announced from the pulpit that he had been to the troubi! 1 of bringing down a new organist, and that certain officers et the church bad prevented the new importation from fulfill" lug his duties. The vicar, moreover, expressed his deter- mination that the old organist should sot play the instrumeot however long he might wait to do so. As the congrego. tion, sidesmen, and churchwardens gathered for the forenoon service last Sunday, it was noticed that the nets' organist was again in his place by the order of the vicar, and certain persons were also engaged to " blow " the orgae for him. On this becoming known, however, the sidesmen went behind the organ with the object of preventing anyous " blowing" for the new organist, and at the same time be " blow " the instrument while the old organist playet There were thus two organists and two lots of " blowers,', which gave promise of plenty of " blows " being exchange° before ths performance was brought to a close. Shortly before the time for the commencement of service the old organist, who had been ordered to leave the chancel by the vicar, took a seat near the instrument, and at once com— menced to play. The vidar and curate then entered tbe church from the vestry, attired in their sarplicee,. and. 01 reaching the reading desk, the vicar announced to the con° gregation that there would be no service whatever in tb: church that day, The statement drew forth loud hisses e° hooting, whereupon the vicar hurriedly retired into the vestry, and one of the vicar's friends, who had promised to, blow the organ for the new organist, was et the same thee somewhat violently bustled 00t of the church. The choir and congregation thee resumed their seats, while the old organist played on the instrument, after which one of the sidemen of the church stepped forward, and, addressing tbs congregation, said he could not strongly enough express; ble regret at the scenes they had witnessed in the name of tett' gion and in the house of God. At this point the vicar en tired from the vestry, and having looked at the sidesman who was speaking, left the church again, amid hisses and groans. After the Doxology had been sung, the choir gathered up all their hymn and music books and left the church "on strike!' And that is as far as the Sande,/ amusements reached in the church on Sunday. It is Vie' that a sort of open-air gala was held in the fields in the evenieg, when some of the sidesmen addressed the conga- gation in denunciation of the vicar, but this could not be described ae anything like the success that the morning Per"' formancatad been in the churdh. It is, however, thought probable that a very attractive programme may again be arranged for next Sunday morning, and persons desiring to' engage reserved seats should make early application. Theo if the vicar, or either of the organists, gets his eyo blackened and his nose smashed en Sunday, it is considered possible that the Bishop may interfere to arrest the progtee6 of the amusements for the future, bat it is not likely that be will intervene until the chorus and " blowers " on BOA have actually struck something.

HOUSEEIOLD STORES TEA PAP.TY. AND, CONCERT. One of the most popular gatherings in the year, sofa Earlestown is concerned, has hitherto been that promote,' by Mr. Thomas Molyneux, of the Household Store, Market-street, and the proceedings on Tuesday prove that it has lost none ef its favour with the public.
