Too MUCH A MAN OF CUFFS AND COLLARS—THOU TBZ sTREET-VAGRANT'S POINT OF VIZIV.—The policeman. A lady of a certain age says that the reason an old maid is generally so devoted to her cat is that, not having a hus- band, she naturally takes to the next most treacherous

" OusTa."—Pater: "Knowledge my bey, is better than wealth." Filius: "Well, d'you "Knowledge, sir, I think I prefer the inferior article! • SaIIETRING To BE READ TO BETTER HALVES.—" If in our school-days the rule of three' is proverbially trying how tench harder, in after-life," writes a melancholy one, "do we feel the rule of one l" Mrs. Thrifty, to shopman : "If you will cut me a small sample of this, I will find out from my dressmaker how many yards I need, and can send for the goods by post." Awful child "Why, mamma, that's just what you said in all the ether shops! " A DEsat-ATIc Duo.—Scene—Highland cottage; time— Sunday morning. Duncan: "Are you in, Tonal ? " No answer. Duncan; " Ah, wed, am gaun awa' ! A cam' tae treat you, though, Tonal." Tonal, earnestly : "Stop, stop, Dancan--she'll be in noo ! Och, ay—och, ay I "—Bailie. Scandal would be rare if everybody were like the Moham- Laden official to whom Sir Austen, then Mr., Layard, the • eastern explorer, wrote for some statistics of the city in Which he lived. The official's reply ran as follows :—" My Illustrious Friend and Joy of my Liver,— The thing you ask of one is both difficult and useless. Although I have passed all ray days in this place, I have neither counted the houses nor have I inquired into the number of inhabitants ; and, as 'to what one person loads on his mules and the other stows away in the bottom of his ship, this is no businesa of mine. Ilut, above all, as to the previous history of this city, Heaven only knows the amount of dirt and confusion that the infidels may have eaten before the coming of the sword of Islam. It were unprofitable for us to inquire into it. 0 _MY soul, 0 my lamb, seek not after the things that concern "tee not! Thou cemest unto us, and we welcome thee. go peace." SKR OBLIGED HlN.—Edwin Booth, the American actor, ~/reo once playing Petruehio with an actress considerably larger than himself, and he thought she let go the whip too readily when, as Petruchio, he wrested it from the hand of Yatharina. So, after the play was over, he said, " You must hold on to the whip with more firmneea to-morrow night. Grabp it as hard as you can; I'll get it away from never fear!" The next performance of Shakespere's 14fting of the Shrew came, and the melancholy-eyed trage- L"ao, who, for the nonce, was essaying comedy, attempted 'toile the instrument of flagellation from his female aUPPOrt." It was of no use. She held on to it with a Teel) of 'iron, and the audience soon began to see the joke, and ~,,,„.,aPPlauded the actress to the echo. Finally, out of pure she unloosed her hol4, and the play pro- Ceedod the curtain fell, the actor had no further ad- Tice to give. An anusing incident occurred at Fortress Monroe on the breaking out of the war between the North and South. The fortress commanded the entrance to Chewaneake Bay, and thy sentinels were ordered to hail all passing boats and make them "heave to," in order that they might be searched for contraband articles. Early one morning a sentinel saw the eyster-fleet passing by, a negro slave in command of each boat. The sentinel hailed the fleet, and ordered the boats to "heave to;" but the ignorant negroes, not recognising the right of the sentinel, kept straight on for Norfolk. In a few minutes a shot was fired ahead of the foremost boat, and then another and ano her, until one was sent right over a boat's stern. This wastes° much for the negro captain to stand. Raising himself to his fall height, he shouted to the soldiers "Quit your foolishness! You'll be killing a valuable nigger if you don't mind! I'm gwine straight home and I'll tell massa. Do ye heah ?" And he did. When his master told him that war had been declared, and he must not go 'GI oystering" any more, the negro was bewildered. "Well, massa," ke exclaimed, scratching his head, "what will ,become ef misses and the children? I ain't got any odder

_ way to s'pote 'em !" Ittnucan Him To Comm—During the high water a man vraa seen going down the Arkansas on a log. As he was Passing Little Rock several men sprang into a skiff, rowed -out to the lone navigator and said: Climb in." "Climb in whar ?" "In the skiff, hurry up." "Wall, strangers, I'm pretty well fixed. Don't take no work to move along." "Where are you going ?" "Down the river." "We know that. Where are you from ?" "From up the river." "Of 401111345 you are, but—" "What made you ax, then ?" " What are Ton doing on that log ?" "Travellin'." "What 410 you want to fool with us for? Don't you know you'll *own if you keep on in this way ?" "Won't drown if I beep on this er way. Ef I wuster to git off in the water I IWOut drown." "How far have you come this way ?" "I've conae this way all er long." "But where were you when you got on the log?" "On the log" "Of course, but where Was the log ?" "In the river." "Certainly, but how far from here ?" "Ain't made no calculation." "Where do You live when you are at home?" "At home." "Of course, but where is y our home?" " Whar I live." "Where is Your family ?" "Scattered er long." "Did your house .Wa'sh away?" "Sorter. ,My wife's back yonder on a cot- "_mwood log, an' my son Bill's cumin' along "som'ers on a Poplar." "Why don't you come to the shore ?" ‘. cause it don't cost nuthin' ter ride." "You'd bettor come out and get a drink of whisky." "Dinged if I don't do it. Feller ,back here wanted me to come out an' hear him preach, but r didn't have the right kin' o' gospel. Now, fellers, put fur the shore as fas' as yer ken."

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

- DOITELE CHARGE AGAINST A HUSBAND—At the Town Hall, St. Helens, on Saturday, before Alderman Harrison and Mr. Sinclair, a young man named Patrick Hart, who had been apprehended en a warrant, was fined 5s and 79 6d costs for assaulting his wife by striking her in the face. Prisoner was afterwards arrested by the Prescot police on a charge of neglecting to maintain his wife and family, he having deserted them about ten months since. The woman had been in the workhouse for one week in July last, and the bench remarked that it was a shame to put the warrant .in force against him now. SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY—On Monday Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy-coroner, held an inquest at the Rifle Corps Inn, Windle, on the body of Thomas Davis, 5 years of age, son of John Davis, collier, Lowe-street, who died on the previous Thursday from injuries accidentally received. On the Wednesday morning preceding, about seven o'slock, the deceased came downstairs and stood too near the fire. His clothes got ignited and were soon all in dames. The poor lad's screams brought his mother to his assistance, but not before serious injuries had been inflicted all over his body, of which he died on the following day. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." BAD rism —A large amount of bad fish was seized at St. Helens railway station last week by Dr. McNicoll, the medi- cal officer-of health, and Inspector Coughtrey. On the pre- vious Monday 1D boxes of mackerel arrived at St. Helens, from Kinsale, via Holyhead. They were consigned to Wm. DUO, St. Helens, and en Monday the fish were believed to he in good condition. Dean, however, only paid the carriage of four boxes, which he removed, leaving the others until he could pay for their carriage. Bat as he did not return for the remaining 15 boxes (containing about 1,800 mackerel) the inspector's attention was called to them, and after an inspection they were found to be unsound and un- fit for human food, and the whole of the fish was at once condemned. FIRE AT A Sr. HEINNS CHEMICAL WORlES.—Between four and five o'clock on Wednesday afternoon an alarm was given at the St Helens Fire Brigade Station that a fire had broken out at the chemical works of Mr. Thos. Walker, Merton-road, Parr, and wi h all possible haste the fire engines and brigade were despatched to the works in ques- tion. It turned cut, however, that their services were scarcely needed. It appears that a " finishing pot" of caustic burst, and the liquid leaking out and spreading itself in the slack below caused an immense quantity of smoke. The men prevented any serious consequences by covering up the caustic with slack, and so smothering the fire. It is understood, however, that .£lOO will hardly cover the damage. SERMONS AND LECTURE BY RET. P. MACIENZIE.—The Rev. P. Mackenzie visited the Nutgrove Wesleyan Chapel, Thatto Heath, on Easter Monday, when a special effort was made in aid of the chapel fund. Service was held in the afternoon, and there was a large congregation, who listened with marked attention to the sermon by the Rev. P. Mac- kenzie. Subsequently a large number of persons partook of tea in the schoolroom, after which Mr. Mackenzie delivered hi popular lecture on " J.seph and his brethren." There was a very large attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Clarke, of Ditton, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Superintendent Johnson, who bad been announced to pre- side. The lecture was a very interesting one, pointing out the chief events in the life of Joseph, and the lessons that were to be learned therefrom. At the close a hearty vote of , thanks was accorded to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. , James Fogg, seconded by Mr. John Lyon. A Youranur. GAMESTER.—Before W. W. Pilkington and A. Sinclair, Eeqs., at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday 1 morning, John Riley, 12 years of age, was charged with gaming with cerde that morning.—The prisoner pleaded not , guilty.—P.C. Clarkson said that about a quarter-past ten I that morning he saw the prisoner in company with two 1 other boys playing with cards in Bold-street, Windle. They I were passing money backwards and forwards, and on seeing him (the constable) dray ran away, leaving some of the cards. He picked up the cards and followed them. The prisoner ran into a house, and witness caught him therein. The lad would not give his name or address, and the con- stable was obliged to bring him to the office.—The prisoner said he was not playing at cards, but was watching the others.—ln reply to the Bench, P.C. Clarkson added that the prisoner had some of the cards in his possession when he apprehended him.—The prisoner was ordered to be detained in custody for one day and then discharged. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON POLICEMEN.—At the St. Hel ens Police Court on Monday morning, before W. W. Pilking ton and A. Sinclair Esqrs., Edwin Jones, a young fellow was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Liverpool-road and also with assaulting P C.'s Huret and Ewalt. The prisoner said he did not recollect anything at all about the assaults.—P.C. Ewart deposed that the prisoner was very disorderly and violent, and he kicked him (the witness) several times, besides biting him severely on the band.— P.C. Hurst stated that the prisoner had kicked him on the face—leaving a mark on hie bottom lip.—The prisoner called a female witness who alleged that the constables had used unnecessary violence towards the prisoner. She said they both kicked him and struck him, and added that the mark on P.C. Hurst's face was not caused by a kick but by the handcuffs which accidentally hit him in the struggle.— The Bench fined the prisoner ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and 10s. and costs in each case of assault. In default of payment he would be committed to prison for seven days in each case. SERIOUS ASSAULT BY A YOUNG WomAar.-e-On Saturday at the St. Helens Town Hall, before Aldermen Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair, Elizebetn Borman, a young woman, was charged with unlawfully wounding a young man named Thomas Oleave, who resided in Cowley-street Superinten- dent Johnson stated that both parties worked at the Cowley Hill glass-works, and on the Friday afternoon the prisoner and her mother went to the prosecutor's house regarding some alleged familiarity. It was alleged that the prisoner struck him violently on the head with some hard substance which she held in her hand.-The prosecutor deposed that the prisoner struck him on the head with a large stone, which rendered him insensible and caused five wounds.—Dr. Don- nellan said he found prosecutor suffering from four wounds on the back of the head. They were punctured and lacerated wounds, but were not dangerous unless erysipelas set in.— The.prisoner alleged that the prosecutor had behaved very improperly towards her whilst she had been at work, and she had had to complain to the manager of the room about R.—She was fined 10s. and costs. _

CAPTURE OP JUVENILE BURGLARS AT ST. HELENS: IN- DUSTRIAL SCHOOL BOYS IN TROUBLE —Before C. J. Bishop, Esq., at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday morning, Robert Anwyle and John Breckland, lads, were charged with burglariously breaking and entering the dwelling-house of John Brockbank, pork butcher, Baldwin-street, and steal- ing therefrom one loaf, six cakes, some pig's head, and black puddings, value 2s 6d.—The prisoners admitted having ab- sconded from the Liverpool Industrial School farm at Newton-le-Willows.—Prosecutor said that between two and three o'clock that morning 1.13 heard a noise in the shop underneath his bedroom, and be went downstairs and called for the police. On searching the premises with Police- constable Lowe, one of the boys was found lying on one of the shelves in the cellar, and the other was underneath the counter in the shop. A hammer and chisel, which were not prosecutor's, were also found in the shop; and the articles named in the charge were placed on a chair. Three boots were found in the cellar, and one boot and an apron were found on the cellar grid, which bad been removed and a wire netting broken. An entrance had thus been effected. Both prisoners were with- out boots. A further charge was pref .rred against both prisoners of effecting an entrance through the cellar grid of the house, 60, Orrnskirk-street, and stealing therefrom an apron, value 6d, the property ef Mrs. Isabella Barris, grocer. Prosecutor said the apron was safe in a basket in the cellar at ten o'clock on the previous night; but that morning she noticed that the basket had been upset and the apron was gone. She found a knife, which did not belong to her, in the cellar, the grid of which had been disturbed. Both prisoners, who had nothing to say, were committed to the Assizes for trial.

TAMIN' A WIFE.

--- BY HENRI' YATES. "Jemmy t' Clogger," as fooak co'd him, wer a blade, an allus hed bin fro bein' a child. Th' only son of his feyther, he'd bin pampered au' spoiled a bit in his young days, an' when t' time coom for his dad to try an' mek someat on him in his own trade he'd a bigger job than he reckoned on, for reyt deawn mischief ther wornd his equal fro' St. Helens to Runcorn Brig. He'd poo fooaks signs deawn an' swop 'em, hid fooaks shutters, poo flags up an' cut their gas off, ged grocers to believe as black travel° wer beawn to rise an god em to lay in a big stock, an' then gooa up an' deawn to t' grocers' customers, an' tell 'ern they shouldn'd use traycle if they dudn'd want t' yellow fayyer. He's bin known to god o' t' childsr th' street, wi' bribin"em wi' a penny, to gooa to a perticular shop, au' ax for a bottle o' Yorkshire Relish, when he knew at t' same time thad shop never speculated i' owt o' th' sooart, an' god t' grocer as kept id to be persuaded wi' t' next traveller as co'd to take a gross o' bottles o' thad peppery stuff, thinkin' ther wer beawn to be a rare demand for id. A drinkseller 'Would as lief see th' Owd Lad come into his heawse as Jemmy, for he'd bin known to use burnt red pep- per at dances, drug their snuff wi' helibore, an' poo t' bungs eavrt e' ther casks, an' put allicker in. He's bin known to , chain a cat up in a piano to help t' music, an' stop fiddles 1 wi greosin' their strengs ; an aw've heard when he wer wed heaw his owd dad thanked his stars, thinkin' id would be t' I escorts o' mekkin' him meoar sensible. But astid o' this i Jemmy went woes o' t' two after he wer wed, for his wife bein' a daycent sooart of a woman couldn'd bide to hear of his carryins on, an' hoo tkowt hoo'd do her best to cure him bi' givin' him a sermon two or three times a day whol he , wer peighlen' away at his cloggin', allus finishin up wi'— "It's o for thi' own good, Jemmy." Whol Jemmy would sometimes sing, bein' a bit of a rhymer : Aw know it's for t' good, it's o for ml good Bad physic's for t' good too, they say; An' it's o just for t' good o' good leather, ml lass, As it's leather'd on t' lapstene each day. Gig me but ml lungs, an' o't' women their tongues, An aw'll sing whol yo preych abeawt me, For ther's nowt here on earth nobbut music an' mirth As con bring real contentment to me. Aw know it's for t' good, it's o for ml good To be talked to booath mornin' an' nest, An' at dinner time too, to be co'd a big foo, An' thee t' wisest wife i' o t' street. It's bin sooa sin' aw swaggered abeawt ml frock, When aw supp'd ml fost strong seeny tay, To be le bi ml nooas like a child i' long clooas Sermonised for mi good every day. Sooa'yo may guess this sermonisin' dudn'd gnoa deawn wi' Jemmy so wool. After o, an' when he thowt he'd had enough on id, he put his wits to work one day when his wife hed gie'n him an extra dose. "Aw'll cure her," said Jemmy to hissel, as he went eawt to visit an owd crony of his where he could hey a quiet glass an' bethink tassel wed to do; an' 800 a. after glass an' glass hed bin swallowed, an' Jemmy hed stared i'th' fire awhile 'till he thowt his wife would be i' bed, he wished t' landlord "good neet," an' set off deawn t' back street to some stables wheer ther wer a varra young donkey. This young donkey hed getten quite used to Jemmy an' he'd nod mich trouble i' geddin' id away fro th' owd jenny-ass, id mother, sooa, puttin' a kind of a hawter on id, he led id away to his own hooam, an' when he'd getten theer slowly poo'd his shoon off an' led t' donkey across th' shop floor to th' bottom o't' stairs, wheer he chained id tip, an' then quietly went upstairs to bed hissel. "Is thad thee, Jemmy ?" his wife axed, when he wer just tnrnin' t' leet up. "Ay," said Jemmy. "Aw think aw'm comin' to bed for t' last time." " Heaw's thad? Are ta ill ? ' " Avem welly deod," said Jemmy.

" Wheer are ta ill ?" Astid o' anawerin' her last question, Jemmy geet bed an' started o' rowlin' up an' deawn like a horse i'th' bally wertch. Wed ever mon aw do? Wod mon aw do, Jemmy?" hoo axes. "Hem ta oay brandy i'th' heawse ?" Jemmy answered. " Nowe, but aw can mon fntch some," he° said. "Well, be sharp, then, an' durn'd keawr cheer an watch me dee," said Jemmy, as he gave another rowl o'er i'th' bed. "Ther's nowt but triable i' this world," muttered Jemmy's wife, as hoo put her dressing gown on an slippers, whol Jemmy gave another turn over i' bed, an' Wl' eawt- stretched arm knocked booath t' candle ale t' matches to t' other side o' t' room off table aside on him. Ther wer nowt left but for Jemmy's wife to grope her way deawn t' stairs th' darkness, which hoo did. As soon as his wife wer heeard gooin carefully deawn t' stairs, Jemmy jumps eawt o' bed an' listens at t' top o'th' stairs tisee heaw hoo took to th' company at t' bottom. An' he hedn'd long to wait befoor he wer cenvinced as his wife wodn'd preych ageon for a day or two. Jemmy !" coons to him i' soft fn eten'd voice. "Jemmy !" a second time, in an agony- " Jemmy !!" a third time, like as hoo wer werning somebry to get eawt o'th' gate of a railway engine at Belthorn. "Is thad thee 7' axes Jemmy, putting his heyd o'er t' ballusters. "Ay ; an for t' sake of us booath, be sharp an' cone dea otn, for the devil's i'th' heawse," hoo said. Jemmy turned his face to laugh, bat he thought he'd plague her a bit longer. "What's thad—wod is ther i'th' heawse ?"

' The devil ; come deawn•for t' sake of us booath." "For t' sake of us booath ? "Ay !" "But he nobbut wants one, or else he'd come upstairs," said Jemmy. "Come deawn for t' sake o' me, then, for aw know aw've bin a bad un." "But aw'm a bit freetened mysel; an beside, it's happen for thi good as he's corned," put in Jemmy. Jemmy bed gone rayther too far, for he'd hardly getten t' last words eawt befoor his wife fell of her back an fainted at t' bottom o'th' stairs, an ther wer nowt left but for Jemmy hissel to gooa an look for sone brandy to bring her reawnd, aa' to ged t' jackass eawt o'th' Beet as soon as he could. It took mony a month after that befoor Jemmy's wife could believe as id war nowt but a jackass as freetened her thad neat, but it's bin "o for her own good," an Jemmy's too, for he hesn'd had as mony sermons fro' her as he had befoor' but Jemmy says its o because hoo cornd stand to be tovrd abeawt the devil comin' for her, because " hoo knew hoo'd bin a bad un."

The Nottingham Corporation has resolved to withdraw their opposition to the Trent Navigation Bill, and to buy the undertaking, representing a paid-up capital of £26,000, for £21,000. FRAUD ore CsceisTs.—At the Wolverhampton Quarter Sessions, on Thursday, Frederick Cooper was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for fraud Prisoner resided at Wolverhampton, and although out of business, advertised himself as a bicycle manufacturer. He thus got orders and money for bicycles which he never sent, By advertising in the Exchange and Mart he also obtained goods from per. Sons in various parts of the country under the pretence of exchanging them for bicycles. OIITBRBAK OF SMALLPDX AT SKI:MM.—At a meeting of the Sedgley sanitary authority, on Thursday, it was reported that five cases of smallpox had broken out in the district through a woman persisting in visiting her friends when suffering from smallpox. The 'medical officers said thgt unless something was done to stop the visiting the disease would be prevalent throughout the district. The orders of the officers wire treated with contempt by the people. It was decided to prosecute some-of the offenders. In the pedestrian races the quarter-mile ' handicap was won by L. Grainger, and the mile handicap by W. Rolley. FACTORY LlowszazioN.-51r. A. Belgrave, the Chief In- spector of Factories; has presented his report for 1883 to the Home Secretary. The Chief Inspector notices that it is now 50 years since the passing of the first effective Fac- tory Act, and remarks that the year 1883 may be distin- guished as the " jubilee" of facory legislation. It is stated lii an appendix to the report that in the twelve months ended the 31st of October last, accidents arising from machinery happened to 8,996 persons, and that the fatal easel were 395 males and five females.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1884.
A farmer named Cuff and his wife were buined to death at Kilbeg village, within half a mile of Claremorris, through their hotse taking fire, on Sunday night. The affair is at-

tributed to wilful outrage. SINGING IN ELEMENTAHT SCHOOLS.—A return issued by the Education Repartment shows that the encouragement given in the code to singing by note is hearing practical fruit. The proportion of schools in England and Wales teaching singing by ear has sunk from 83 4 per cent. to 79 6 per cent. In Scotch schools singing by note is much more COMIIIOII than in English, only 36 3 per cent no, th of the , tweed teaching singing by ear. In England end Wales the number of departments has increased during the year by 351, while the number singing by ear has decreas.d by 609; the number using the staff notation has increased by 96, and the number using the tonic sol-fa notation has increased by 900. Taking England, Wales, and Bcotland together, the percentage of schools singing by ear is 74 8; of those that teach singing 6y note the staff notation is used by 21 per cent., and the tonic sol-fa by 762 per cent. Goon TRILPLABS ANNUAL SESSIONS—The eighth annual session of the North-Western Grand Lodge of England, comprising the counties of Lancashire, Cheshire, Derbyshire, and the Isle of Man, was held at the Good Templar Hall, Warwick-street, Liverpool, on Monday, Bro. John Pritchard, W.C.T., presiding. There was a large attendance. The Grand Lodge decree was conferred on a large number of members. The G.W.C.T. read his report, which stated that the lodges in Cheshire were doing much better than last year. St. Helens and Present were holding their own ; Blackburn, Accrington, and Macclesfield rimorted good work dens. In the Isle of Man a new start had been made, with every prospect of success. A new lodge bad recently been opened in Douglas; a sew lodge at Prescot, and one in Col- quilt-street, Liverpcol. They had only a few friends in Manchester, Rochdale, Buxton, and Bury, which was a matter of great surprise, all places being noted for gcod tem- perance workers. As a matter of general interest, the , G.W.C.T. was not aware of any application for relief being made by any member of the order within the jurisdiction , of the North-Western Grand Lodge during the past year. The G W. Secretary (Bro. J. W. Chialitolm), the G.W. Treasurer (Bro. J. Parkin), and the General Superintendent of Juvenile Template (Bro. W. H. Kelly) also submitted their reports, which were highly satisfactory. A congratu- latory telegram was received from the North of England Provincial Grand Ledge, in session at Sunderland, and a suit.ble reply sent. The Grand Lodge next proceeded to the election of officers for the ensuing year, the following being chosen :—Bro. Samuel Capper, G.W.C.T. (Manches- ter); Bro. John Pritchard, P.G.W C.T. ; Bro. J. W. Chis- holm, G.W.C.•, Sister Morris, G.W.V.T ; Bro. Nicholson, G W.S. ; Bro. Parkin, G.W. (treasurer); Bro. Whitelock, G.W.M. ; Bro. Wild, G.W. (chaplain); Sister Kelly, G.D.M. ; Bro. Ackary, G. Messenger; Bro. Jacob Christian, G. Guard ; Bro. Sefton, G.A. (secretary ) ; Bro. W. H. Kelly, G.S.I.T. I Bro. Hathaway, P.G.W.C., in an able speech, recounted his I experiences during the Boer war, and urged increas d , earnestness in the work of the order. A motion coegratu- lating temperance friends on the acceptance of the Local Option resolution was adopted. The installation of officers then took place' and after some other business the Grand : Lodge closed. The annual session of the Good Templars' 1 Grand Lodge opened at Leicester, en Monday. The report I of Grand Worthy Chief Templar MalMs states that on the whole the order is in a satisfactory condition. Eighty thou- sand lodge sessions, 30,000 juvenile sessions, and 12,000 public meetings were held during the year ' • and while in , some places the Blue Ribbon movement has helped, in others it has hindered work. The naval and military lodges have I got over their internal troubles. The report recommended the appointment of a Grand Lodge Political Action Corn- mittee, with considerable powers. The hon. secretary : (Councillor Wood, Hartlepool), reports that on November 1 last there wereB6,ol4 members in 1 720 lodges, being a de- Crease of 45 lodges and 5,400 members; but against this it is stated that the first quarter of the current year gives a I considerable increase, the actual present membership , being in adult lodges 90,0000 and in the juvenile branch nearly 50,000. div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse ea Tuesday, Mr. Mclntyre presiding. There were present the Rev. John Lockwood, Messrs. J. Aehron, J. Derbyshire, E. A. Wallington, J. Warburton, Pickering, Stokes, C. Rigby, Acton, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). THIS CLIIRICS SeLLUir.—On the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. J. Ashton, the clerk's salary was Axed at £6O for the past 12 months with £25 added fk extra , 11111TFiCell. TEN MEDICAL OFFICRR.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Dr. Adams as medical officer until a successor to hr. Bride was appointed. MaDiOar. OFFICER'S &max.—Dr. Adams presented his quarterly report, which stated that during the quarter end- ids March 31st the Registrar's returns record 140 births and 94 deaths in the three districts comprised in the Rural Sanitary district of the Runcorn Union. Of the births 86 were males and 54 were females, representing a birth-rate of 7'2 per 1,000. against 144 births with a birth-rate of 74 ; per 1,000 in the corresponding quarter of 1883. Of the deaths 43 were males and 51 were females; death-rate 4 8 . per 1,000, against 85 deaths, with a death-rate ot 44 per , rin the corresponding quarter of 1883. Of the deaths wo ers persons under 5 years of age, 19 of these being one year and under ; while 61 were 5 years of age and up- wards. Ten deaths resulted from bronchitis, 7 from in- • flamruation of the lungs, 1 from congestion of the lunge; that was to say, that 16-8 per cent ot the total deaths re- sulted from inflammatory diseases of the orgAna of respira- tion, and this notwithstanding the extraordinary mildness of the weather daring the quarter of the year just ended. Be- sides these there were 2 deaths from scarlet fever, 2 from .neasles, 2 from whooping cough, 3 from typhoid fever, and from infantile diarrheas, together with 8 coroner's in- quests. 58R10175 OUTERRAIL OF :iCARLIIT FEVER AT WESTON.— The Medical Officer Jlso presented a special report, in which he stated that an exteosive outbreak of scarlet fever had taken place in the township of Weston. Up to Satur- day last he had a.scertained that the following persons had been attacked with the disease :—At a house occupied by John Todmore, in Sweetnam's-cottages, Maria Todmere, his wife, aged 37, Etizaiseth rodmore. aged 5 years, and Mar- garet Todmore, aged 3 years; at a house in Main-street, oc- cupied by James Mort, Annie Mort, his daughter, aged 4 years now convalescent; at a house in Main-street, occu- pied by George Douglas, Frederick William Douglas, aged 6 yeare, Jane ehotton Douglas, aged 2 years and 9 months, and Edith Douglas, aged 1 yeaqall programing favourably ; at a house in Pritcuard'a-row, behind Main-street, occupied by Frank Ligtatfoot, Richard Lightfoot, aged 3 yeats, John Lightfoot, aged 9 years, and Thomas Light toot, aged 6 years; at a house in Ford Benk, occupied by Wm. Norman, William Ernest Norman, aged 3 years. Frederick James Norman, aged 1 years, and Robert Norman, aged 8 years; at a house in Ford Bank, occupied by William Henry Wil- liams, Percy Herbert Williams, aged 6 years, and Charles Iderbert Williams, aged 4 years. Besides the cases reported above, he had reason to bedeve that the disease existed at other houses in the township, and he should endeavour to I I them all before the Authority at the next meeting. The cause of this outbreak was, in his opinion, to be found in the nearness of Weston and Runcorri, at which latter place scarlet fever, he was told, was very prevalent. He had taken all aeceesary steps in these cases. The diseese at present was of a mild type, and he trusted they should be able to keep this outbreak from further extension.—ln reply to a question, Dr Adams said he understood there were np- wards of a hundred cases of fever in Runcorn. F lIODSHAN WATER SUPPLY. The Frodsham Water Supply Committee tied held a meeting, and resolved that the consideration of all the claims, except Mr. Stretch's, be deferred, and that the solicitor to the Authority be instructed to make an offer of £5O to Mr. Stretch without prejudice, and inform him that the average quantity of water going down to Cattenleall is 620,000 gallons in 24 hours, and the quantity of water to be abstracted in 24 hours would be 42,000 gallons. PAROCILIAL COMMITTEE FOR FRODSILARL—Mr..I. Ashton give notice that at the next meeting he would move that a Parochial Committee be appointed for Frodeham and Frod- sham Lordship, and that the Authority delegate to that committee all the powers necessary. RUNCORN BO eILD OF GUARDIANS. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the forthightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there were present the Rev-. J. Lockwood, Mews. J. Ashton, Stokes, Norman, Challoner, Whittaker, P. Speakman, R. Ashton, Weir, Percival, W. Whitlow, Hamilton. Pickering, Warburton, Mclntyre Smith, Neild, Acton, E. A. Walling- ton, C. Rigby, W. Handley, J. Derbyshire, H. Linaker (clerk) and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). FINANCH Cosi. or RuNcoes Erscriote.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amount- Mg to £472 17s 2d, which included £64 5s 104 expenses incurred in the late elections for Runcorn and Weston. (Mr. Weir: It's abominable.) The sum included £165 8s LI for Mr. Timmins repairing the well; £73 13s 41, vaccination, registration and extra medical fees; £163 tis Id, mainten- ance of lunatice ; and £6 ss, nurse.—The Rev. J. Lockwood moved, and Mr. Norman seconded, the adoption of the

Tan WORKHOUSE DRAINIOE.—Mr. Derbyshire, as chair- man of the Workhouse Drainage Committee, observed that the drainage works were completed and everything seemed to be right. He understood there was a claim likely to be made for the cutting of the sewer across the "top field." The committee had not yet received a claim, and they were strongly of opinion that none could be reasonably made.— Mr. Rigby: He ought to pay us £5 for cutting the draie across his stiff stubborn field. I shall be strongly against paying one halfpenny. Tun DAY or MEETING.—Mr. Challoner moved, and Mr. Percival seconded, that the day of meeting be altered from Tuesday to Thursdity„ but the motion was lost by eleven votes to ten.

The CLERIC'S REMIINERATION.—The Deputy-Clerk read a report from the Assessment Committee, which stated that the committee had considered the remuneration to be paid the clerk, and had resolved that for ordinary duties in con- nection with the committee for the year ending Lady Day, 1884, he should be paid the same amount as last year—£7s. It was also resolved that in consideration of his additional labour in the revaluation of railway property, gas works, isc., he should be paid £llo.—Mr. R. Ashton said he had great pleasure in moving the adoption of the report. He wished to make a few remarks showing why the committee thought Mr. Linaker entitled to this remuneration. In 1872, when the railway property was re-valued by Messrs. Corbett and Co., the assessment was raised to £23,923, but it was afterwards reduced by appeals, and the total increase in the assessment was £5.000. Those appeals cost the Union £587. In 1878, six veers later, the committee asked the clerk to undertake the work of revaluation. He consented, and be met the managers of the railway company, and it was satisfac- torily arranged to increase the assessment by £6,535, which was done without any appeals whatever. The Board granted Mr. Linaker £lOO for his extra services, which he was not bound to undertake. Last year he had revalued the railway company's property, arid the assessment had been increaaed £4,313, while the assessment of the alkali works, Frodshare gas works, and other works, had also been increased by 'Mont £2,083. The total increase in the assessments for the last year was therefore £6,396, and the revenue of the Union would be increased by about £BOO per annum. Mr. Linaker was engaged in this work about 20 days outside his office, besides the besinees he would have to do in his office; and he left it to the members to judge whether the remuneration proposed was not well earned. Messrs. Corbett and Co. charged the Beard 10 per cent, on the increased valuation, but Mr. Linaker's remuneration was not quits 2 per cent.— Mr. Neild had great pleasure in seconding the motion.—Mr. Challoner observed that these increased valuations saved the farmers' pockets—(hear, hearl—and Mr. Linaker was entitled to the proposed remaneration if not more,—Mr. Handley and Mr. Norman supported the motion, 'which was carried unanimously.—The Clerk said he was very much obliged to the Guardians for confirming the decision of the i committee. He did not take these extra duties with. the I intention of making money out a f them. (Hear, hear.) If ha were employed by private parties be should get a grew deal more money, but he did not look upon his connection with the Union in that way. He did his duty to all fairly, whether it was the Board of Guardians, the Assessment Committee, or the Rural Sanitary Authority. In one Union recently the revaluation of the railways had cost .21,065 14s, and this did not include all the expenses, so that he thought the Runcorn Union in paying him £llO got very well out of it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Derbyshire remarked that Mr. Jones was entitled to some extra remuneration for services he had rendered with respect to drainage—(hear, hear)—and he should be glad if the committee coald meet to conaidar the matter. ( Efear, bear.)—On the proposition of the Rev. J. Lock wood, seconded by Mr. J. Ashton, Mr. Linakees na.lary as clerk to the School Attendance Committee was deed at £35 per annum. ATTENDANCE AT THB ABSESSMENT COMMITTEE. In accordance with a resolution, the attendances of members of vw.3 Assessment Committee were read. Out of a possible 12, llle.srs. C. Reynolde, bad made 9, A. Thomas, J.P., 11, E. A. vVrieht, J.P., 8. Colonel Talbot, J.P., 0, Thomas Norman 11, William Handley 10, John Weir 10, Joseph Knowles 9, John Clhallcner 7, Robert Ashton 7, Elenry Neild 6, Peter Percival 4. VOTES OF THANas —Mr. J. Ashton proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for his uniform kincienesps, and iiB never cour- tesy in the chair during the past year. found the proceedings of ether Boards of Guardians conducted so harmoniously as their own—(bear, hear)—and while the good temper of the members might aid this, he thought it was due in a great measure to the chairman. (Applause) —Mr. Norman seconded the proposition. The (Thairman had not been well for the past few months, and he was sure ' the members were highly pleased to see hien amongst them again. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Derbyshire supported the motion, which was carried by loud aoclamation.—The Chairman, in replying, observed that he was glad to see that the interests of the Board had not suffered during his absence, and this was to be attributed to the vice-chairman, Colonel Ashton, and also to the invariable good temper which had characte-ised the members of the Board. There might have been differences, but thSy had been few and far between, and had been settled in a courteous and amicable manner, and it was a great pleasure to preside over snch a Beard.—The Rev. .7. Lockwood moved, and Mr. W. Hind. ley seconded, a vote of thanks to the Vice-chairman, which was carried with acclamation, and Mr. Ashton suitably replied.—A similar compliment was paid to the Clerk and Depnty-Clerk. on the motion of Mr. Cballoner, seconded by _Mr R. Ashton, both gentlemen speaking of the able and

efficient way in which the business of the Board was carried on.—The Clerk observed that such a tribute was wholly un- expected, and he could only say he was very much obliged to them. He daresay he was the oldest official or member connected with the Board, having attended the meeting for upwards of 35 years. Of course the members paid him in other ways than by votes of thanks, which he did not expect. He might say that whether inside the office or outside the office, or in that room, he would always gladly give information to members of the Board whenever asked. ("Hear, hear," and applause.) He also returned thanks for I his deputy. The members then commenced to deal with the relief cases. INDUCTION AT ST. AMBROSE'S CHURCH. On Tuesday, toe Rev. S. A. Spooner, M.A.. was inducted to the living of the newly-consecrated church of St. Am- brose, Halton View, near Widnes' by the Bishop of Liver- pool. There was a fair congregation. Amongst the clergy present were the Revs. George Bond, M.A., vicar of Fame worth; J. Holden, curate of Farnworth : J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes; G. H. Spooner, vicar of Litherland ; E. 8. Jackson, vicar of Sankey; F. Lee, curate of Prescot ; and S. I A. Spooner. The deed of institution to the adrowson con- tained the names of the following gentlemen, as trustees:— Row. George Bond. Messrs. T. Sutton Timcnis, George Pil• , kington, Enstace Carey, and John Stock, each of whom was present. His lordship delivered a practical and appropriate discourse from 1 Cor. ii., 2: "I determined not to know any- thing about you save Christ and Him crucified." He com- menced nis remarks by a rate:, ace to the state of luxury which prevailed in Corinth at the time when Paul visited that city, and the many references to the apostle's personal experience in that city as compared with the scarcity of , them in other letters to the Christian churches. He pro- ceeded to say that they were met upon a very solemn and serious occasion—viz., that of the public induction of a new minister into the perpetual curacy or incumbency of St. Ambrose's Church. A gentleman taking upon him the sacred office in connection with a new building and' a new district ought to be the object of their deep interest and sympathy. His lordship went on to observe that when be was a young man it was the cus- tom in Surrey to induct the minister in private. He had always felt that to adopt such a course was to throw away, as it were, a great occasion; and when he was appointed to the honourable office of bishop of that diocese, he •felt he should like such a ceremony to be a public one. 'He had acted upon that principle in publicly inducting Mr. Spooner that day. He commended their minister to their hearty sympathy and help in the arduous work he had undertakes, and pronounced before all of them his biasing upon all that Mr. Spooner might do. His lordship then urged upon the candidate the paramount necessity of following the noble example set by Paul in subordinating everything in his teaching to the cardinal truth of "Christ and Him cruci- fied." He next referred to the wonderful and abiding in- fluence of the name of Christ, though His public ministry was of such short duration. Infidels might sneer and cart the lip at some of the stories related in the Bible but they had never been able to fleda reasonable explanation of the wondrous Influence wielded by One who came without the weight of a great name and without money and power. Nelson at Trafalgar died on the way to victory; and Wolfe on the ladighte of Abraham, at Quebec, died listening to the words, "They fly, they fly ;" but when the Saviour expired every- thing appeared to have gone against Him. After a reference to the importance of preaching the verity of Christ's death as a satisfaction for the sins of the world, the speaker pro- ceeded to sketch the effects of a true preaching of the Gospel as instanced in the work of the Apostles in Asia Minor, and the power which was in Martin Luther's pro- clamation of the old doctrine of justification by faith. It was this pure gospel preaching which wrought such a won- derful influence by means of Whitefield, Wesley, and Romaine, about a hundred years ago, when church and chapel were alike asleep. The declaration of this grand doctrine of "Christ and Him crucified," would, if pro- claimed in the neighbourhood of Halton View, prove a blessing to the ministry of Mr. Spooner, to whom he hoped Almighty God would grant every success. A collection was then made, and the proceedings ter- minated in the usual manner.

div.head: WARRINGTON VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: WARRINGTON VESTRY MEETINGS.

PARISH CHURCH. The annual vestry meeting was held on Tuesday. The Rector of Warrington, the Rev. W. Quekett, presided, and amongst those present were the following : Messrs. Dooley (vicar's warden), Wright (people's warden), H. B. White (vestry clerk), Hunt (chief constable), S. Higham, J. E. Wright, Cowley, J. Morris S. Davies, J. R. Buckton, Tanranac, Porter W. S. Howard, H. Orford; Jones Whittle, J. P. Leigh, Reid ' , Francomb, Dewhurst, Scotson,Hutchin- son, Heminvway, Chidlaw, &c.—Mr. Buckton and Mr. Tauratiac then proceeded to audit the accounts, which gave a total income of £297 7s 2.1, leaving a balance in hand of £7 Os 7d, the expenditure having been £290 6s 7d. On the Church Repairs Fund account the total receipts had been Jl3OO 153 2d, and the expenditure £2BB 14s 41, leaving a balance in hand of £1.2 Os 10d. There was a bill of £l6 108 yet to be received.—Theaccounts were passed on the motion of Mr. Highatn, seconded by Mr. Portor.—Mr. Tauranac thought Mat it would be wise if the accounts were in future audited before the meeting, and pro- posed that two auditors be appointed.—Mr. Dooley did not think they could carry out that plan and asked what would be done if one of the persons ap- pointed died before the time of the meeting.—After a short discussion an amendment to the effect that the accounts be audited at the vestry meetings as usual was carried.—The Chairman wished to make a few observations. It had been his hope, be said, to continue the next year as had been the case in the past, and he did not wish for any changes, but circumstances had occurred that caused his present church- warden not to wish to again take the position. Mr. Dooley had served him faithfully for live years; he heartily thanked him for doing so. He thought that it was cus- tomary when a vicar's warden had to be chosen to appoint the people's warden,-and so he had nominated Mr. Wright as his warden for the ensuing year. He (the Chairman) had the anxious wish to live in friendliness with everyone, and hoped that whoever might be appointed the people's churchwarden would be loyal and friendly towards the Rector. He should be very sorry to have any unpleasant- ness, and there were so many connecting links between the Rector and the wardens.—Mr. Francomb was then appointed people's warden, and the following were appointed sides- men :—Messre. Moores (Mr. Wright's), J. Dewhurst (Mr Francomb's). Morris, Gill, Cawley, and Percival.—A volun- tary church rate of 3d in the £ for the ensuing year was laid, on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr: Cawley. —Mr. Buckton and Mr. Webster were re-appointed lay re- presentatives, on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. Dewhurst.—A. vote of thanks was passed to the chair- man.

BT. PAUL'S. The vestry meeting of the parishioners of St. Pawl's was held on Monday morning. The vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkin- son, occupied the chair, and there were ale° present Messrs. Jolley (vicar's warden), Sutton (people's warden), Jeans (vestry clerk), W. Finney, Leeson, Parry, Gibson. LaWloeB, Pollitt, Hough, Holbrook. Bebington, and Lawton.—Mr. Sutton, on laying the statement of receipts and expenditure before the meeting, said that they had commenced the pre- vious year with a debt of upwards of £BO owing to trades- men, which was, in fact, a sort of legacy left to himself and Mr. Jolley when they took office. Their income having , been limited to the pew rents, the church collections and 'the proceeds of the annual tea party, they had not only been unable to reduce their liabilities, but the liabilties were increasing instead of diminishing. In consequence they decided, two years ago, to have collections made every Sun- day evening instead of every other Sunday. According to 1 the accounts their income for the past year had. been £l7O 1148 30, which was made up as follows :—Pew rents £32 19s, Sunday evening collections £9B 148 Bid, the annual tea party £39 7s, The accounts also showed that their expenditure for the same period, in- cluding payment of the old debts of £BO, had been £221 5s lid, an excess of £5O odd of expenditure over income. The expenditure was made up as follows : Salaries £95 14s 10d, tradesmen's bills for repairs, dec., £42 Is Ad, old accounts due to tradesmen £B2 78 51d, fees, ttc., it 2s. 'To enable them to make the whole of these pay- ments and clear off the old debts they were indebted to the liberality of Sir Gilbert Greenall, But., who, learning that they were in debt, had, with his ,usual generosity, volun- tarily come forward with a promise of £5O to help them through their difficulties. They might now really consider themselves out of debt, and they might congratulate them- selves that they stood in a better position at the commence- ment of the present year than they did at the last. He thought they had now got rid of their legacy, and hoped that they would be able to steer clear of debt in the future. —Mr. Jolley thought the statement just made a yery gratifyiog ene.—The Chairman said that it was very satis- factory, through the liberality of Sir Gilbert Greenall, to find themselves once more free men.—The accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. Finney, seconded by Mr. Lee- son, and a vote of thanks was accorded to Sir Gilbert Greenall for his promised donation, on the motion of Mr. Gibson, seconded by Mr. Parry.—The Chairman, in re- appointing Mr. Jolley as his warden, thanked him warmly for his past services. Tne y must also allow him to thank the people's warden, Mr. Sutton, and the eight gentlemen who had acted as sidesmen. It was a great pleasure .to transact their business at the vestry meeting in such a united manner as they were then doing. In the charchwai dens of St. Paul's they had men respected throughout the town, and who had the interests of the parishioners at he art.—Mr. Jolley, in reply, remarked On the improvements that had taken place since the chairman cams to the pariah, and proceeded to say that the church, situated in such a populous neighbourhood, was becoming more and more a workingmen's church, and he theught that if the rich people in the parish only knew the good that was being done to their workpeople, they would give the church their aid, as the improvements could not be con- Maned without money. He suggested that it would be a good plan to improve and beautify the ground around the church, and he thought, if that were done, tbe public would help to share the exp-nse, as it would be like a little p irk in that densely populated neighbourhood. It could be done I at a little cost, and he thought that if the idea was carried , ont many pecitile would help them—Mr. Finney said that it had been his privilegetopropose occasion,,t a t and Mr. hteadVidiriliobt" kind obwe people's warden on several that he had ever had greater pleasure than at present in so doing. They were blessed with St. Paul's in having two good churchwardens who took a great interest in all that concerned the welfare of the parish. Charles Fisher and Mr. Harry Bretherton were was another phase of the question that was worth consider- elected lay representatives, and the usual votes of thanks ing, and that was the conservancy of rivers and prevention concluded the meeting of floods. He thought they would all agree that it was high Ilan time some steps were taken to regulate the unequal discharge of water in the rivers. There was an immense source of power running rapidly past them at one time, and then in a few hours it might be that they had hardly enough water to drown a cat. All this WRS capable of regulation, and un- til they got that regulation they should have to endure periodical and inopportune floods with their consequent damage and inconvenience. It was not for them there to ' discuss the system upon which this conservancy should be carried out, nor how the expenses of so doing should be levied. Let the legislature determine. It was apparent, from the figure he had given, that the great bulk of the water was gathered on the uplands above Manchester, and the rivers having sharn inclinations discharged their volume with immense rapidity upot those who dwelt upon the fiats; and it would go hard with these latter if they had to bear the entire cost of any works in- curred for the relief of floods. There was no doubt, if the , Ship Canal was made, the discharge of this river would be ' entirely altered, as by locking the canal there would be a series of settling ponds into which the water would be gathered and passed off systematically at regular and fre- quent intervals; and at the same time sufficient water would be ensured to those now using it for trading purposee ; nor would there be any danger of the old channel silting up, as sluices would be fixed in various places to pass, when raised, a volume of water that would thoroughly scene the deposit in :the bed of ;he river. If the Ship Canal be not con- structed, then they should have to endure the existing order of things for very many years, as it was quite certain Par- liament was given up to Egypt and reform, it would be many sessions hence before such a practical and useful measure as the Rivers Conservancy Bill would beceme law. The question was no doubt a comprehensive and intricate one, but it was one that must be dealt with sooner or later. It was not in the nature of things that the owners of the low lying lands would stand by much longer and see them depreciating, nor would the agriculturist in these times be prepared to let his crops be destroyed without a loud murmur. He hoped that those of them who were members of the Town Council and the Chamber of Commerce would not lose sight of the importance of ever keeping the question promi- nently before them. In conclusion, he hoped that he had been able to show them what a great power in the material prosperity of the country their dirty river was. One hun- dred ye ire ago it supplied the power to turn these water wheel, and turbines that set the early machinery in motion, thus being the great sustainer of those industries which had so rapidly grown in this part of England. About the same era, too, ire waters were diverted into those wonderful canals by which Brindley revolutionised the whole system of in- terne' communication. As the use of steam crept in the water power was abandoned, and the grit was need for a con- tensing with huge workehops. When sanitary reformers &ming pond, end the river side became more thickly celled the attention of the people to the danger of using the surface wells and the much-cherished pumps, another source of eupply was sought, and engineers at once went to. the heads of the valleys and tapped the bright streams and rivulets, damming them up before they reached the rivers and forming some of the most magnificent systems of water supply in the world. Who could say then that the most had not been made of their river? (Applause.) Mr. T. G. SOITILWORTH-WITH-CROFr ocHOOL WA/D.-The monthly meeting at the above Board was hel4l at the Board School, on Tuesday evening. Present: Messrs. Richard Turner (vice-chairman), James Hatton, Lewis, Birchall, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer). The attendance officer reported that the average attendance at the Board School for the past month had been 120. He also gave the names of several children in irregular attendance at school, whose parents will be summoned 'before the magistrates next month, unless they send their children more regularly to school. Several accounts having been passed, the proceed- ings terminated. Vromairr ASSAULT ow Tun POLICE.—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. John Fairclough (in the chair) and Alderman Chandley. James Farrell, a labourer, last from Rochdale, was charged with being drunk on the previous afternoon in Bank-street; with assaulting P.C. Williams whilst in the execution of his duty at the same time and place; also with assaulting Mary Farrell, Margaret Carter, and William Forester, and with doing damage to the extent of 108 61 to the trousers of William Barrows.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) informed the Bench that the assaults committed by the prisoner had been of a most violent and unprovoked character. He as- saulted his sister and P.O 's Williams and Johnston saw him acting in a most disorderly manner in Bank-street. Without remonstrating with him, as he was indiscriminately assault- ing anyone, the officers proceeded to take him into custody. A Mr. Dobson would tell the Bench that he saw the prisoner threw alarge stone and hit as little child in the face. When taken into custody he began to kick the officers. Mr. Bur- rows, County Court bailiff, was near at the time and as- sisted the constables, and he was also assaulted. The prisoner had been brought up for similar offences a number of times before, but never for a worse offence than the pre- sent. —P.C. Williams was then called, and said that at six o'clock on the previous afternoon he was called to Bank- street by the prisoner's sister. fie there saw the prisoner drunk and assaulting people. Witness told him he must go to the police-station with him, whereupon the prisoner cursed and swore, and said that he would not. P.C. John- Mon and witness then got hold of him, and got him down. Ile then kicked violently, witness receivingone of the kicks on his face. Mr. Burrows came to their assistance, and with great difficulty they got him to the police-station. On the way prisoner assaulted Mr. Burrows and tore his trousers.— PC. Johnston, in corroborating, said that the prisoner kicked him once in the back and twice on the legs.—A Mr. Dobson said that he heard the row, and saw the prisoner dancing about the street and defying everybody near. Wit- ness did not know whether he was drunk or mad, but should think that he was mad drunk. He saw prisoner strike an old lady who never spoke to him. He then picked up a stone and hurled it some distance. A woman was standing near with a child in her arias, and the stoma narrowly missed the child and struck a little girl. Prisoner was then taken away.—Mr. Runt: It took four or five to bring him.—Mr. Burrows deposed to assisting the police, and to receiving severe blows on the leg and arm. His trousers were very , much torn.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said that he would never get drunk again.—Mr. Hunt said that he believed when the prisoner was drunk he was quite nn• accountable for his action:l.—Prisoner said that be never interfered with anyone when he was seber.—Mr. Hunt: That is tree ; when he is sober he is quite enough.—Pri. sonar was committed to prison for four months with hard labour, the Bench deciding that Mr. Burrows should be ;remunerated.

Mr. BURGESS moved that the following gentlemen form the new Council :-President, Mr. T. G. Rylands ; vice-presi- dent, Rev. Canon Dodd ; hon. treasurer, John Dun; council, Mews. H. Blackly, R. Davies, C. Broadbent, Rey. Gibson Smith, and C. White, and J. R Young (hon. secs.) The double character of the society, Mr. Burgess said, was to some extent maintained by appointing Mr. Rytands as-pre- sident. Canon Dodd had represented their literary side and Mr. Rylands represented their philosophical side. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Mounts seconded the proposal, which was car- ried unanimeusly.—On taking the chair Mr. RYLANDS said the time woald come, sooner or later—and better sooner than later---when the young men in that society would have to come forward and take their share in its proceed- ings. That they could do it they had abundant proof that night. He suggested that they should take steps to gradu- ally lead the members to take more interest in the proceed- ings of the society, and he invited any member to send in any suggestion which they thought might operate to the benefit of the society.—A. vote of thanks to Canon Dodd. the president of last year, moved by Councillor BuoannarrT, and seconded by Mr. Yocum, Was carried; as was also a vote of thanks to the hon. secretaries (Messrs. White and Young).—The meeting then terminated.

THE DEATH Eln DROWN/MG.—On Saturday afternoon ani inquiry was held at the Three Pigeons, Tanners'-ape, War- I rington, before Mr. liueband, deputy-coroner, into the cir- cumatances attending the death of a boy named Benjamin Cox (10), son of Joseph Cos, of Pitt-street, Warrington, who was drowned on Wednesday afternoon in the canal at Bewsey-lochs, as reported in our last issue.—lienry Harper (11); Albert-street, a Tompanion of the deceased, gave evi- dence to the effect: that on Wednesday afternoon he was playing with the deceased near the edge of the water. The deceased over-balanced hianaelf and fell in. Wits tried to pull him Out but could not,,as he only rose once, aad was then about a yard frornAhe aide. The body was recovered by some flatmen.—The jury returned a verdict of " Acci- dental death."

ALLEGED FRAUD.—At the Warrington Police Court, on Friday, James Newton', an carter living in Orford-lane, was - charged with having obtained eight tons of manure, value 50s, from Mr. John Longshaw, brielsmaker, Lyinm, with intent to defraud kirn.—A., man named Mania Ward, of Cartwright-street, stated that on the =ad ult. the prisoner visited the yard where the manure was kept. and, represeat- ing that Mr. Longsbarrisaduold it to him, got possession of the manure in question.—The prosecutor said it was not true that be had sold the manure to the prisoner, but the Bench said they were not eatisfied as to the case, and would consequently adjourn it for a week, in order to allow of the appearance of a farmer to whowliewton said he had sold the manure.

FUNERAL OF COUNCILLOR WOOLFALL.—The mortal re- mains of the late Councillor WooVali, whose death was announced in our last issue, were interred in the Warrington cemetery on Saturday. The funeral cortege left the resi- , deuce of the deceased shortly before noon and proceeded to the cemetery, where the service was conducted by the Rev. P. W. P. Montgomery, curate of the Parish Charch. The following members of the Town,Council atteuded, viz.: —The Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Kean, Bar- gees, Webster, and Pickrnere ;. Councillors J. Pierpoint, Joseph ashton, J. Brown, W. Pierpoint, Taylor, Caldwell; and Messrs. J. L. Whittle (deputy-tows clerk), and T. Lengdin (borough surveyor.) Amongst the other mourners present were Mr. Hunt (chief constable), Dr. White, and Messrs. D. W. Finney, Hampson, W. Fairhurst, G. Mackey. J. Shaw Green, William Dickens, J. Smethurst, A. Woollen. , (son of the deceased), Edward Middleton, William Whitley, Charles Middleton, F. Taylor, Smith, Platen. Howard, kc. GIVING HER ANOTHER CEancn. —At the Warrington , Police Court, on Tuesday mornibg. a wornae named Mar- garet Fleming was brought befora-Captain Litton on a charge ; of being drunk and disorderly in Burtermarket-street on the previous eyeaing.—lnspecter. Berry said that oa his request- jug the prisoner net to obstruct the footpath she commenced ,to be very disorderly, and caused a crowd to assemble. Coe- sequently he locked her up.—Mr, Hunt (Chief-Constable) said that last year the prisoner was committed to two • months' bard labour, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months. She had behaved herself very well recently. • He was wishful that the officers should.use a little kindness and leniency towards this class of persons, for he believed that the prisoner was one if thoee who could be led by kindness and leniency rather than roughness. A young ;man with whom the prisoner bad been keeping company had been sent to gaol for 14 days for felony, and probably that S had upset her.—Captain Litton dismissed the prisoner, ex- pressing the hope that she would lead a better life. A FOL/CEIIANiw DIFFIMILTIES.—At the Warrington I Borough Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman Chandley, James Turnbell was charged with being druith whilst in charge of two horses at Latchford on the 7th inst., and also with furiously driving an entire horse.-.P.0 10 said that at about 6-30 on the evening of the date in question hswas standing on the Wilderepool crossing, when he saw the defendant passing , the Norton Arms riding a pony, and leading an entire horse! by the reins. The defendant was galloping down the road at the rate of about 14 or ld a' hoar. There were a ; good deal of people in the road at the time, and the defend- 1 ant nearly ran into a donkercart. Witness Stopped the , .defendant, and found that he could scarcely sit on his horse. When witness was asking him for his name and I 'address, the defendant put spurs into his horse and tried to I run over him. At the same time a milk cart drove up and I knicked witness down, passing over his body. Whilst on., the ground one of the horses troden his hand. Defendant drove off, and witness followed him in a milk cart, bnt, failed to overtake him—Defendant was fined 20s and costs in each case, making £3 altogether. STREET ACCIDENT : A CHILD• KILLED.—An inquest wee held at the Unicorn Inn, Warrington, on Wednesday after- noon, before Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, touching the death of a child named Ashton, the son of James Ashton, stonemason, 42, Geueral-street, which occurred on Monday morning, under the following circumstances. On the pre- vious afternoon (Sunday) the child :was on Pinner's Brcw, playing with other children, when a horse and two-wheeled trap came up the Brow, driven by James D. Morgan, baker, 41, Henrietta-street, Leigh,,andoontaining four persons, In- cluding the driver. The deceased was playing on the foot- path at the time, and attempted, to cross the road when about a dosen yards in front of the horse. The drlver pulled up as sharp as possible to endeavour to save the child, and jumped out of the trap, but he was too late, as the child was knocked down,.struok try the horse's legs, and run over. It was at once taken to the house of Dr. Adams, and afterwards to its parents, but it succumbed to the in- juries that it had received on Monday morning. From the evidence adduced it appeared that the driver, after the ac- cident occurred, expressed the greatest sorrow, and that in jumping out of the trap he hurt his foot rather severely. The deceased was two years and five months old. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," entirely ex- onerating Mr. Morgan from blame.

GOOD FRIDAY AT PICIATETR.—The Wesleyans of Penketti devot.d the day to a •tea meeting sea counter-attraction to the sports held et the Ferry, 8049 to. keep the Sunday; school scholars from taking part in. the wakes. At five o'clock there sat down about 135:persons to an excellent tea, which was under the aaperiatendence of Misses Parker,.Briscoe, A. Moses, A. Wynn, &a. after tea there was a miscellane- ous entertainment, coma:mein,' at I p.m.; whet, the follow- ing programme was gone through, Mr. R. Gareett presiding with his usital ability :—Piano solo, Miss Helen. Garnett*,; , reading, "The psalm of life," Mr„ William Moores; duet (piano), Miss Fildes (Stretford) and Miss H. Garnett,: read- ing, "Mr. Winkle," Mr. P. Johnson; piano solo, Miss Fildes ; chorus, "Sport of the flowers," ths children;. reading, "The burial of Jacob," Mr. John Mainley; verses, of Scripture, by the scholars; meg, ',Consider:, the lilies," Miss Garnett; reading, Mr. Ca E. Parker; piano solo, Miss. Helen Garnett; reading, "Overcome evil with good," Mr. J. Watson; duet and chorus, "Green hills far away," Mine Marian Ashton, and Master Joe Smith and children; ad- dress by Mr. James Dedds, on. "The progress of the Bible," Which vras heartily applauded; solo, duet, and choral, "Give me the wings of faith to. rise," Miss Margaret Boat- ledge, and Master Phillip. Hughes and children. The vari- ous parts were well ,rendered, and each was heartily ap- plauded. Mr. Hobson gave a report on the working of the Sunday school. There was a crowded attendance. Ale rsORATEFVL Flamm—A young man named John Itedfearn WAS on Menday charged at the Warrington Police Court with having stolen ata ad in silver and copper from the shop of John Davis,. 58a Winwick-street, at a quarter- past four o'clock on Saturday afternoon.--Chief Constable Hunt stated that the prosecutor was a hairdresser, and had a shop in Wine:tick-street, and the defendant was stated to be is slater's labourer,. residing at 9, Portland-street. From what he had heard, the prosecutor and, ptisoner had been companions, and 'had been a great deal in each other'S com- pany. Defendant had.besa in the habit of frequentics prose- cutor's shop. He had been out of employ a good number ct weeks, and the complainant had been very kind to him by giving him money, &c. On Saturday afterncon they left complainant's shop, in charge of a girl and went to the I,,atn's Read together, and afterwards to anotlaer heuse, where some difference arose between, them, and the prisoner was ej.cted from the house. Prisoner seemed then to have :gone straight back to the shop in Winwick-stree4 and there succeeded in,extractimg the stolen money from,the tilL— Evidence in support of this statement was given hy the coma- plainant and the little girl who had been left in charge of the shop.—The prisoner denied, having taken., the money, and to account foe is 611 that was found in his possession said a gentleman. had given him. Ss 64 for carrying a 'aox between the Central and Bank Quay Stations.—The Mayor : You don't often find gentlemen so liberal as that one do you 2—Pt:boner : Not often, alt.—The Mayor said prisoner would Imam to go to gaol for a, fortnight with, hard lobour. lie also cautioned the complainant about leaving his. shop in charge of so young a girl. DRAMATIC ENTRIITAINIVANTS AT TALE BARRACES,—OR Wednesday and Thursday evenings dramatic entertainments were given in the Theatre Royal, Orford Sarracks, by mem- bers of the sth and 40th Regimental districts. They provid an undoubted soccese, thesoom being crowded each evening with the military and their friende. The entertainm,ent was given, under the patronage of Colonel H. J. Bell and officer% and Sergeant-Major M. Cope. ably superintended the arrangements. The programme each evening commenced with an overture by the orchestra, followed by the. drama "Ban Bolt" and a miscellaneous prograherne, the farce " The Limerick boy" concluding the whale.. "Ban Bo;" was put upon the boards in e capital, manner. Colour-Sergeant Neild as Christian Comfort, "the master to kind and so true," did . justice to a difficult part; and, Colour-Sergt. Sullivan as Aeon /ronfinkthe indispensable calculating villains ful- filled his role with coolness and skill. Bon 8014 the hero of the piece, and: his sweetheart,. Alice, the heroine, were admirably impersonated by Sergeant Ccaper and Mae. Bur- gess. The minor parts, which were also very comonandably anstaieed, were undertaken by the fotlowing, Viz..—Spar- bolt, the Miller's man, Private Sutton; Cblia, A rustic, Lance-Corporal Wells; Reulen Rags, a wanderer, P.-M.-S. Collins ; Will Watch, of the Preventive Service,Dr. Sergt. 0' Brien; Mary Moonlight, servant at the school, Mrs. Price. The scenery—representing in the first act " Morn- ing," the, mill, school-house, the village church on the beach ofr "Rock Head Ferry;" and in the second" Night," dilapidated school-house ail rootless mill, the churchyard, , and "slab of granite eo grey "—was painted by . Sergeant Walk,' and did him gveat credit. The drama was followed bye selection by the orchestra;' a oomic duet, "Ihl3 bold Militiaman," by Lae-Corporal Wells and Private Delay; selection by the hand-bell ringers; duet, "Laeboard watch," Lance-Corporal Wells and Private Daley. The , farce was diverting, and was productive of much laughter. rho caste was as follows :—Paddy Miles, Private Lowry ; Dr. Coates, Colour-Sergeant Sullivan; Henry, his son, Ser, , geant-Doctor O'Brien ; Job, a gardener, Collins; Reuben, Sergeant Cooper; Mrs. Picket, Airs, Price; Jima her daughter, Mrs. Burgess,
